The company has suspended all deposits and withdrawals while it works with law enforcement to secure its infrastructure and locate stolen funds. The hack originated from a compromised laptop, it said, which allowed “an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” “The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B,” Binance said late Thursday on X. About $3 billion of crypto assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said. Binance will “cover all losses” from the hack, it said, adding, “User funds are safe.” “We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice,” it said. Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars’ worth of digital currencies on the exchange. Unlike traditional bank deposits, funds kept in accounts with companies like Binance are not automatically insured against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges. The previous record for a crypto heist was $1.5 billion that hackers from North Korea stole from Bybit in February 2025. Binance cautioned that the full value of assets affected by the hack, as well as assets recovered or frozen, could change. “This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets,” it said. Bitcoin was down about 4.3%, while Ethereum lost 4.6% of its value. Two major stablecoin issuers, Tether and Circle, said they had identified billions of dollars in assets connected to the hackers and had frozen them. The massive breach of Binance occurs at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence. In 2025, Coinbase disclosed that thieves had stolen customers’ personal information and tried to extort the company for $20 million. Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, said, “As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.” Zhao stepped down as the CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money-laundering laws.

sources.title: Binance's $6.3 billion hack: How crypto insurance works
passages: Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance in the world's biggest crypto heist, highlighting how cryptocurrency exchanges insure their digital assets against theft and cyberattacks.However, insurance protection varies widely.

Binance established the Secure Asset Fund for Users in July 2018 as an emergency reserve to protect users in extreme cases, such as security breaches or platform-level incidents.As of 2026, the SAFU fund holds crypto assets worth roughly $1 billion, entirely in bitcoin, according to Binance's website.

While cyber policies can cover both first-party losses and third-party liabilities, including forensic investigations, customer notifications and legal expenses, they generally exclude the loss or transfer of funds.As a result, standalone cyber policies typically do not cover the full value of stolen cryptocurrency unless specific digital asset coverage has been added.How do insurers assess crypto theft claims?Insurers examine how a breach occurred, which systems were compromised and whether the resulting loss falls within the policy's coverage.They may also assess whether the exchange followed the required security procedures, including controls over private keys, wallet access and transaction approvals.The distinction between an external hacker stealing credentials and an employee deliberately transferring assets can determine whether a crime or cyber insurance policy covers the loss.

Your assets are safe," Teng said on social media. Binance said it has money set aside in a Secure Asset Fund for Users to handle extreme cases, such as security breaches. Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a separate social media post Friday morning that customer withdrawals should resume within 48 hours. "We are rebuilding the withdrawal service, and we are not switching it back until it passes rigorous testing," noted Teng on Friday. "We are very hopeful that users will be able to withdraw prior to the Sunday deadline." Teng said the hack was not carried out by one person. Initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop, but further review revealed broader security breaches. "This was a complex attack," Teng said. "The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers." The attack has rattled crypto markets and related stocks. Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) tumbled 5% to hover below $77,000 on Friday. Other major crypto assets also tumbled after the hack, with ether ( ETH-USD ) dropping 4% to around $2,200. Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also plunged by more than 6%. Crypto-related stocks traded lower, led by shares of Circle, trading platforms Coinbase ( COIN ) and Robinhood ( HOOD ), and digital-asset Treasury giant Strategy ( MSTR ). Binance said that about $3 billion in assets have been "frozen on-chain so far." The frozen assets include over $2 billion in stablecoins. Tether, the world's largest stablecoin issuer, "froze more than 1.567B" of its USDT stablecoin in relation to the hack," CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X . The second-largest issuer, Circle ( CRCL ), froze another $800 million "in coordination with law enforcement," CEO Jeremy Allaire said. World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency venture co-founded by President Trump and his sons, said it froze $27 million of its stablecoin, USD1, associated with the hack, according to CEO Zack Witkoff. Although details are still emerging, the hack is shaping up to be the largest crypto theft in history, far exceeding the previous record set in February 2025, when attackers stole $1.5 billion from the crypto derivatives exchange ByBit. Blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Elliptic have linked the theft to North Korean hackers, with TRM attributing it "with high confidence" to a group known as TraderTraitor, the same group responsible for last year's Bybit hack. Elliptic estimated Friday that about 44% of the stolen assets have been frozen, with stablecoins accounting for nearly all of those funds. The hackers appear to have compromised Binance's wallet-signing infrastructure, allowing them to authorize transactions that drained billions of dollars in cryptocurrency across multiple blockchains, according to the firms. Binance, in its preliminary stage, has conducted an investigation into the hack, which suggests the incident may have begun with a compromised engineer's laptop. "That meaningfully reduces the risk of a negative feedback loop involving withdrawals, forced selling, tighter credit, and broader deleveraging," he added. Binance's initial investigation suggests hackers gained access to the firm's withdrawal systems and were able to make unauthorized transfers from the exchange's crypto wallets, according to the company . The company says it has found no evidence that the private keys controlling those wallets were leaked and is still investigating the full scope of the breach. The company says it will cover customers' losses . Binance maintains a roughly $1 billion emergency fund known as SAFU, which was created to protect customers in the event of a security breach. The company initially said SAFU and company funds would cover the losses, and has since said it has set aside more than $6.3 billion of its own funds. For crypto investors, the Binance breach highlights one of the risks of keeping assets on an exchange. While exchanges make it easier to buy, sell and store crypto, what happens after a hack can vary widely, including whether customers get their money back. Crypto exchange hacks aren't uncommon. Hackers stole roughly $1.5 billion from Dubai-based exchange Bybit in 2025, while Seychelles-registered Bitget lost more than $387 million in a hack in September 2026. But a hack doesn't necessarily mean customers will lose their money permanently. Stolen assets can sometimes be recovered or frozen — preventing the hackers from moving or cashing them out — and exchanges may also have insurance, dedicated emergency funds or other company resources available to cover losses. In Binance's case, roughly half of the affected assets have already been frozen, preventing some of the stolen crypto from being moved. Its roughly $1 billion SAFU emergency reserve provides another backstop, if needed. Customers don't always recover stolen digital assets quickly. New Zealand exchange Cryptopia was forced into liquidation months after a 2019 hack in which about NZ$30 million in crypto was stolen. The liquidation process stretched on for years, with the first distributions finally beginning in 2024 . "When you leave crypto on an exchange, you are relying on that company's controls and its balance sheet," says Martin Mulyadi, YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting and professor of accounting at Shenandoah University. "A pledge to make customers whole is only as strong as the resources behind it." When considering where to transact in and hold crypto, start by researching the exchange itself. The Securities and Exchange Commission recommends searching for customer complaints and checking how the exchange is regulated. U.S. customers can also check whether an exchange is registered with the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, using its online database . Registration can help confirm that you're dealing with an identifiable business operating within the U.S. regulatory system, though FinCEN cautions that registration isn't an endorsement of the company. Look for language explaining who owns your crypto and what the exchange can do with it. Phrases such as "you retain title" or assets being "held for your benefit" are good signs, Mulyadi says. Check whether customer assets are kept separate from the exchange's own, which can offer extra protection if the company fails. And find out whether the exchange can lend or otherwise use your crypto, which can expose your assets to additional risk. In the user agreement, check the exchange's limitation-of-liability section, Mulyadi says, and look at what insurance coverage the exchange offers and what it actually covers. "If a refund after a hack is at the exchange's discretion, it's a goodwill gesture, not a promise," Mulyadi says. Even strong language in the terms isn't a guarantee that your assets will be safe. FTX, the popular crypto exchange that collapsed in 2022, misappropriated billions of dollars in customer funds even though its terms said those assets belonged to customers, Mulyadi says. If you don't want to hold your crypto through an exchange, there's another option known as "self-custody." With self-custody, you use your own crypto wallet and control the private keys used to authorize transactions on the blockchain. Wallets typically come with a recovery phrase — essentially a master password that can be used to restore access to the wallet if you lose it. That gives you control of your crypto without relying on an exchange, but it also makes you responsible for keeping that information safe. And for anyone who's ever lost or forgotten a password, the risks of self-custody are real. With self-custody, there is "no help desk if you lose your recovery phrase," Mulyadi says. For many investors, Mulyadi says a middle ground is keeping only what they actively trade on an exchange and holding longer-term assets themselves, as long as they understand how to safely store and recover them. "Coins on an exchange are a promise from a company; coins in your own wallet are a responsibility you can't hand off," Mulyadi says. sources.title: Binance targeted in $6.3 billion crypto heist, the largest ever
passages: The digital currency exchange Binance says it was the target of a $6.3 billion crypto heist Thursday, believed to be the largest ever recorded.
The previous record for a crypto heist was $1.5 billion that hackers from North Korea stole from Bybit in February 2025.
Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars’ worth of digital currencies on the exchange.

The hack originated from a compromised laptop, it said, which allowed “an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” “The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B,” Binance said late Thursday on X.
About $3 billion of crypto assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said.

Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, said, “As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.” Zhao stepped down as the CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money-laundering laws.

Unlike traditional bank deposits, funds kept in accounts with companies like Binance are not automatically insured against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges.
Binance cautioned that the full value of assets affected by the hack, as well as assets recovered or frozen, could change.

The massive breach of Binance occurs at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence.

The company has suspended all deposits and withdrawals while it works with law enforcement to secure its infrastructure and locate stolen funds. The hack originated from a compromised laptop, it said, which allowed “an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” “The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B,” Binance said late Thursday on X. About $3 billion of crypto assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said. Binance will “cover all losses” from the hack, it said, adding, “User funds are safe.” “We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice,” it said. The previous record for a crypto heist was $1.5 billion that hackers from North Korea stole from Bybit in February 2025. Binance cautioned that the full value of assets affected by the hack, as well as assets recovered or frozen, could change. “This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets,” it said. Bitcoin was down about 4.3%, while Ethereum lost 4.6% of its value. Two major stablecoin issuers, Tether and Circle, said they had identified billions of dollars in assets connected to the hackers and had frozen them. Jeremy Allaire, CEO of stablecoin issuer Circle, said the company had also frozen hundreds of millions of dollars of assets and was coordinating with law enforcement. The massive breach of Binance occurs at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence. In 2025, Coinbase disclosed that thieves had stolen customers’ personal information and tried to extort the company for $20 million. Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, said, “As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.” Zhao stepped down as the CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money-laundering laws.

sources.title: Binance's $6.3 billion hack: How crypto insurance works
passages: Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance in the world's biggest crypto heist, highlighting how cryptocurrency exchanges insure their digital assets against theft and cyberattacks.However, insurance protection varies widely.

Binance established the Secure Asset Fund for Users in July 2018 as an emergency reserve to protect users in extreme cases, such as security breaches or platform-level incidents.As of 2026, the SAFU fund holds crypto assets worth roughly $1 billion, entirely in bitcoin, according to Binance's website.

While cyber policies can cover both first-party losses and third-party liabilities, including forensic investigations, customer notifications and legal expenses, they generally exclude the loss or transfer of funds.As a result, standalone cyber policies typically do not cover the full value of stolen cryptocurrency unless specific digital asset coverage has been added.How do insurers assess crypto theft claims?Insurers examine how a breach occurred, which systems were compromised and whether the resulting loss falls within the policy's coverage.They may also assess whether the exchange followed the required security procedures, including controls over private keys, wallet access and transaction approvals.The distinction between an external hacker stealing credentials and an employee deliberately transferring assets can determine whether a crime or cyber insurance policy covers the loss.

sources.title: Apple satellite patent takes big step toward stable communication
passages: Sun machine This kind of stable connection is of course essential to support voice calls and internet browsing, though Apple might not be thinking about a future satellite communications service in quite the same way.
voice calls Apple has big plans for satellite services, a new patent filing confirms.

Apple has built a handy little visual guide to help you point your device at the best available satellite, but connection takes time —and as the satellite drifts over head on its orbit, you might eventually find you must reconnect to another station.

Carriers, including AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, are also now working with satellite services to provide messaging and other features to devices, and Apple will not be investing billions in its satellite partner, GlobalStar, simply to be a bystander in this race.
As first spotted by Patently Apple, the new patent describes a handover procedure that means the connection a device has with one satellite will smoothly shift over to a second.
The idea is that each satellite then acts as a “transparent network relay mode,” according to the patent.
If you’ve been able to use any of the company’s satellite services, you’ll already know that it takes a while to reach a connection with your nearest satellite.
What’s new is that Apple now appears to have achieved a way that could enable that.

It is also interesting, given the quantity of data shared with mobile networks, that Apple’s filing makes particular mention of this: “It is well understood that the use of personally identifiable information should follow privacy policies and practices that are generally recognized as meeting or exceeding industry or governmental requirements for maintaining the privacy of users.
It’s the latest nugget of information to roll down Apple Confidential mountain, a plan to make it much easier for devices to maintain connectivity as they move between satellites.

Ultimately, it’s all about demand management, and satellite (particularly as 5G tech advances and 6G looms) has a part to play in the tapestry of solutions emerging to help handle the rapidly growing pressure on communications networks.

sources.title: Satlyt takes another step toward turning satellites into space data centers
passages: Naturally, Rama Afullo’s first reaction was, “Let’s GOOOO,” he said.
His company, Satlyt , is building software to turn existing satellites into data processing networks, similar to the orbital data center concept.
And he just took another step closer to that.
Afullo, who previously worked at Google and SpaceX, founded Satlyt in 2024 to turn spacecraft into virtual data centers.

Its software helps operators run AI and other applications onboard, processing data closer to where it is collected and reducing dependence on downlinks, where satellites send data back to Earth, and ground-based analysis.
Still, Satlyt which was in the top five of TechCrunch Disrupt Battlefield this year, calls this a win.
“It’s a building block toward satellites sharing computing work,” he said.

“We also need usable communication links, permission from participating operators, secure transfers, resource scheduling, and recovery when a connection of computers becomes unavailable.” Satlyt is also researching applications beyond low Earth orbit, including supporting 4K video streaming from the Moon through its NASA-funded work.
That’s what virtual AI data centers in space mean to us.”
Afullo said NASA missions face the same constraints that Satlyt hopes to address — “limited computing resources, intermittent communication, and the need to get useful information back to people.”
Its software is already on three satellites in orbit and the first step to that vision was this test.
In this test, the company created a simulated network with four computers, four users, and eight services.
The software then assessed how to assign and run tasks on those computers, accounting for compute and communication availability.

The test proved that Satlyt’s software can generate plans on hardware in orbit, but more testing will be done to see how those computers transfer information amongst each other in practice when multiple physical computers are used.
Satlyt said it still needs to test its own software under various workloads, hardware, and connectivity conditions.

They also found an issue in how their software was time-referencing delays, Afullo said — it was stamping it as arrival time (the time it arrived) rather than elapsed delay (how long it took to arrive), which is a different metric.

extraction.body: Naturally, Rama Afullo’s first reaction was, “Let’s GOOOO,” he said. His company, Satlyt , is building software to turn existing satellites into data processing networks, similar to the orbital data center concept. And he just took another step closer to that. After 13 months of work, the company had a successful test earlier this month. Working with the University of Houston on a NASA-funded research project, the test showed how the startup’s software can spread out tasks among computers while in orbit based on communication and available compute. He said the goal is to create software that connects to multiple satellites to share computing assignments. Users of the system “will only need to define permissions, priorities, and operating limits,” while the software will make decisions within those limits, Afullo told TechCrunch. Its software is already on three satellites in orbit and the first step to that vision was this test. While the test used NASA-funded research, the agency has not yet selected it for any particular mission or chosen it to deploy its technology. Afullo said NASA missions face the same constraints that Satlyt hopes to address — “limited computing resources, intermittent communication, and the need to get useful information back to people.” In this test, the company created a simulated network with four computers, four users, and eight services. The software then assessed how to assign and run tasks on those computers, accounting for compute and communication availability. One physical computer aboard a spacecraft ran the experiment, evaluating a simulated network of four computing hosts, then returned the results to Earth. The test proved that Satlyt’s software can generate plans on hardware in orbit, but more testing will be done to see how those computers transfer information amongst each other in practice when multiple physical computers are used. “The finding is a trade-off,” he said. One approach worked best, though it required more computing power than the others. Still, Satlyt which was in the top five of TechCrunch Disrupt Battlefield this year, calls this a win. “It’s a building block toward satellites sharing computing work,” he said. NASA already has a technology network designed to move data through space even when communication links face delays. It started using this tech earlier this year and has already tested it on aircraft. Afullo, who previously worked at Google and SpaceX, founded Satlyt in 2024 to turn spacecraft into virtual data centers. Its software helps operators run AI and other applications onboard, processing data closer to where it is collected and reducing dependence on downlinks, where satellites send data back to Earth, and ground-based analysis. For example, if a spacecraft sees a wildfire on Earth, such software can help it transmit relevant information much faster. “The goal is to get useful answers to people sooner and make better use of limited communication windows,” he said. “This experiment tested one planning component of that broader capability.” Satlyt said it still needs to test its own software under various workloads, hardware, and connectivity conditions. They also found an issue in how their software was time-referencing delays, Afullo said — it was stamping it as arrival time (the time it arrived) rather than elapsed delay (how long it took to arrive), which is a different metric. It doesn’t mean the experiment failed, however. “The software development, onboard execution, and return of outputs succeeded,” he said. But Afullo said much work remains. “We also need usable communication links, permission from participating operators, secure transfers, resource scheduling, and recovery when a connection of computers becomes unavailable.” Satlyt is also researching applications beyond low Earth orbit, including supporting 4K video streaming from the Moon through its NASA-funded work. “Our next technical steps are broader validation and integration, followed by demonstrations of computing work shared across separate spacecraft,” he said. “Longer term, we want developers to build applications for space without having to rebuild the infrastructure for every mission. That’s what virtual AI data centers in space mean to us.”

extraction.body: One of the biggest arguments against data centers is how much power they require -- and whether the power grid can reasonably accommodate them. Data centers are estimated to consume 4% to 5% of electricity in the U.S. today, but that's expected to increase to as much as 17% by 2030, according to data from the Electric Power Research Institute. Blue Origin and Space Exploration Technologies are among the companies that have proposed orbital data centers -- harnessing the power of solar energy to avoid tapping into Earth's resources. But it's Alphabet ( GOOG -1.45% ) ( GOOGL -1.40% ) that is taking the first concrete step by a major tech company toward that goal. On Oct. 1, the company is planning to launch an experimental satellite outfitted with Google's tensor processing units (TPUs) and solar panels. The launch, which is part of the company's Project Suncatcher, is part of the company's effort to eventually put data centers in orbit to run artificial intelligence programs. The satellite, which will be put into orbit from a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, will have the computing power of one data center server and operate on 1 kilowatt of solar power to answer simple AI queries. The satellite is expected to operate for a year. Google announced Project Suncatcher a year ago as a long-term project to determine if space could support the infrastructure to power machine learning and AI. Google scientists believe that satellites can generate eight times as much solar power as solar panels on Earth because they receive near-constant sunlight. By linking multiple satellite constellations, the company believes it can manage large AI workloads from orbit. It's a similar effort that SpaceX plans to make with its Starmind AI satellites, powered by Nvidia chips, which SpaceX believes will begin deploying in the fourth quarter of 2027. SpaceX has plans to deploy up to 1 million orbital data centers, according to CEO Elon Musk . Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has said orbital data centers are a reasonable long-term goal, although he thinks timelines of two or three years are a "little ambitious." However, his Blue Origin space company has filed plans to deploy more than 51,000 data-processing satellites in low-Earth orbit. Google's Oct. 1 launch will determine if the chips can withstand the vibration and acceleration that comes with a 10-minute rocket trip from launch to orbit. Once the satellite is in position, engineers will learn whether solar events, cosmic rays, and radiation affect the TPU's ability to function. And engineers will need to find a way to cool the chips in space before they overheat without relying on airflow. In an interview with The New York Times , Google's senior vice president for research, James Manyika, said the company is still in the early phases of its testing and research. "We don't expect, to be perfectly frank, that we'll have anything usefully operational in the next few years," he said. While Google is tempering expectations about the launch, it's clear that the ambitious space-faring project is building on Alphabet's existing AI investments -- Google Cloud, Gemini, and its TPU chips that are emerging as a viable alternative to Nvidia's GPUs. Orbital computing is a long way away, but it could eventually be a significant expansion of Google's AI infrastructure. And the company is undoubtedly taking a leading role in testing the technology. Investors shouldn't expect any near-term financial contributions from Project Suncatcher. But it is another example of Alphabet's deep pockets and willingness to compete across all facets of AI. If the company can eventually figure out how to commercialize the effort, including providing reliable hardware, connectivity, and cooling, then Project Suncatcher could be a significant long-term catalyst for Alphabet stock . passages: On October 1, 2026, a small satellite carrying four of Google’s AI chips rode a SpaceX Falcon 9 into low Earth orbit.
It is not a data center, and it is not close to being one.
Google Research announced Project Suncatcher on November 4, 2025, alongside a preprint describing a scalable system design for machine learning in space .
AI’s appetite for electricity is colliding with grid limits, land constraints, and growing public resistance to data centers.
Project Suncatcher is best understood as a bet on a constraint rather than a product launch.
Google has not put a date on it, and the company has been careful to call Suncatcher research.

The next milestone is a two-satellite optical link demonstration planned for 2027, and any gigawatt-scale orbital data center would depend on the launch costs the paper projects only for the mid-2030s.

Nicknamed MVP and about the size of a refrigerator, it was built in partnership with the Earth-imaging company Planet, flew as part of SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, and Google confirmed shortly afterwards that the satellite was operating as expected .
The research behind it is now published as a peer-reviewed paper in Joule .
At that point, the cost of launching and operating a space-based data center could become broadly comparable to the energy costs of an equivalent ground-based facility.
It is one reason the company argues compute should happen in space in the first place so that only conclusions travel down.

The same constraint sits at the center of the three real bottlenecks analysts have identified in orbital data centers : radiation, thermal management, and the economics of moving data between Earth and space.
SpaceX, meanwhile, has made space data centers a headline part of its pitch to investors since its June 2026 listing.
What success looks like for now is unglamorous: hardware that survives, links that hold, and models that run. “Some things can only be tested in space,” Beals wrote when the satellite reached orbit.

As Scientific American reported ahead of the launch , the chips run Gemini models in stretches of about 15 minutes before they must shut down and cool, a direct consequence of how badly a vacuum sheds heat.
Over the coming weeks, Google will gather in-orbit data on how its TPUs handle launch stress, radiation, and the temperature swings of space.
The roadmap after that is deliberately modest:
Google frames the project as another long-horizon moonshot, in the spirit of its quantum computing program and Waymo.

coreStoryFacts.text: Sun machine This kind of stable connection is of course essential to support voice calls and internet browsing, though Apple might not be thinking about a future satellite communications service in quite the same way.
voice calls Apple has big plans for satellite services, a new patent filing confirms.

Apple has built a handy little visual guide to help you point your device at the best available satellite, but connection takes time —and as the satellite drifts over head on its orbit, you might eventually find you must reconnect to another station.

Carriers, including AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, are also now working with satellite services to provide messaging and other features to devices, and Apple will not be investing billions in its satellite partner, GlobalStar, simply to be a bystander in this race.
As first spotted by Patently Apple, the new patent describes a handover procedure that means the connection a device has with one satellite will smoothly shift over to a second.
The idea is that each satellite then acts as a “transparent network relay mode,” according to the patent.
If you’ve been able to use any of the company’s satellite services, you’ll already know that it takes a while to reach a connection with your nearest satellite.
What’s new is that Apple now appears to have achieved a way that could enable that.

It is also interesting, given the quantity of data shared with mobile networks, that Apple’s filing makes particular mention of this: “It is well understood that the use of personally identifiable information should follow privacy policies and practices that are generally recognized as meeting or exceeding industry or governmental requirements for maintaining the privacy of users.
It’s the latest nugget of information to roll down Apple Confidential mountain, a plan to make it much easier for devices to maintain connectivity as they move between satellites.

Ultimately, it’s all about demand management, and satellite (particularly as 5G tech advances and 6G looms) has a part to play in the tapestry of solutions emerging to help handle the rapidly growing pressure on communications networks.
Naturally, Rama Afullo’s first reaction was, “Let’s GOOOO,” he said.
His company, Satlyt , is building software to turn existing satellites into data processing networks, similar to the orbital data center concept.
And he just took another step closer to that.
Afullo, who previously worked at Google and SpaceX, founded Satlyt in 2024 to turn spacecraft into virtual data centers.

Its software helps operators run AI and other applications onboard, processing data closer to where it is collected and reducing dependence on downlinks, where satellites send data back to Earth, and ground-based analysis.
Still, Satlyt which was in the top five of TechCrunch Disrupt Battlefield this year, calls this a win.
“It’s a building block toward satellites sharing computing work,” he said.

“We also need usable communication links, permission from participating operators, secure transfers, resource scheduling, and recovery when a connection of computers becomes unavailable.” Satlyt is also researching applications beyond low Earth orbit, including supporting 4K video streaming from the Moon through its NASA-funded work.
That’s what virtual AI data centers in space mean to us.”
Afullo said NASA missions face the same constraints that Satlyt hopes to address — “limited computing resources, intermittent communication, and the need to get useful information back to people.”
Its software is already on three satellites in orbit and the first step to that vision was this test.
In this test, the company created a simulated network with four computers, four users, and eight services.
The software then assessed how to assign and run tasks on those computers, accounting for compute and communication availability.

relevantPassages.text: Sun machine This kind of stable connection is of course essential to support voice calls and internet browsing, though Apple might not be thinking about a future satellite communications service in quite the same way.
voice calls Apple has big plans for satellite services, a new patent filing confirms.

Apple has built a handy little visual guide to help you point your device at the best available satellite, but connection takes time —and as the satellite drifts over head on its orbit, you might eventually find you must reconnect to another station.

Carriers, including AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, are also now working with satellite services to provide messaging and other features to devices, and Apple will not be investing billions in its satellite partner, GlobalStar, simply to be a bystander in this race.
As first spotted by Patently Apple, the new patent describes a handover procedure that means the connection a device has with one satellite will smoothly shift over to a second.
The idea is that each satellite then acts as a “transparent network relay mode,” according to the patent.
If you’ve been able to use any of the company’s satellite services, you’ll already know that it takes a while to reach a connection with your nearest satellite.
What’s new is that Apple now appears to have achieved a way that could enable that.

It is also interesting, given the quantity of data shared with mobile networks, that Apple’s filing makes particular mention of this: “It is well understood that the use of personally identifiable information should follow privacy policies and practices that are generally recognized as meeting or exceeding industry or governmental requirements for maintaining the privacy of users.
It’s the latest nugget of information to roll down Apple Confidential mountain, a plan to make it much easier for devices to maintain connectivity as they move between satellites.

Ultimately, it’s all about demand management, and satellite (particularly as 5G tech advances and 6G looms) has a part to play in the tapestry of solutions emerging to help handle the rapidly growing pressure on communications networks.

extraction.body: Naturally, Rama Afullo’s first reaction was, “Let’s GOOOO,” he said. His company, Satlyt , is building software to turn existing satellites into data processing networks, similar to the orbital data center concept. And he just took another step closer to that. After 13 months of work, the company had a successful test earlier this month. Working with the University of Houston on a NASA-funded research project, the test showed how the startup’s software can spread out tasks among computers while in orbit based on communication and available compute. He said the goal is to create software that connects to multiple satellites to share computing assignments. Users of the system “will only need to define permissions, priorities, and operating limits,” while the software will make decisions within those limits, Afullo told TechCrunch. Its software is already on three satellites in orbit and the first step to that vision was this test. While the test used NASA-funded research, the agency has not yet selected it for any particular mission or chosen it to deploy its technology. Afullo said NASA missions face the same constraints that Satlyt hopes to address — “limited computing resources, intermittent communication, and the need to get useful information back to people.” In this test, the company created a simulated network with four computers, four users, and eight services. The software then assessed how to assign and run tasks on those computers, accounting for compute and communication availability. One physical computer aboard a spacecraft ran the experiment, evaluating a simulated network of four computing hosts, then returned the results to Earth. The test proved that Satlyt’s software can generate plans on hardware in orbit, but more testing will be done to see how those computers transfer information amongst each other in practice when multiple physical computers are used. “The finding is a trade-off,” he said. One approach worked best, though it required more computing power than the others. Still, Satlyt which was in the top five of TechCrunch Disrupt Battlefield this year, calls this a win. “It’s a building block toward satellites sharing computing work,” he said. NASA already has a technology network designed to move data through space even when communication links face delays. It started using this tech earlier this year and has already tested it on aircraft. Afullo, who previously worked at Google and SpaceX, founded Satlyt in 2024 to turn spacecraft into virtual data centers. Its software helps operators run AI and other applications onboard, processing data closer to where it is collected and reducing dependence on downlinks, where satellites send data back to Earth, and ground-based analysis. For example, if a spacecraft sees a wildfire on Earth, such software can help it transmit relevant information much faster. “The goal is to get useful answers to people sooner and make better use of limited communication windows,” he said. “This experiment tested one planning component of that broader capability.” Satlyt said it still needs to test its own software under various workloads, hardware, and connectivity conditions. They also found an issue in how their software was time-referencing delays, Afullo said — it was stamping it as arrival time (the time it arrived) rather than elapsed delay (how long it took to arrive), which is a different metric. It doesn’t mean the experiment failed, however. “The software development, onboard execution, and return of outputs succeeded,” he said. But Afullo said much work remains. “We also need usable communication links, permission from participating operators, secure transfers, resource scheduling, and recovery when a connection of computers becomes unavailable.” Satlyt is also researching applications beyond low Earth orbit, including supporting 4K video streaming from the Moon through its NASA-funded work. “Our next technical steps are broader validation and integration, followed by demonstrations of computing work shared across separate spacecraft,” he said. “Longer term, we want developers to build applications for space without having to rebuild the infrastructure for every mission. That’s what virtual AI data centers in space mean to us.”

extraction.body: One of the biggest arguments against data centers is how much power they require -- and whether the power grid can reasonably accommodate them. Data centers are estimated to consume 4% to 5% of electricity in the U.S. today, but that's expected to increase to as much as 17% by 2030, according to data from the Electric Power Research Institute. Blue Origin and Space Exploration Technologies are among the companies that have proposed orbital data centers -- harnessing the power of solar energy to avoid tapping into Earth's resources. But it's Alphabet ( GOOG -1.45% ) ( GOOGL -1.40% ) that is taking the first concrete step by a major tech company toward that goal. On Oct. 1, the company is planning to launch an experimental satellite outfitted with Google's tensor processing units (TPUs) and solar panels. The launch, which is part of the company's Project Suncatcher, is part of the company's effort to eventually put data centers in orbit to run artificial intelligence programs. The satellite, which will be put into orbit from a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, will have the computing power of one data center server and operate on 1 kilowatt of solar power to answer simple AI queries. The satellite is expected to operate for a year. Google announced Project Suncatcher a year ago as a long-term project to determine if space could support the infrastructure to power machine learning and AI. Google scientists believe that satellites can generate eight times as much solar power as solar panels on Earth because they receive near-constant sunlight. By linking multiple satellite constellations, the company believes it can manage large AI workloads from orbit. It's a similar effort that SpaceX plans to make with its Starmind AI satellites, powered by Nvidia chips, which SpaceX believes will begin deploying in the fourth quarter of 2027. SpaceX has plans to deploy up to 1 million orbital data centers, according to CEO Elon Musk . Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has said orbital data centers are a reasonable long-term goal, although he thinks timelines of two or three years are a "little ambitious." However, his Blue Origin space company has filed plans to deploy more than 51,000 data-processing satellites in low-Earth orbit. Google's Oct. 1 launch will determine if the chips can withstand the vibration and acceleration that comes with a 10-minute rocket trip from launch to orbit. Once the satellite is in position, engineers will learn whether solar events, cosmic rays, and radiation affect the TPU's ability to function. And engineers will need to find a way to cool the chips in space before they overheat without relying on airflow. In an interview with The New York Times , Google's senior vice president for research, James Manyika, said the company is still in the early phases of its testing and research. "We don't expect, to be perfectly frank, that we'll have anything usefully operational in the next few years," he said. While Google is tempering expectations about the launch, it's clear that the ambitious space-faring project is building on Alphabet's existing AI investments -- Google Cloud, Gemini, and its TPU chips that are emerging as a viable alternative to Nvidia's GPUs. Orbital computing is a long way away, but it could eventually be a significant expansion of Google's AI infrastructure. And the company is undoubtedly taking a leading role in testing the technology. Investors shouldn't expect any near-term financial contributions from Project Suncatcher. But it is another example of Alphabet's deep pockets and willingness to compete across all facets of AI. If the company can eventually figure out how to commercialize the effort, including providing reliable hardware, connectivity, and cooling, then Project Suncatcher could be a significant long-term catalyst for Alphabet stock . passages: On October 1, 2026, a small satellite carrying four of Google’s AI chips rode a SpaceX Falcon 9 into low Earth orbit.
It is not a data center, and it is not close to being one.
Google Research announced Project Suncatcher on November 4, 2025, alongside a preprint describing a scalable system design for machine learning in space .
AI’s appetite for electricity is colliding with grid limits, land constraints, and growing public resistance to data centers.
Project Suncatcher is best understood as a bet on a constraint rather than a product launch.
Google has not put a date on it, and the company has been careful to call Suncatcher research.

The next milestone is a two-satellite optical link demonstration planned for 2027, and any gigawatt-scale orbital data center would depend on the launch costs the paper projects only for the mid-2030s.

Nicknamed MVP and about the size of a refrigerator, it was built in partnership with the Earth-imaging company Planet, flew as part of SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, and Google confirmed shortly afterwards that the satellite was operating as expected .
The research behind it is now published as a peer-reviewed paper in Joule .
At that point, the cost of launching and operating a space-based data center could become broadly comparable to the energy costs of an equivalent ground-based facility.
It is one reason the company argues compute should happen in space in the first place so that only conclusions travel down.

The same constraint sits at the center of the three real bottlenecks analysts have identified in orbital data centers : radiation, thermal management, and the economics of moving data between Earth and space.
SpaceX, meanwhile, has made space data centers a headline part of its pitch to investors since its June 2026 listing.
What success looks like for now is unglamorous: hardware that survives, links that hold, and models that run. “Some things can only be tested in space,” Beals wrote when the satellite reached orbit.

As Scientific American reported ahead of the launch , the chips run Gemini models in stretches of about 15 minutes before they must shut down and cool, a direct consequence of how badly a vacuum sheds heat.
Over the coming weeks, Google will gather in-orbit data on how its TPUs handle launch stress, radiation, and the temperature swings of space.
The roadmap after that is deliberately modest:
Google frames the project as another long-horizon moonshot, in the spirit of its quantum computing program and Waymo.
The flight also arrived months ahead of schedule.

Google originally planned to send two purpose-built satellites up in early 2027; instead, it fit its chips into a spacecraft Planet had already built, a shortcut that meant accepting added risk to reach orbit sooner, according to Eric Stevens, a director of systems engineering at Planet, as reported by The New York Times .
AI is already woven into orbit in quieter ways.
The Cold War version of this problem was solved by dropping film canisters out of spy satellites.

extraction.body: On October 1, 2026, a small satellite carrying four of Google’s AI chips rode a SpaceX Falcon 9 into low Earth orbit. Hours later, Google’s team confirmed contact and reported that the spacecraft was working as expected. It is not a data center, and it is not close to being one. It is the first piece of hardware for Project Suncatcher , Google’s research moonshot to run machine learning on solar-powered satellites, and it turns a long-running thought experiment about moving AI infrastructure into orbit into a mission engineers can actually measure. The timing is not accidental. AI’s appetite for electricity is colliding with grid limits, land constraints, and growing public resistance to data centers. This guide covers what Project Suncatcher is, what Google launched, the hurdles that stand between a four-chip prototype and a working orbital data center, and why getting answers back down to Earth may be the hardest problem of all. Google Research announced Project Suncatcher on November 4, 2025, alongside a preprint describing a scalable system design for machine learning in space . The concept is deceptively simple: instead of building ever larger terrestrial campuses, fly compact constellations of solar-powered satellites carrying Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), wired together with free-space optical links, the laser equivalent of a fiber connection between spacecraft. The energy argument comes first. In the right orbit, a solar panel can be up to eight times more productive than one on the ground and can generate power almost continuously, sharply reducing the battery mass a satellite has to carry. Google frames the project as another long-horizon moonshot, in the spirit of its quantum computing program and Waymo. The reference design in the paper is specific. The satellites would fly in a dawn-dusk sun-synchronous low Earth orbit, where they stay in sunlight for nearly the entire orbit. An illustrative configuration places 81 satellites in a cluster only one kilometer across at a mean altitude of about 650 kilometers, with next-nearest neighbors oscillating between roughly 100 and 200 meters apart as Earth’s gravity tugs at the formation. sources.title: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom

extraction.body: Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down. Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips. Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns. The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again. A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses. Alphabet provided the clearest example of that this week. Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027. Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google’s AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company’s money-maker. Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it. Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday. Meta is also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week. Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank . It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year. Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand. These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions. Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence. Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications. The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again.

Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it.

Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday.

Meta is also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week.

Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank .

According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year.
Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand.

Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions.

Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year and said spending should continue rising in 2027.

At the same time, Google’s AI Mode chatbot is built into Search, the company’s major advertising business. Search advertising accounts for roughly half of Alphabet’s revenue, but growth slowed to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. The company is investing heavily in AI technology that could put pressure on the search business funding that investment.

The market reaction was swift. The Nasdaq fell 2.9% on Friday. Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom fell more than 5% and Qualcomm declined 11%. Alphabet, after plunging 12% on Thursday in its worst day on record and losing $500 billion in market value, fell again.

Amazon reported negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive free cash flow of $14.8 billion in the prior year. The company expects capital spending of $220 billion this year.

Its cloud business, AWS, grew revenue 39%. Still, Amazon shares fell 7% after the company reported earnings Thursday. The contrast captures the tension facing investors: demand for cloud computing is growing, but the infrastructure needed to serve it carries a steep bill.

Meta also reported negative free cash flow, at $2.1 billion in the third quarter, as capital spending exceeded operating cash. The company is guiding for as much as $145 billion in capital spending this year. Its ad revenue grew 26%, but Meta shares still lost 10% last week.

Meta has described Muse, its new free personal AI agent, as expensive to operate. Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg said it is “very compute-intensive to run.” That makes the investment question more direct: even a popular AI feature can add substantial computing costs, while the company still depends on advertising revenue.

Microsoft was the only one of the four to report positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, recording $18.6 billion. Capital spending came to $45.2 billion, below the $50 billion the company had projected.

Microsoft said the lower figure did not reflect a deliberate retreat from AI investment. It blamed delays in capacity from third-party providers, a development that also sent shares of smaller companies renting out AI computing power lower.

The spending boom is also being financed through borrowing and securities sales, not only through profits. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence.

Demand for AI computing remains strong, and Google, Amazon and Microsoft all recorded gains in their cloud businesses. The pressure falls on whether those gains can justify the cost of meeting demand. For investors, that question now sits alongside the companies’ latest cash-flow figures and spending plans.

sources.title: Cracks emerge in AI borrowing boom as CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank debt worries grow - The Business Times
passages: The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out.
Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s.
Not every data centre developer worries bond investors equally.
The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals.
The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked.
It now costs more than US$40,000 to insure against US$1 million of SoftBank debt.
At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000.
Those questions burst into the forefront this past week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data centre company, CoreWeave.

Prices of its bonds – the company has accrued US$72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centres – crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 per cent likelihood that CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations.
Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects.
SoftBank has borrowed heavily to make one of the biggest bets – by dollar value – on OpenAI.
The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first US$500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested US$30 billion more.
That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due.
Some of the debt has traded around US$0.90 on the US dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan.
CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description.
Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts with those of the troubled office-space provider WeWork.
Oracle planned to pay back the borrowed money on the Texas facility helped by profits from the latter complex, called Project Lighthouse, which it expected to be operational by 2028.
In response to questions about SoftBank’s increasing debt, Alex Clavel, CEO of the SoftBank Vision Funds, said the amount of debt as a percentage of SoftBank Group’s assets had not changed.
TRILLIONS of dollars in borrowed money have powered the artificial intelligence boom.
First, CoreWeave buys Nvidia and other AI chips.
Then, as with WeWork, which leases space inside office buildings owned by others, CoreWeave contracts with data centre owners to use the structures for AI computing for 15 years or more.
CoreWeave then sub-leases the space to customers, including Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI, for a shorter time frame.
Several investors said they worried about whether hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future.
Alternately, they are wary of whether the data centres could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire.
Oracle faces similar permitting issues at a data centre project in New Mexico.
The project’s developer, investment firm Blue Owl, has started construction on the facility, but Oracle is struggling to get state permits to provide enough power.

The rub is that CoreWeave is on the hook for costs on both ends: It must pay to assemble and operate the facilities before any tenant is in place, and it is committed to the space for longer than its customers may stick around.

extraction.body: TRILLIONS of dollars in borrowed money have powered the artificial intelligence boom. But now there is growing uncertainty around just how easily more money can be obtained – and how much of it will be paid back. Those questions burst into the forefront this past week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data centre company, CoreWeave. Prices of its bonds – the company has accrued US$72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centres – crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 per cent likelihood that CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations. Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s. At the same time, Wall Street investors have been bidding up the price of some complicated financial instruments that insure corporate debt against default, like those insuring SoftBank, the Japanese technology colossus that has borrowed heavily to bet its future on a partnership with OpenAI. The recent market moves could spell losses for investors that own the companies’ existing bonds and could mean the companies will be forced to pay higher interest rates when they borrow again, raising the costs of their already wildly expensive AI projects. The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out. Five decades of milestones and moments that shaped Singapore’s success story - told through our headlines. The spread, or extra premium that investors demand to put their money into risky AI debt investments, has shot up more than 50 per cent over the past six months, according to Barclays, the investment bank. “The market is on a knife’s edge everywhere,” said Alexandra Coleman, founder of Azraq, a data centre risk researcher. A lot is riding on the continuation of the borrowing binge. Every week lately, economists, banks and private equity firms project higher and higher amounts of debt that they say will be needed to finance the AI systems that their boosters assert will run the world in a few years. Virtually every major mutual fund company, insurer and private equity firm has been buying up the AI debt, to say nothing of the scores of individual investors who have poured money into skyrocketing AI companies. The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals. Investors have also sold out of some these companies’ existing debt, though the drop in bond prices has been less steep than for CoreWeave. CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description. Then, as with WeWork, which leases space inside office buildings owned by others, CoreWeave contracts with data centre owners to use the structures for AI computing for 15 years or more. The rub is that CoreWeave is on the hook for costs on both ends: It must pay to assemble and operate the facilities before any tenant is in place, and it is committed to the space for longer than its customers may stick around. Several investors said they worried about whether hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future. Alternately, they are wary of whether the data centres could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire. A CoreWeave spokesperson, Lia Davis, said the company disagreed with the WeWork comparison. “The complexity of our financing reflects discipline, which is a point of pride for us,” she said in a statement. Another worry is the growing number of US data-centre projects being delayed by permitting issues or, in some cases, falling through. Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects. In 2025, the company easily borrowed US$38 billion from a group of banks to build, with the help of project developers, a pair of data centres, one in Texas and another on about 809 hectares of farmland in Port Washington, Wisconsin. Oracle planned to pay back the borrowed money on the Texas facility helped by profits from the latter complex, called Project Lighthouse, which it expected to be operational by 2028. Aterio, a data centre researcher, said it was looking less likely that Project Lighthouse’s four data centres would start operating before 2029. That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due. Some of the debt has traded around US$0.90 on the US dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan. The project’s developer, investment firm Blue Owl, has started construction on the facility, but Oracle is struggling to get state permits to provide enough power. Some of the US$18 billion in debt tied to the project has recently sold at steep discounts, roughly US$0.80 on the US dollar, according to two people familiar with the trades. The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked. It now costs more than US$40,000 to insure against US$1 million of SoftBank debt. At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000. Some investors see a potential silver lining to the troubles. John Lloyd, the global head of multisector and corporate credit at asset manager Janus Henderson, said slowing down the financing for projects “makes existing projects and existing AI infrastructure even more valuable.” NYTIMES

sources.title: AI spending is soaring, but where is the revenue? Anand Shah flags cracks in the boom
passages: Anand Shah, CIO of PMS & AIF at ICICI Prudential AMC, sees cracks emerging in the artificial intelligence investment boom as revenue generation fails to keep pace with spending on infrastructure.
He believes the sustainability of the massive investment cycle will depend on how effectively AI companies convert spending into revenue.“Today, the boom is in AI investment.

We are not seeing a big boom in terms of revenue,” Shah told CNBC-TV18 in an interview.He pointed to pressure on companies supplying AI infrastructure, including chip manufacturers and businesses benefiting from electrification, alongside revenue concerns among AI companies.

He argued that the country would continue to need foreign direct investment and foreign institutional investor flows unless exports increased significantly relative to imports.Shah also noted that the securities transaction tax had become a source of revenue for the government, while saying the future direction of equity taxation remained uncertain.“We need to be mindful that, unlike many other economies that run surpluses, exporting more than they consume or producing more than they consume, India is much more dependent on foreign flows,” he said.He added that attracting foreign investment would remain important until India built sufficient manufacturing strength to export substantially more than it does today.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

Shah expects the resulting revenue growth to create operating leverage, with additional capital expenditure and expenses remaining relatively limited compared with the opportunity.India needs foreign investment until exports strengthenOn equity taxation, Shah said India needed to remain mindful of its dependence on foreign investment flows to fund its deficit.

Shah added that rupee depreciation against the Chinese yuan had created a tailwind for Indian manufacturers competing with China, while making Chinese goods and raw materials more expensive for Indian buyers.Consumer companies face rising costs and tougher competitionIn contrast to manufacturing, Shah said consumer-facing businesses were dealing with higher input costs and intensifying competition, making it harder for companies to protect profitability.He pointed to the paint industry, where the number of major players had increased from four to seven or eight.
The transition from 4G to 5G has been slower than the earlier shift from 3G to 4G because fewer immediate use cases have developed, he said.

Shah expects the resulting revenue growth to create operating leverage, with additional capital expenditure and expenses remaining relatively limited compared with the opportunity.India needs foreign investment until exports strengthenOn equity taxation, Shah said India needed to remain mindful of its dependence on foreign investment flows to fund its deficit.

He argued that the country would continue to need foreign direct investment and foreign institutional investor flows unless exports increased significantly relative to imports.Shah also noted that the securities transaction tax had become a source of revenue for the government, while saying the future direction of equity taxation remained uncertain.“We need to be mindful that, unlike many other economies that run surpluses, exporting more than they consume or producing more than they consume, India is much more dependent on foreign flows,” he said.He added that attracting foreign investment would remain important until India built sufficient manufacturing strength to export substantially more than it does today.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

sources.title: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom

extraction.body: Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down. Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips. Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns. The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again. A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses. Alphabet provided the clearest example of that this week. Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027. Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google’s AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company’s money-maker. Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it. Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday. Meta is also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week. Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank . It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year. Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand. These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions. Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence. Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications. You can contact or verify outreach from Rebecca by emailing [email protected] or via encrypted message at rebeccabellan.491 on Signal.

It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales.
