extraction.body: Reach Africa's business leaders, investors and decision-makers. Binance was hacked with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets. Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far. The exchange pledged to cover all losses, while blockchain investigators linked the attack to North Korea and analysts assessed the potential financial risks. Bitcoin was under pressure on Friday and was trading below $78,000. Freezing cryptocurrency prevents it from being transferred, but recovering the funds requires a separate legal process, according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs and a former U.S. federal prosecutor and Treasury official. “A freeze stops the money from moving, and recovery follows through legal process,” Redbord told CNBC. Redbord said law enforcement typically obtains a court order or seizure warrant before working with stablecoin issuers to release or reissue assets and return them to their rightful owners. “Stablecoins are the most recoverable asset class in crypto because the issuer controls the token contract,” he said. “Tether and Circle can freeze, burn and reissue, which allows frozen USDT and USDC to be returned to a victim.” But recovering bitcoin and ether is more challenging because they have no issuer that can directly freeze the assets. Instead, investigators must trace funds through exchanges and other crypto services where they can potentially be intercepted, added Redbord. Eric Jardine, head of research at blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, said returning frozen assets requires coordination among law enforcement, exchanges and token issuers. “There is no standard recovery timeline. A technical freeze may happen quickly, while returning funds can take months or years,” Jardine told CNBC. Jardine added that while bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen by an issuer, they can still be traced and potentially recovered. Investigators can trace the funds on public blockchains and intervene when they reach a cooperating exchange or another centralized platform, he said. TRM Labs attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit, based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence. The FBI previously identified the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, according to the company’s insights. TRM Labs said the Binance attack shared characteristics with previous North Korea-linked incidents, including preparations made well before the theft and transaction signatures obtained in advance. The firm estimated that approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, with most transferred within about 20 minutes. TRM Labs said preparations for the attack began at least 36 hours before the theft, with the attackers using Tornado Cash, a cryptocurrency mixing service, to fund their wallets ahead of the breach. Chainalysis also pointed to North Korea, with co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin saying the firm assessed that the $6.4 billion Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, citing links to previous attacks. The attack does not currently appear to pose a significant solvency risk for Binance, according to Sean Farrell, head of digital asset strategy at Fundstrat Global Advisors. “The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance,” Farrell said. Farrell estimated that around $3.3 billion in assets remained unfrozen. Assuming frozen stablecoins are eventually returned, Binance’s SAFU emergency fund, worth approximately $1.2 billion, could cover roughly a third of the remaining losses, with the balance coming from the exchange’s own funds. Farrell said the key indicators to watch were how quickly Binance resumes withdrawals and whether outflows remain orderly. He added that a shortfall in customer assets could force the exchange to sell reserves, potentially triggering broader selling across crypto markets. “I do not think that is the setup we are dealing with, but the key tell will be how quickly withdrawals resume and whether outflows stay orderly,” Farrell said. The Binance hack underscores the need for stronger cybersecurity standards and greater coordination among governments, according to Chris Perkins, head of Franklin Crypto at Franklin Templeton. Speaking to CNBC’s “Squawk Box Asia,” Perkins said the industry must address cybersecurity challenges to reach its full potential, calling for stronger defenses and policies to hold cybercriminals accountable. “We need to make sure standards are incredibly high, but we have to really focus on the criminals,” Perkins said. Perkins called for greater international cooperation to address cybersecurity threats, pointing to regulatory coordination among G20 countries following the global financial crisis as a potential model. He also said AI could help improve cybersecurity by identifying and addressing vulnerabilities, even as the technology is used by both attackers and defenders.

extraction.body: The $6.3 billion security breach at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has renewed concerns about the safety of digital assets and the risks of keeping investments on centralised trading platforms. While the exchange has pledged to cover all losses and around $3 billion worth of assets have reportedly been frozen, the incident raises a larger question: how can crypto platforms prevent such attacks rather than simply compensate investors after a breach?Binance's preliminary investigation has pointed to a possible compromise of a developer engineer's laptop, which may have allowed an attacker to access an internal service and initiate unauthorised withdrawals. The incident highlights the risks associated with internal access to systems handling large amounts of digital assets.Vineet Budki, Partner and CEO of Sigma Capital, believes the solution lies in stronger security measures, better industry cooperation and greater investor awareness.In an interview with CNBC-TV18, Budki said cyberattacks were not new to the digital world, but the growing use of online platforms for financial transactions had increased the potential consequences of a security breach. He also emphasised that investors and exchanges need to rethink how crypto assets are stored and protected.Here is what the Binance hack tells us about the vulnerabilities of crypto platforms and the measures needed to address them.Why are crypto exchanges vulnerable to hacks?Budki believes crypto hacks are part of a wider cybersecurity problem that has affected internet platforms and financial institutions for years. Web 3 has taken this further by allowing people to transact through digital platforms.This has increased the financial stakes involved in cyberattacks."Anything that involves a transaction carries the risk of being hacked," Budki said.He pointed to incidents such as the theft of $80 million from the Bank of Bangladesh in 2016 and the Mt. Gox and WazirX hacks to underline that security breaches are not unique to any one segment of the digital economy.The Binance incident also raises questions about the security of internal systems. If an employee's compromised device can provide access to services that authorise transactions, exchanges need to ensure that such access cannot be exploited to move large amounts of assets.According to Budki, technology will continue to improve, but attackers will also find new ways to exploit vulnerabilities. This makes security an ongoing challenge for platforms handling digital transactions.What should crypto investors do to protect their assets?The Binance breach also highlights why investors should not concentrate their cryptocurrency holdings on a single exchange.Budki said risk diversification should extend beyond the choice of asset classes to include how digital assets are held. Investors should consider their overall exposure to crypto alongside investments in real estate, gold and other assets.He also advised against keeping all cryptocurrency holdings on one trading platform. Instead, investors should consider splitting their holdings between exchanges and private wallets.This brings self-custody into focus. Unlike assets held on an exchange, cryptocurrency stored in a private wallet gives investors greater control over how their holdings are accessed and transferred."Not your wallet, not your money," Budki said.His point is that investors who leave their assets on an exchange depend on the platform's security systems and controls. Even established exchanges with substantial security resources can face breaches, making it important for investors to avoid relying entirely on a single custodian.Why refunding investors is not enoughBinance has pledged to cover the losses arising from the breach. While Budki believes such a commitment can restore confidence in the founder, he does not see compensation as a long-term answer to the industry's security challenges.A founder's ability to reimburse investors can provide reassurance, particularly when the exchange has sufficient financial resources. However, returning money after a hack does not address the weaknesses that allowed the breach to happen.Budki compared this with the banking system, where the focus should be on strengthening institutions and scrutinising their processes rather than relying on refunds after a collapse.He believes the cryptocurrency industry needs similar safeguards. This could include a dedicated body to develop solutions against hacking groups such as the Lazarus Group, which has been linked to attacks on several exchanges.The objective should be to establish stronger preventive mechanisms so that exchanges are better equipped to identify threats and stop attacks before they result in substantial losses.What security measures should crypto exchanges strengthen?Budki believes exchanges need multiple layers of security, backed by independent oversight and continuous monitoring.He identified third-party security audits as an important measure and suggested that exchanges could also explore using banks as custodians to strengthen the protection of digital assets.Another critical area is the management of hot and cold wallets.Cold wallets are not connected to the internet and are therefore less exposed to online attacks. Hot wallets, by contrast, are accessible through the internet and are needed to facilitate transactions.Since exchanges need to maintain some assets in hot wallets to process withdrawals and other transactions, securing these systems is particularly important.Budki said exchanges should deploy multiple security solutions and have independent teams monitoring their systems around the clock. The speed at which funds can be moved during an attack makes the ability to detect suspicious activity and respond quickly crucial.Referring to the Binance breach, in which most of the funds were reportedly moved within about 20 minutes, he questioned whether better monitoring could have stopped the attack much earlier."Could it have been stopped in five minutes? Could it have been stopped in under one minute?" he asked.Can the crypto industry prevent stolen funds from moving?Security measures within individual exchanges are only part of the solution. Budki believes companies across the cryptocurrency ecosystem also need to work together to restrict the movement of stolen assets after a breach.He pointed to the response by Tether and Circle, which froze cryptocurrency worth hundreds of millions of dollars following the incident, as an example of what industry cooperation can achieve.Such coordination could help limit the movement of stolen funds, although the same approach is not possible with every cryptocurrency. Budki noted that freezing assets such as Bitcoin and Ethereum is not possible in the same way.He believes exchanges, stablecoin issuers and other industry participants need to work towards more effective ways of responding to attacks.Budki also suggested exploring insurance products for cryptocurrency deposits, with large providers potentially offering protection against losses arising from security breaches.For the industry, the challenge is to move beyond relying on individual exchanges to deal with attacks after they happen. Stronger internal security, faster responses and cooperation between market participants will be essential to reducing the risks faced by investors.The Binance breach may be followed by compensation for affected users, but Budki's argument is that lasting confidence in crypto platforms will depend on their ability to prevent such incidents in the first place.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

The company, which worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets, also said it will cover all customer losses.In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."Crypto industry analysts say the hack against Binance is the largest cyber heist ever.

We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice." "An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," the firm said.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.

In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world. Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as the company's CEO. Zhao posted Thursday on social media that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that, while he no longer manages Binance, "As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered." The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab. "This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet. Binance said on social media it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

The rest exceeds Binance’s insurance fund, and the man promising to make users whole isn’t supposed to be running the company. A notorious North Korean cybercrime group has stolen around $6.4 billion in cryptoassets from multiple hot wallets a belonging to Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, and still controls around $3 billion of it after stablecoin issuers and other protocols froze what they could. These estimates are still in flux as various platforms work to freeze tokens or otherwise thwart the attacker from cashing out, and as both Binance and independent security researchers continue their investigations. Unlike many supposedly “multi-billion dollar” crypto hacks, where the headline figure relies on the notional value of illiquid assets that could never be sold for anywhere near that amount, the majority of these stolen assets were major stablecoins, bitcoin, ethereum, and other fairly liquid tokens. Binance has estimated the total theft at $6.3 billion; external estimates later revised the total up to around $6.4 billion. At least $5.5 billion of these were liquid assets. Tether announced they had frozen at least $1.567 billion of the stolen USDT, and Circle has frozen around $800 million of stolen USDC. World Liberty Financial froze the $27 million in USD1 stolen by the attacker, and the Arbitrum ethereum layer-2 network froze an additional $30.5 million that had moved to its network. The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion . Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who is legally not allowed to have any active role with the company [ I98 ] yet still has remarkable amounts of inside knowledge into its inner workings, posted on Twitter less than an hour after the theft that “User funds are safe!”, adding early estimates of how much Tether and Circle had frozen. He added, “I don't manage Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.” He later tweeted “Loss might be a bit higher than [$1 billion], but will cover.” (Why a person who is barred from any control over Binance would be the one promising this is an exercise I will leave to the reader.) Binance keeps an emergency insurance fund in case of exploits or other crypto disasters. Its most recent balance report puts it at around $1.3 billion. 1 Unless more is recovered, Binance will either fail to make users whole or dip into its own balance sheet — potentially to the tune of 10 figures. Binance later wrote that their "initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop", which allowed an attacker to “submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” They estimated the total theft at around $6.3 billion, with approximately $3 billion frozen. 2 While the assets frozen by Tether and Circle will likely easily be returned to Binance, other non-centralized assets frozen by various protocols may be inaccessible both to the attacker and to Binance. Blockchain security firm TRM Labs has attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group. 3 The group has been linked to other massive cryptocurrency heists, including a massive $1.5 billion theft from the Bybit cryptocurrency exchange in 2025 [ W3IGG ]. This Binance hack has now surpassed the Bybit hack for the largest cryptocurrency theft. I’ve written more about North Korea’s crypto thefts, how they launder the funds, and what the money pays for in a follow-up. The contagion also threatens to spread beyond Binance. Aave, a defi lending project, paused some of its markets to stop the attacker from depositing stolen assets as collateral and borrowing against them — a move that could otherwise leave it holding significant bad debt. Protocols that are slower to respond may not be so lucky. The Binance theft came within hours of a separate, much smaller theft of around $2.7 million from Polymarket users [ W3IGG ], and some people wondered whether the two were connected. I doubt it. Polymarket has blamed its incident on a compromised third-party vendor, which an attacker apparently used to inject a malicious script into the site’s frontend and steal user funds. The Binance attacker got access to the exchange’s own hot wallets. They’re very different attacks, and nothing besides timing ties them together so far. North Korean hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance , the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, in a lightning-fast theft that an insider has called “the largest bank heist in human history.” Cybercriminals swiped the digital coins out of Binance wallets within a mere 20 minutes starting at 4:30 p.m. ET Thursday, exploiting the system by hacking into an engineer’s laptop, according to analytics firm TRM Labs and industry insiders. In an update Friday, Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, said the company’s security team has “uncovered additional points of breach,” suggesting it was a complex attack carried out by more than one person. The culprits targeted just a few accounts, including one crypto wallet holding nearly $800 million, Idan Ofrat, co-founder of Fireblocks, told The Post. TraderTraitor, the North Korean hacking group suspected of the crime, is known for pulling off unparalleled lootings by using algorithms to spread the riches across global crypto networks faster than any human could – making them virtually impossible to recover. US officials have said cybercrime attacks fund roughly half of North Korea’s missile program. Binance said Friday it has started to recover some of the stolen assets. About $2.8 billion was quickly frozen by stablecoin providers – but roughly $3 billion is likely gone forever, as it was unable to be frozen, according to analytics firms. The crypto exchange added that it’s on track to allow customers to make withdrawals within two days and that it has set over $6 billion of company funds aside to cover customers’ losses. It suspended withdrawals and vowed to cover all losses immediately after the attack. Meanwhile, co-CEO Changpeng Zhao tried to stop Tesla and SpaceX billionaire Elon Musk from adding to the chaos online, telling him that it’s a “bad time to troll.” Musk posted several laughing- and grimacing-face emojis on X, his social-media platform, reacting to the news. Zhao responded by reminding Musk that Binance holds a stake in his businesses worth more than $1 billion. “Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop,” Zhao wrote. “Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!” Bitcoin dropped below $80,000 for the first time in a month, ether fell to a two-month low of $2,230 and crypto-related stocks plummeted as the hack served as a stunning reminder that the crypto industry still remains a largely unregulated Wild West. “You could probably say it was the biggest hack ever in terms of monetary value,” Nic Puckrin, CEO of Coin Bureau, told The Post. Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, also called it the “largest bank heist in human history.” Binance said it is working with law enforcement, including the Secret Service; blockchain intelligence firms; token issuers; and other exchanges to trace and recover the stolen funds, promising to do everything possible to “ensure that these bad actors will be held accountable.” Crypto and law enforcement officials are now in a “cat and mouse game” against the North Korean hackers, racing to recover the stolen crypto before it’s turned into fiat currency and hidden forever, CNBC reported. Stablecoin providers – which tie digital assets to currencies like the dollar with a 1:1 ratio – could reissue the tokens, potentially recovering the losses. But the hackers have already sold the stablecoins and borrowed ether, which is more difficult to freeze, according to CNBC. The exchange is also conducting a full security review across the company, including endpoints, cloud and key management, according to Teng. The company said there is no evidence of the hacker still having direct access to funds. TRM Labs, the US-based blockchain intelligence firm that pinned the attack on TraderTraitor, described the cybercriminal group as North Korea’s elite hacking unit. “We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said, noting that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.” Chainalysis co-founder Jonathan Levin also suspected North Korean hackers, writing that they “are up to their old tricks.” A massive $1.5 billion heist targeting crypto exchange Bybit last year was also pinned on the North Korean cybercrime group, given the code name TraderTraitor by the FBI. Last month, North Korean groups were suspected in the theft of over $350 million in crypto in a hack of crypto exchange Bitget. State-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor was formed around 2016 and tasked with stealing cryptocurrency, according to the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, a group of 11 nations including the US that tracks North Korean sanctions violations. Binance maintains a $1 billion bitcoin reserve asset fund for users designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. While the loss is severe and marks a record theft for the industry, it’s still just a fraction of Binance’s total balance sheet. The exchange holds a total of $167 billion in crypto assets across its digital wallets, according to blockchain analytics firm Nansen.

Meanwhile, co-CEO Changpeng Zhao tried to stop Tesla and SpaceX billionaire Elon Musk from adding to the chaos online, telling him that it’s a “bad time to troll.”

Musk posted several laughing- and grimacing-face emojis on X, his social-media platform, reacting to the news. Zhao responded by reminding Musk that Binance holds a stake in his businesses worth more than $1 billion.

“Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop,” Zhao wrote. “Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!”

Bitcoin dropped below $80,000 for the first time in a month, ether fell to a two-month low of $2,230 and crypto-related stocks plummeted as the hack served as a stunning reminder that the crypto industry still remains a largely unregulated Wild West.
“You could probably say it was the biggest hack ever in terms of monetary value,” Nic Puckrin, CEO of Coin Bureau, told The Post.
Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, also called it the “largest bank heist in human history.”

Binance said it is working with law enforcement, including the Secret Service; blockchain intelligence firms; token issuers; and other exchanges to trace and recover the stolen funds, promising to do everything possible to “ensure that these bad actors will be held accountable.”

Crypto and law enforcement officials are now in a “cat and mouse game” against the North Korean hackers, racing to recover the stolen crypto before it’s turned into fiat currency and hidden forever, CNBC reported.

Stablecoin providers – which tie digital assets to currencies like the dollar with a 1:1 ratio – could reissue the tokens, potentially recovering the losses. But the hackers have already sold the stablecoins and borrowed ether, which is more difficult to freeze, according to CNBC.
The exchange is also conducting a full security review across the company, including endpoints, cloud and key management, according to Teng.
The company said there is no evidence of the hacker still having direct access to funds.
TRM Labs, the US-based blockchain intelligence firm that pinned the attack on TraderTraitor, described the cybercriminal group as North Korea’s elite hacking unit.
“We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said, noting that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.”
Chainalysis co-founder Jonathan Levin also suspected North Korean hackers, writing that they “are up to their old tricks.”
A massive $1.5 billion heist targeting crypto exchange Bybit last year was also pinned on the North Korean cybercrime group, given the code name TraderTraitor by the FBI.
Last month, North Korean groups were suspected in the theft of over $350 million in crypto in a hack of crypto exchange Bitget.

State-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor was formed around 2016 and tasked with stealing cryptocurrency, according to the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, a group of 11 nations including the US that tracks North Korean sanctions violations.
Binance maintains a $1 billion bitcoin reserve asset fund for users designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website.

While the loss is severe and marks a record theft for the industry, it’s still just a fraction of Binance’s total balance sheet. The exchange holds a total of $167 billion in crypto assets across its digital wallets, according to blockchain analytics firm Nansen.

coreStoryFacts.text: A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean cyber unit was likely behind an attack that stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.Binance said on Friday that deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals were suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two.

The company, which worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets, also said it will cover all customer losses.In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."Crypto industry analysts say the hack against Binance is the largest cyber heist ever.

We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice." Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.
"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," the firm said.
What is TraderTraitor?In a post on its website Thursday, tech security firm TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit.

The Justice Department alleged in 2018 that the Lazarus Group was responsible for an attack on Sony Pictures Entertainment four years earlier that leaked a massive amount of sensitive company data online.Working "around the clock" Binance said on social media that its "teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017.

A notorious North Korean cybercrime group has stolen around $6.4 billion in cryptoassets from multiple hot wallets a belonging to Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, and still controls around $3 billion of it after stablecoin issuers and other protocols froze what they could.

These estimates are still in flux as various platforms work to freeze tokens or otherwise thwart the attacker from cashing out, and as both Binance and independent security researchers continue their investigations.
This Binance hack has now surpassed the Bybit hack for the largest cryptocurrency theft.
I’ve written more about North Korea’s crypto thefts, how they launder the funds, and what the money pays for in a follow-up.

Binance later wrote that their "initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop", which allowed an attacker to “submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” They estimated the total theft at around $6.3 billion, with approximately $3 billion frozen.

2 While the assets frozen by Tether and Circle will likely easily be returned to Binance, other non-centralized assets frozen by various protocols may be inaccessible both to the attacker and to Binance.
" North Korea Steals USD 6.36 Billion From Binance in the Largest Hack in History , TRM Labs. ↩
At least $5.5 billion of these were liquid assets.
The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion .
Binance keeps an emergency insurance fund in case of exploits or other crypto disasters.
1 Unless more is recovered, Binance will either fail to make users whole or dip into its own balance sheet — potentially to the tune of 10 figures.
It is independently published by Molly White, and entirely supported by readers like you.

He later tweeted “Loss might be a bit higher than [$1 billion], but will cover.” (Why a person who is barred from any control over Binance would be the one promising this is an exercise I will leave to the reader.)

extraction.body: Stablecoin issuers froze about $2.4 billion of the roughly $6.4 billion stolen. The rest exceeds Binance’s insurance fund, and the man promising to make users whole isn’t supposed to be running the company. A notorious North Korean cybercrime group has stolen around $6.4 billion in cryptoassets from multiple hot wallets a belonging to Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, and still controls around $3 billion of it after stablecoin issuers and other protocols froze what they could. These estimates are still in flux as various platforms work to freeze tokens or otherwise thwart the attacker from cashing out, and as both Binance and independent security researchers continue their investigations. Unlike many supposedly “multi-billion dollar” crypto hacks, where the headline figure relies on the notional value of illiquid assets that could never be sold for anywhere near that amount, the majority of these stolen assets were major stablecoins, bitcoin, ethereum, and other fairly liquid tokens. Binance has estimated the total theft at $6.3 billion; external estimates later revised the total up to around $6.4 billion. At least $5.5 billion of these were liquid assets. Tether announced they had frozen at least $1.567 billion of the stolen USDT, and Circle has frozen around $800 million of stolen USDC. World Liberty Financial froze the $27 million in USD1 stolen by the attacker, and the Arbitrum ethereum layer-2 network froze an additional $30.5 million that had moved to its network. The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion . Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who is legally not allowed to have any active role with the company [ I98 ] yet still has remarkable amounts of inside knowledge into its inner workings, posted on Twitter less than an hour after the theft that “User funds are safe!”, adding early estimates of how much Tether and Circle had frozen. He added, “I don't manage Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.” He later tweeted “Loss might be a bit higher than [$1 billion], but will cover.” (Why a person who is barred from any control over Binance would be the one promising this is an exercise I will leave to the reader.) Binance keeps an emergency insurance fund in case of exploits or other crypto disasters. Its most recent balance report puts it at around $1.3 billion. 1 Unless more is recovered, Binance will either fail to make users whole or dip into its own balance sheet — potentially to the tune of 10 figures. Binance later wrote that their "initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop", which allowed an attacker to “submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” They estimated the total theft at around $6.3 billion, with approximately $3 billion frozen. 2 While the assets frozen by Tether and Circle will likely easily be returned to Binance, other non-centralized assets frozen by various protocols may be inaccessible both to the attacker and to Binance. Blockchain security firm TRM Labs has attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group. 3 The group has been linked to other massive cryptocurrency heists, including a massive $1.5 billion theft from the Bybit cryptocurrency exchange in 2025 [ W3IGG ]. This Binance hack has now surpassed the Bybit hack for the largest cryptocurrency theft. I’ve written more about North Korea’s crypto thefts, how they launder the funds, and what the money pays for in a follow-up. The contagion also threatens to spread beyond Binance. Aave, a defi lending project, paused some of its markets to stop the attacker from depositing stolen assets as collateral and borrowing against them — a move that could otherwise leave it holding significant bad debt. Protocols that are slower to respond may not be so lucky. The Binance theft came within hours of a separate, much smaller theft of around $2.7 million from Polymarket users [ W3IGG ], and some people wondered whether the two were connected. I doubt it. Polymarket has blamed its incident on a compromised third-party vendor, which an attacker apparently used to inject a malicious script into the site’s frontend and steal user funds. The Binance attacker got access to the exchange’s own hot wallets. They’re very different attacks, and nothing besides timing ties them together so far. North Korean hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance , the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, in a lightning-fast theft that an insider has called “the largest bank heist in human history.” Cybercriminals swiped the digital coins out of Binance wallets within a mere 20 minutes starting at 4:30 p.m. ET Thursday, exploiting the system by hacking into an engineer’s laptop, according to analytics firm TRM Labs and industry insiders. Binance initially said the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop. In an update Friday, Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, said the company’s security team has “uncovered additional points of breach,” suggesting it was a complex attack carried out by more than one person. The culprits targeted just a few accounts, including one crypto wallet holding nearly $800 million, Idan Ofrat, co-founder of Fireblocks, told The Post. TraderTraitor, the North Korean hacking group suspected of the crime, is known for pulling off unparalleled lootings by using algorithms to spread the riches across global crypto networks faster than any human could – making them virtually impossible to recover. US officials have said cybercrime attacks fund roughly half of North Korea’s missile program. Binance said Friday it has started to recover some of the stolen assets. About $2.8 billion was quickly frozen by stablecoin providers – but roughly $3 billion is likely gone forever, as it was unable to be frozen, according to analytics firms. The crypto exchange added that it’s on track to allow customers to make withdrawals within two days and that it has set over $6 billion of company funds aside to cover customers’ losses. It suspended withdrawals and vowed to cover all losses immediately after the attack. Meanwhile, co-CEO Changpeng Zhao tried to stop Tesla and SpaceX billionaire Elon Musk from adding to the chaos online, telling him that it’s a “bad time to troll.” Musk posted several laughing- and grimacing-face emojis on X, his social-media platform, reacting to the news. Zhao responded by reminding Musk that Binance holds a stake in his businesses worth more than $1 billion. “Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop,” Zhao wrote. “Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!” Bitcoin dropped below $80,000 for the first time in a month, ether fell to a two-month low of $2,230 and crypto-related stocks plummeted as the hack served as a stunning reminder that the crypto industry still remains a largely unregulated Wild West. “You could probably say it was the biggest hack ever in terms of monetary value,” Nic Puckrin, CEO of Coin Bureau, told The Post. Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, also called it the “largest bank heist in human history.” Binance said it is working with law enforcement, including the Secret Service; blockchain intelligence firms; token issuers; and other exchanges to trace and recover the stolen funds, promising to do everything possible to “ensure that these bad actors will be held accountable.” Crypto and law enforcement officials are now in a “cat and mouse game” against the North Korean hackers, racing to recover the stolen crypto before it’s turned into fiat currency and hidden forever, CNBC reported. Stablecoin providers – which tie digital assets to currencies like the dollar with a 1:1 ratio – could reissue the tokens, potentially recovering the losses. But the hackers have already sold the stablecoins and borrowed ether, which is more difficult to freeze, according to CNBC. The exchange is also conducting a full security review across the company, including endpoints, cloud and key management, according to Teng. The company said there is no evidence of the hacker still having direct access to funds. TRM Labs, the US-based blockchain intelligence firm that pinned the attack on TraderTraitor, described the cybercriminal group as North Korea’s elite hacking unit. “We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said, noting that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.” Chainalysis co-founder Jonathan Levin also suspected North Korean hackers, writing that they “are up to their old tricks.” A massive $1.5 billion heist targeting crypto exchange Bybit last year was also pinned on the North Korean cybercrime group, given the code name TraderTraitor by the FBI. Last month, North Korean groups were suspected in the theft of over $350 million in crypto in a hack of crypto exchange Bitget. State-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor was formed around 2016 and tasked with stealing cryptocurrency, according to the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, a group of 11 nations including the US that tracks North Korean sanctions violations. Binance maintains a $1 billion bitcoin reserve asset fund for users designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. While the loss is severe and marks a record theft for the industry, it’s still just a fraction of Binance’s total balance sheet. The exchange holds a total of $167 billion in crypto assets across its digital wallets, according to blockchain analytics firm Nansen.

extraction.body: Russia vetoed the UN Security Council resolution on Western Sahara today. The resolution received 11 votes in favor, three abstentions, and one vote against, from Russia. As a permanent member of the Security Council, Russia's vote against constituted a veto, preventing the adoption of the resolution. The Russian veto came after the United States, acting as the penholder on the Western Sahara file, circulated a comprehensive draft resolution aimed at advancing the UN-led political process and addressing several longstanding aspects of the dispute. The US proposal sought to reshape the mandate and future role of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO), including changing its name to the UN Mission in Western Sahara (MINUSO), while placing Morocco’s Autonomy Proposal at the center of negotiations. However, Russia failed to support the international community's efforts seeking to end the dispute over Western Sahara. As a permanent member, Moscow’s negative vote constituted a veto, preventing the draft resolution from being adopted. The vote undermines Washington’s latest diplomatic effort to move the dispute toward a negotiated settlement under Morocco’s autonomy proposal. The veto also comes against the backdrop of Russia’s longstanding strategic relationship with Algeria, one of its major partners in North Africa. Algiers challenges Morocco’s territorial integrity and sovereignty over its southern provinces and backs outdated narratives against the Autonomy Plan, which has been supported by over 135 countries. While Russia’s vote reflects its stated objections to the draft, its close ties with Algeria add another dimension to the diplomatic divisions surrounding the Western Sahara file. The veto does not permanently close the matter, as the United States or any other Security Council member can submit a new draft resolution. Council members may revise the text to address objections raised during negotiations, seek compromise on disputed provisions, and circulate an amended proposal for another vote. The US-drafted resolution proposed several significant changes to the UN's approach to the Western Sahara dispute, including a revision of the mandate and structure of MINURSO. One of its most notable proposals was to rename MINURSO as MINUSO, effective November 1, removing the reference to a referendum from the mission's name. The draft also proposed extending the mission's mandate until October 31 in 2027. It further requested the UN Secretary-General to submit, no later than January 30, 2027, detailed proposals concerning the mission's future structure and staffing. The draft also called for renewed negotiations involving all parties to the dispute, including Algeria, using Morocco's expanded and updated Autonomy Proposal as the basis for discussions. It took note of US President Donald Trump's call for the parties to engage without delay, using Morocco's proposal as the framework for negotiating a mutually acceptable solution. Another significant provision concerned the role of the UN Personal Envoy for Western Sahara, Staffan de Mistura. The draft requested him to consult a broad range of Sahrawi constituencies and interlocutors, including those outside the negotiating parties, in Western Sahara, the refugee camps, and the diaspora, and to reflect these consultations in the Secretary-General's reporting. This provision carries particular significance for Morocco's position that the Polisario Front is not a representative of the Sahrawi population. Rather, it recognizes the importance of hearing from different Sahrawi constituencies, including those living in Morocco's southern provinces in Western Sahara, the Tindouf camps, and abroad. The draft further called on the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) to complete the registration of the refugee population in the Tindouf camps within six months, in accordance with international law, particularly international refugee law, and UNHCR standards and practices. 80% of the population in the camps consists of Tuareg people stemming from countries across the Sahara desert, including Niger, Chad, Mali, Algeria, and Libya, according to the two former Polisario operatives. The proposal also condemned the May 5 attack against Es-Semara, which targeted civilians in southern Morocco, and deplored the failure of one party to engage substantively in negotiations facilitated under Resolution 2797 (2025). Reports said a woman was injured and taken to the hospital, with authorities reportedly denying any significant material damage. This is not an isolated incident, as the separatist group has carried out several attacks seeking to undermine Morocco’s territorial integrity and security. Under its current composition, the UN Security Council comprises 15 members, including five permanent members – China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States – and 10 non-permanent members: Bahrain, Colombia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Denmark, Greece, Latvia, Liberia, Pakistan, Panama, and Somalia.

The US proposal sought to reshape the mandate and future role of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO), including changing its name to the UN Mission in Western Sahara (MINUSO), while placing Morocco’s Autonomy Proposal at the center of negotiations.
However, Russia failed to support the international community's efforts seeking to end the dispute over Western Sahara.
As a permanent member, Moscow’s negative vote constituted a veto, preventing the draft resolution from being adopted.
The vote undermines Washington’s latest diplomatic effort to move the dispute toward a negotiated settlement under Morocco’s autonomy proposal.
The veto also comes against the backdrop of Russia’s longstanding strategic relationship with Algeria, one of its major partners in North Africa.
Algiers challenges Morocco’s territorial integrity and sovereignty over its southern provinces and backs outdated narratives against the Autonomy Plan, which has been supported by over 135 countries.
While Russia’s vote reflects its stated objections to the draft, its close ties with Algeria add another dimension to the diplomatic divisions surrounding the Western Sahara file.
The veto does not permanently close the matter, as the United States or any other Security Council member can submit a new draft resolution.
Council members may revise the text to address objections raised during negotiations, seek compromise on disputed provisions, and circulate an amended proposal for another vote.
The US-drafted resolution proposed several significant changes to the UN's approach to the Western Sahara dispute, including a revision of the mandate and structure of MINURSO.
One of its most notable proposals was to rename MINURSO as MINUSO, effective November 1, removing the reference to a referendum from the mission's name.
The draft also proposed extending the mission's mandate until October 31 in 2027.
It further requested the UN Secretary-General to submit, no later than January 30, 2027, detailed proposals concerning the mission's future structure and staffing.
The draft also called for renewed negotiations involving all parties to the dispute, including Algeria, using Morocco's expanded and updated Autonomy Proposal as the basis for discussions.
It took note of US President Donald Trump's call for the parties to engage without delay, using Morocco's proposal as the framework for negotiating a mutually acceptable solution.
Another significant provision concerned the role of the UN Personal Envoy for Western Sahara, Staffan de Mistura.

The draft requested him to consult a broad range of Sahrawi constituencies and interlocutors, including those outside the negotiating parties, in Western Sahara, the refugee camps, and the diaspora, and to reflect these consultations in the Secretary-General's reporting.
This provision carries particular significance for Morocco's position that the Polisario Front is not a representative of the Sahrawi population.
Rather, it recognizes the importance of hearing from different Sahrawi constituencies, including those living in Morocco's southern provinces in Western Sahara, the Tindouf camps, and abroad.

The draft further called on the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) to complete the registration of the refugee population in the Tindouf camps within six months, in accordance with international law, particularly international refugee law, and UNHCR standards and practices.

80% of the population in the camps consists of Tuareg people stemming from countries across the Sahara desert, including Niger, Chad, Mali, Algeria, and Libya, according to the two former Polisario operatives.

The proposal also condemned the May 5 attack against Es-Semara, which targeted civilians in southern Morocco, and deplored the failure of one party to engage substantively in negotiations facilitated under Resolution 2797 (2025).
Reports said a woman was injured and taken to the hospital, with authorities reportedly denying any significant material damage.
This is not an isolated incident, as the separatist group has carried out several attacks seeking to undermine Morocco’s territorial integrity and security.

Under its current composition, the UN Security Council comprises 15 members, including five permanent members – China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States – and 10 non-permanent members: Bahrain, Colombia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Denmark, Greece, Latvia, Liberia, Pakistan, Panama, and Somalia.

UNITED NATIONS (AP) — Russia vetoed a U.S.-drafted resolution Friday that would have supported Morocco’s demand for sovereignty over the disputed Western Sahara and ended the U.N.’s 35-year peacekeeping mission, which was charged with helping to prepare a referendum on the future of the mineral-rich territory. The U.N. Security Council then defeated a Russian-drafted resolution to extend the mandate of the peacekeeping mission for a year. The 3-1 vote with 11 abstentions meant the United States didn’t have to use its veto because the resolution failed to get the minimum nine “yes” votes in the 15-member body. The U.N. mission’s mandate will now expire on Saturday, bringing an end to its operations. Morocco annexed Western Sahara, a former Spanish colony also believed to have considerable offshore oil deposits, in 1975, sparking a conflict with the Polisario Front, which represents the indigenous Sahrawi people. The United Nations brokered a ceasefire in 1991 and established a peacekeeping mission to monitor the truce and help prepare a referendum on the territory’s future. It has never taken place because of disagreements on who is eligible to vote. Last year, the U.N. Security Council approved a resolution backing Morocco's claim to the Western Sahara, a significant shift that aligns with the Trump administration’s support for the North African country. That resolution referred to Morocco's proposal for wide-ranging autonomy for the territory as the basis for negotiations and made no mention of a referendum on self-determination. Morocco's plan to maintain sovereignty over the territory also is backed by Britain, France and others, while Russia and China have long favored holding a referendum that includes independence as an option. The U.S.-drafted resolution put to a vote Friday went much further. It would have ended the peacekeeping mission on April 30, 2027, and created a new political mission no longer preparing for a referendum. It would have affirmed “that genuine autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty is the only feasible solution to negotiate a mutually acceptable solution.” Russia's rival resolution would have simply extended the current mandate of the peacekeeping mission until Oct. 31, 2027. U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz said Russia’s veto prevents “historic steps toward finally ending a 50-year conflict." But he said the United States will continue working with U.N. special envoy Staffan de Mistura and both parties “to negotiate a lasting peace.” Morocco’s royal palace, which oversees the kingdom’s foreign policy, said, however, that the Western Sahara conflict should no longer remain on the Security Council’s agenda. “The UN political process, which has unfortunately been marked by the procrastination of the other parties, their stubbornness in creating a blockage and perpetuating the status quo, is thus suspended,” the palace said in a statement. Russia’s U.N. Ambassador Vassily Nebenzia blamed those who opposed Moscow’s resolution for the demise of the mission. He said Russia vetoed the U.S. draft because it sidelined the longstanding proposal for “a just, free and fair solution on the basis of self-determination” for the Sahrawi people. Sidi Omar, the Polisario Front's U.N. representative, thanked Russia for vetoing the U.S. resolution, saying it "would have undermined the free exercise by the Sahrawi people of their inalienable right to self-determination and independence.” "Moreover, by seeking to legitimize Morocco’s illegal and forcible occupation of Western Sahara, the resolution would not only torpedo the foundations of the U.N. peace process but would also have set a very dangerous precedent that threatens broader regional and international peace and security,” he said. As for the Polisario Front going forward, Omar told reporters, “We remain fully committed to the peace process — but a peace process put back on the right track, a peace process that will lead to enabling our people to exercise their inalienable right to self-determination and independence.” Akram Oubachir contributed to this report from Rabat, Morocco Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. extraction.body: Russia vetoed the UN Security Council resolution on Western Sahara today. The resolution received 11 votes in favor, three abstentions, and one vote against, from Russia. As a permanent member of the Security Council, Russia's vote against constituted a veto, preventing the adoption of the resolution. The Russian veto came after the United States, acting as the penholder on the Western Sahara file, circulated a comprehensive draft resolution aimed at advancing the UN-led political process and addressing several longstanding aspects of the dispute. The US proposal sought to reshape the mandate and future role of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO), including changing its name to the UN Mission in Western Sahara (MINUSO), while placing Morocco’s Autonomy Proposal at the center of negotiations. However, Russia failed to support the international community's efforts seeking to end the dispute over Western Sahara. As a permanent member, Moscow’s negative vote constituted a veto, preventing the draft resolution from being adopted. The vote undermines Washington’s latest diplomatic effort to move the dispute toward a negotiated settlement under Morocco’s autonomy proposal. The veto also comes against the backdrop of Russia’s longstanding strategic relationship with Algeria, one of its major partners in North Africa. Algiers challenges Morocco’s territorial integrity and sovereignty over its southern provinces and backs outdated narratives against the Autonomy Plan, which has been supported by over 135 countries. While Russia’s vote reflects its stated objections to the draft, its close ties with Algeria add another dimension to the diplomatic divisions surrounding the Western Sahara file. The veto does not permanently close the matter, as the United States or any other Security Council member can submit a new draft resolution. Council members may revise the text to address objections raised during negotiations, seek compromise on disputed provisions, and circulate an amended proposal for another vote. The US-drafted resolution proposed several significant changes to the UN's approach to the Western Sahara dispute, including a revision of the mandate and structure of MINURSO. One of its most notable proposals was to rename MINURSO as MINUSO, effective November 1, removing the reference to a referendum from the mission's name. The draft also proposed extending the mission's mandate until October 31 in 2027. It further requested the UN Secretary-General to submit, no later than January 30, 2027, detailed proposals concerning the mission's future structure and staffing. The draft also called for renewed negotiations involving all parties to the dispute, including Algeria, using Morocco's expanded and updated Autonomy Proposal as the basis for discussions. It took note of US President Donald Trump's call for the parties to engage without delay, using Morocco's proposal as the framework for negotiating a mutually acceptable solution. Another significant provision concerned the role of the UN Personal Envoy for Western Sahara, Staffan de Mistura. The draft requested him to consult a broad range of Sahrawi constituencies and interlocutors, including those outside the negotiating parties, in Western Sahara, the refugee camps, and the diaspora, and to reflect these consultations in the Secretary-General's reporting. This provision carries particular significance for Morocco's position that the Polisario Front is not a representative of the Sahrawi population. Rather, it recognizes the importance of hearing from different Sahrawi constituencies, including those living in Morocco's southern provinces in Western Sahara, the Tindouf camps, and abroad. The draft further called on the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) to complete the registration of the refugee population in the Tindouf camps within six months, in accordance with international law, particularly international refugee law, and UNHCR standards and practices. 80% of the population in the camps consists of Tuareg people stemming from countries across the Sahara desert, including Niger, Chad, Mali, Algeria, and Libya, according to the two former Polisario operatives. The proposal also condemned the May 5 attack against Es-Semara, which targeted civilians in southern Morocco, and deplored the failure of one party to engage substantively in negotiations facilitated under Resolution 2797 (2025). Reports said a woman was injured and taken to the hospital, with authorities reportedly denying any significant material damage. This is not an isolated incident, as the separatist group has carried out several attacks seeking to undermine Morocco’s territorial integrity and security. Under its current composition, the UN Security Council comprises 15 members, including five permanent members – China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States – and 10 non-permanent members: Bahrain, Colombia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Denmark, Greece, Latvia, Liberia, Pakistan, Panama, and Somalia.

The vetoes prevent renewal of MINURSO as expiry looms, creating uncertainty over future mission. The UN Security Council left MINURSO’s fate in limbo after Russia and the United States vetoed rival resolutions on Western Sahara, with the mission due to expire on Saturday. Russia vetoed a United States resolution that would bury the option of a self-determination referendum, and Moscow’s blockage forced the U.S. resolution to stay on the drawing board despite 13 of 15 Security Council members voting in favor and China abstaining. The United States vetoed a Russian draft that would have extended MINURSO’s mandate for another year without those changes, and unless the Security Council agrees to a last-minute extension, the mandate would expire on October 31. Oxfam warned that losing the mission could put refugees at risk, while hostilities persisting at low levels since Polisario said in November 2020 that it was resuming "armed struggle". Morocco’s royal palace welcomed the failure to renew the mission and said its personnel and equipment should leave Western Sahara in the coming days. United States Ambassador Michael Waltz said a referendum had never taken place because of longstanding disagreements over voter eligibility, and he argued that UN officials had been telling the Council this reality for 30 years. "Unfortunately, some members of this Council have used their veto to preserve the letter 'R' for referendum in the mission's name," Michael Waltz said, while the United Nations has not been preparing to hold such a vote for decades. Russia’s UN envoy Vassily Nebenzia said the Security Council cannot automatically pre-determine matters relating to sovereignty, and he said, "The Security Council must not give a blessing to such a one-sided approach." Nebenzia also called the U.S. veto "the political murder of the mission," and he said Russia was compelled to block the adoption of the draft. The Russian ambassador presented his alternative as a "technical" extension to renew the mission without changing its structure, while Mike Waltz would reject Moscow’s initiative. Atalayar said the non-renewal of MINURSO’s mandate by the UN Security Council marked a decisive milestone in managing the Western Sahara conflict, and it said the decision paved the way for a definitive closure of the Western Sahara issue within the United Nations. "The United Nations Security Council did not extend MINURSO’s mandate at its meeting today, October 30, 2026," the Royal Cabinet of the Kingdom of Morocco said, and the Mission’s presence in the southern provinces should cease in the coming days. The veto showdown threatened the future of a mission the council has routinely renewed for decades, and the unusual standoff deepened a dispute over a territory most of which is controlled by Morocco but claimed by the Algeria-backed Polisario Front. Oxfam warned that losing MINURSO’s monitoring and de-escalation functions risks undermining security and stability, with serious consequences to civilians and prospects of a peaceful resolution. Russia vetoed a United States resolution that would bury the option of a self-determination referendum, and Moscow’s blockage forced the U.S. resolution to stay on the drawing board despite 13 of 15 Security Council members voting in favor and China abstaining. The United States vetoed a Russian draft that would have extended MINURSO’s mandate for another year without those changes, and unless the Security Council agrees to a last-minute extension, the mandate would expire on October 31.

Oxfam warned that losing the mission could put refugees at risk, while hostilities persisting at low levels since Polisario said in November 2020 that it was resuming "armed struggle". Morocco’s royal palace welcomed the failure to renew the mission and said its personnel and equipment should leave Western Sahara in the coming days.

United States Ambassador Michael Waltz said a referendum had never taken place because of longstanding disagreements over voter eligibility, and he argued that UN officials had been telling the Council this reality for 30 years. "Unfortunately, some members of this Council have used their veto to preserve the letter 'R' for referendum in the mission's name," Michael Waltz said, while the United Nations has not been preparing to hold such a vote for decades. Russia’s UN envoy Vassily Nebenzia said the Security Council cannot automatically pre-determine matters relating to sovereignty, and he said, "The Security Council must not give a blessing to such a one-sided approach."

Nebenzia also called the U.S. veto "the political murder of the mission," and he said Russia was compelled to block the adoption of the draft. The Russian ambassador presented his alternative as a "technical" extension to renew the mission without changing its structure, while Mike Waltz would reject Moscow’s initiative.

Atalayar said the non-renewal of MINURSO’s mandate by the UN Security Council marked a decisive milestone in managing the Western Sahara conflict, and it said the decision paved the way for a definitive closure of the Western Sahara issue within the United Nations. "The United Nations Security Council did not extend MINURSO’s mandate at its meeting today, October 30, 2026," the Royal Cabinet of the Kingdom of Morocco said, and the Mission’s presence in the southern provinces should cease in the coming days. The veto showdown threatened the future of a mission the council has routinely renewed for decades, and the unusual standoff deepened a dispute over a territory most of which is controlled by Morocco but claimed by the Algeria-backed Polisario Front.

Oxfam warned that losing MINURSO’s monitoring and de-escalation functions risks undermining security and stability, with serious consequences to civilians and prospects of a peaceful resolution. Atalayar said the end of MINURSO’s presence implied the suspension of the political process at the UN related to the Sahara, and it said the Security Council would no longer address this issue on its agenda.

UNITED NATIONS (AP) — Russia vetoed a U.S.-drafted resolution Friday that would have supported Morocco’s demand for sovereignty over the disputed Western Sahara and ended the U.N.’s 35-year peacekeeping mission, which was charged with helping to prepare a referendum on the future of the mineral-rich territory. The U.N. Security Council then defeated a Russian-drafted resolution to extend the mandate of the peacekeeping mission for a year. The 3-1 vote with 11 abstentions meant the United States didn’t have to use its veto because the resolution failed to get the minimum nine “yes” votes in the 15-member body. The U.N. mission’s mandate will now expire on Saturday, bringing an end to its operations. Morocco annexed Western Sahara, a former Spanish colony also believed to have considerable offshore oil deposits, in 1975, sparking a conflict with the Polisario Front, which represents the indigenous Sahrawi people. The United Nations brokered a ceasefire in 1991 and established a peacekeeping mission to monitor the truce and help prepare a referendum on the territory’s future. It has never taken place because of disagreements on who is eligible to vote. Last year, the U.N. Security Council approved a resolution backing Morocco's claim to the Western Sahara, a significant shift that aligns with the Trump administration’s support for the North African country. That resolution referred to Morocco's proposal for wide-ranging autonomy for the territory as the basis for negotiations and made no mention of a referendum on self-determination. Morocco's plan to maintain sovereignty over the territory also is backed by Britain, France and others, while Russia and China have long favored holding a referendum that includes independence as an option. The U.S.-drafted resolution put to a vote Friday went much further. It would have ended the peacekeeping mission on April 30, 2027, and created a new political mission no longer preparing for a referendum. It would have affirmed “that genuine autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty is the only feasible solution to negotiate a mutually acceptable solution.” Russia's rival resolution would have simply extended the current mandate of the peacekeeping mission until Oct. 31, 2027. U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz said Russia’s veto prevents “historic steps toward finally ending a 50-year conflict." But he said the United States will continue working with U.N. special envoy Staffan de Mistura and both parties “to negotiate a lasting peace.” Morocco’s royal palace, which oversees the kingdom’s foreign policy, said, however, that the Western Sahara conflict should no longer remain on the Security Council’s agenda. “The UN political process, which has unfortunately been marked by the procrastination of the other parties, their stubbornness in creating a blockage and perpetuating the status quo, is thus suspended,” the palace said in a statement. Russia’s U.N. Ambassador Vassily Nebenzia blamed those who opposed Moscow’s resolution for the demise of the mission. He said Russia vetoed the U.S. draft because it sidelined the longstanding proposal for “a just, free and fair solution on the basis of self-determination” for the Sahrawi people. Sidi Omar, the Polisario Front's U.N. representative, thanked Russia for vetoing the U.S. resolution, saying it "would have undermined the free exercise by the Sahrawi people of their inalienable right to self-determination and independence.” "Moreover, by seeking to legitimize Morocco’s illegal and forcible occupation of Western Sahara, the resolution would not only torpedo the foundations of the U.N. peace process but would also have set a very dangerous precedent that threatens broader regional and international peace and security,” he said. As for the Polisario Front going forward, Omar told reporters, “We remain fully committed to the peace process — but a peace process put back on the right track, a peace process that will lead to enabling our people to exercise their inalienable right to self-determination and independence.” Akram Oubachir contributed to this report from Rabat, Morocco Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. Salesforce is acquiring Rune Technologies, a Washington, DC-based defense startup that builds AI tools for frontline military logistics, for $375 million in a mix of shares and cash, according to two people familiar with the deal. The purchase extends Salesforce's push into national security contracts. The company's military-facing AI enterprise software, Missionforce, has grown 80 percent year over year since its launch in 2025. Rune complements that enterprise work with tactical supply chain tools. "The acquisition of Rune Technologies reflects our long-term commitment to offer the leading commercial AI platform for national security, from the enterprise to the tactical edge," Missionforce CEO Kendall Collins said in a post on X. Rune raised $30 million from investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Point72 Ventures and IQT, formerly known as In-Q-Tel. PitchBook valued the startup at $127 million in its last funding round. David Tuttle and Peter Goldsborough founded the company in 2024. At the time, a wave of American defense tech startups was emerging. Many focused on drones, weapons or battle-focused AI. Tuttle targeted logistics. "I saw a gap in the market, in our national security, and decided to found Rune Technologies to focus that same innovation on one thing only: logistics in the military," Tuttle told Resilience Media this year. Collins echoed that view in his post, calling logistics one of the military problems "that modern technology has yet to fully address." The company built TyrOS, which collects inventory data and helps soldiers determine what they need, when they need it, and the best way to transport it. David Tuttle and Peter Goldsborough founded the company in 2024. At the time, a wave of American defense tech startups was emerging. Many focused on drones, weapons or battle-focused AI. Tuttle targeted logistics. "I saw a gap in the market, in our national security, and decided to found Rune Technologies to focus that same innovation on one thing only: logistics in the military," Tuttle told Resilience Media this year. Collins echoed that view in his post, calling logistics one of the military problems "that modern technology has yet to fully address." The company built TyrOS, which collects inventory data and helps soldiers determine what they need, when they need it, and the best way to transport it. passages: Salesforce bought Rune Technologies, an AI logistics startup for military supply chains, for $375 million in cash and stock. The deal pushes Salesforce deeper into defense contracts through its Missionforce unit, which has grown 80 percent since launching in 2025.

Salesforce is acquiring Rune Technologies, a Washington, DC-based defense startup that builds AI tools for frontline military logistics, for $375 million in a mix of shares and cash, according to two people familiar with the deal.

The purchase extends Salesforce's push into national security contracts. The company's military-facing AI enterprise software, Missionforce, has grown 80 percent year over year since its launch in 2025. Rune complements that enterprise work with tactical supply chain tools.

"The acquisition of Rune Technologies reflects our long-term commitment to offer the leading commercial AI platform for national security, from the enterprise to the tactical edge," Missionforce CEO Kendall Collins said in a post on X.
Rune raised $30 million from investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Point72 Ventures and IQT, formerly known as In-Q-Tel. PitchBook valued the startup at $127 million in its last funding round.

David Tuttle and Peter Goldsborough founded the company in 2024. At the time, a wave of American defense tech startups was emerging. Many focused on drones, weapons or battle-focused AI. Tuttle targeted logistics.

"I saw a gap in the market, in our national security, and decided to found Rune Technologies to focus that same innovation on one thing only: logistics in the military," Tuttle told Resilience Media this year.
Collins echoed that view in his post, calling logistics one of the military problems "that modern technology has yet to fully address."

The company built TyrOS, which collects inventory data and helps soldiers determine what they need, when they need it, and the best way to transport it. Rune landed a $99 million Army contract over the summer.

Salesforce secured a $5.6 billion Army contract in January. Until now, that work centered on back-office administrative record keeping and strategic planning. Rune puts Salesforce at the tactical edge, where frontline units make decisions under time and connectivity pressure, the company wrote in a blog post.
The deal benefits the Rune team. The $375 million price is nearly three times the startup's $127 million valuation.
The acquisition continues a buying spree. Salesforce bought AI marketing firm Braze for $5.99 billion last week and AI agent platform Fin for $3.6 billion over the summer.

The deal points to more consolidation in defense technology. Legacy prime contractors and well-capitalized "neo-primes" like Anduril and Helsing have deep pockets. As early-stage defense startups struggle to raise growth rounds while waiting for contracts, larger players will seek bolt-on acquisitions to strengthen their businesses.
Intel posted its worst day since the 1970s after cutting its forecast, while Amazon fell on a revenue and profit miss as investors question massive AI spending across the sector.

Atech, which Embraer controls, aims to double its operation by 2030 by expanding air traffic management and drone traffic systems abroad, CEO Rodrigo Persico said. The company is building unmanned aircraft traffic management infrastructure and has delivered systems in South Africa.

J-PAL North America launched ARTEMIS, a fully funded program that trains early-career researchers to design randomized evaluations of U.S. poverty policies. The inaugural cohort of 20 began training at MIT Endicott House in June and will receive mentorship through December.

sources.title: Salesforce pushes further into defense tech via Rune acquisition - Washington Technology
passages: By purchasing Rune, Salesforce is aiming to broaden its artificial intelligence portfolio that includes the Missionforce agentic AI offering and push further into operations at the edge like logistics and mission readiness.

“Salesforce is doubling down on national security with our most significant acquisition in this space,” Kendall Collins, president and CEO for Missionforce and government cloud, at Salesforce, said in a release.
“Missionforce is already helping defense organizations modernize operational readiness.
Rune Technologies extends that work into frontline logistics, bringing agent-powered capabilities to the tactical edge – keeping equipment, supplies, and personnel moving.”

Salesforce will look to incorporate Rune’s AI-native tools into Missionforce with the goal of greater automation of complex enterprise processes, connecting frontline and supply movement needs to workflows, and improving visibility into resources and field service activity.

Rune Technologies started in 2024 and exited stealth mode one year later via a $24 million Series C capital raise to further develop TyrOS, an operating system designed to not require constant links to external servers.
Terms of the transaction announced Thursday were not disclosed.
All parties involved expect to close the agreement in the fourth quarter of Salesforce’s current fiscal year, which ends Jan.
In its transaction announcement, Salesforce touts all six branches of the U.S. military as customers including the Army via a potential $5.6 billion contract booked in January .

Rune built TyrOS and other software products to help teams forecast supply needs, optimize resources and make decisions in environments without connectivity that are commonly called DDIL – Denied, Degraded, Intermittent or Limited.
The Army and Marine Corps use TyROS for their logistics efforts.
