sources.title: Nvidia weighs playing the cosigner for Nscale’s AI data center in West Virginia
passages: Nvidia is in talks to guarantee billions in debt financing for AI cloud provider Nscale’s planned Anthropic data center in West Virginia, The Information reported Thursday .
Anthropic has signed a $44.6 billion contract for the project’s first building alone, according to Nscale’s IPO filing .

In essence, the chipmaker would be co-signing a customer’s loans, a sign of how hard the AI industry is working to keep its buildout plans afloat as investors grow jittery about the amounts of money involved.
Anthropic’s contract with Nscale covers the first 460-megawatt building at Nscale’s West Virginia campus, which is expected to use Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips.
The companies are also discussing a second deal worth roughly $45 billion for another building.

Under what’s known as a residual value guarantee, Nvidia would step in if Nscale defaulted on construction payments, temporarily take over the facility, and help find a buyer and new tenant, according to The Information .
Nscale has struggled to get its projects off the ground.
The company had about 25,000 advanced AI chips running in August , a fraction of the nearly 500,000 it plans to deploy.
Runoff from the construction site has flooded nearby homes more than once .
In September, after months of negotiations , the project won state certification.
The stakes are high for Nscale, which is seeking to go public at a valuation of up to $35 billion despite growing concerns about its ability to deliver on ambitious data center projects.
That includes $1 billion in convertible financing committed to Nscale in September.
Anthropic, one of the largest buyers of AI computing power, has spread its infrastructure spending across multiple chipmakers.
Nvidia’s earlier support for cloud providers has mostly covered leases and chip purchases, not construction.
This month, Microsoft pulled out of a planned Nscale site in England after grid power for it was pushed into the 2030s.

sources.title: Nvidia Eyes Cosigning Nscale's West Virginia AI Data Center Loan
passages: Nvidia is weighing an unprecedented move to cosign financing for Nscale's AI data center project in West Virginia, marking a dramatic shift in how chipmakers are supporting infrastructure buildout.
What was once easy money for data center projects has dried up, leaving companies like Nscale scrambling for creative financing solutions.

extraction.body: Nvidia is weighing an unprecedented move to cosign financing for Nscale's AI data center project in West Virginia, marking a dramatic shift in how chipmakers are supporting infrastructure buildout. The potential arrangement comes as investors grow increasingly nervous about the sustainability of AI spending, threatening to choke off capital for the very data centers that house Nvidia's chips. It's a striking reversal - the company that sparked the AI gold rush now finds itself potentially backstopping the picks-and-shovels builders. Nvidia is exploring a financing arrangement that would have been unthinkable just months ago - acting as a cosigner on loans for AI data center construction. The chipmaker is in discussions to back financing for Nscale's planned facility in West Virginia, effectively putting its balance sheet behind the infrastructure buildout that's critical to its own chip sales. The timing reveals just how quickly the AI infrastructure market has shifted. After Elon Musk warned of 'guppy-level death' for smaller GPU providers, capital markets have turned skittish on AI infrastructure plays. What was once easy money for data center projects has dried up, leaving companies like Nscale scrambling for creative financing solutions. Nvidia's potential involvement goes far beyond typical vendor financing. By cosigning the loan, the company would be taking on direct credit risk for a project that exists primarily to buy and deploy its chips. It's a circular arrangement that underscores both the strategic importance of AI infrastructure and the precarious state of its financing. States across the country have been competing aggressively for AI data center projects, offering tax breaks and infrastructure support. West Virginia has positioned itself as a low-cost alternative to traditional tech hubs, with abundant land and power capacity. But even with state incentives, securing financing has become increasingly difficult as lenders question the long-term profitability of AI infrastructure. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been vocal about capital constraints throttling what he calls "neocloud" growth - the wave of specialized AI infrastructure providers that have emerged to serve enterprise customers. The company's willingness to potentially cosign loans suggests it views the capital crunch as a genuine threat to its growth trajectory. If data centers can't get built, chips don't get sold. Companies like Nvidia have long offered technical support, early access to hardware, and even equity investments in promising startups. The company recently backed Indian AI startup Simplismart as it posted explosive revenue growth. But directly cosigning debt takes that support to an entirely different level of financial commitment and risk. Industry observers see the potential Nscale deal as a canary in the coal mine for AI infrastructure financing. If Nvidia feels compelled to backstop loans, it suggests traditional lenders have serious doubts about the sector's fundamentals. The AI data center market has been built on assumptions of endless demand growth and improving economics. But with concerns mounting about AI spending sustainability and environmental impact, those assumptions are facing fresh scrutiny. The move also highlights the growing concentration of power in AI infrastructure. Nvidia already controls the vast majority of AI chip sales. By effectively financing the data centers that house those chips, the company would gain even more leverage over the entire stack. That could raise antitrust concerns, though regulators have so far taken a hands-off approach to AI infrastructure consolidation. For Nscale, landing Nvidia as a cosigner would be transformative. But it would also tie the company's fate even more closely to Nvidia's ecosystem, potentially limiting flexibility in chip selection and strategic direction. The discussions come as massive infrastructure investments continue elsewhere, with SpaceX recently closing a $40 billion debt deal for AI chip infrastructure. Smaller, specialized players like Nscale face a much tougher financing environment, even with strong growth prospects. Nvidia's consideration of cosigning Nscale's data center loan represents more than just a creative financing arrangement. It's a signal that the AI infrastructure boom has entered a new, more precarious phase where even the industry's biggest winners feel compelled to prop up the ecosystem. Whether this becomes a one-off deal or a new template for infrastructure financing will depend on how capital markets evolve in the coming months.

coreStoryFacts.text: Nvidia is in talks to guarantee billions in debt financing for AI cloud provider Nscale’s planned Anthropic data center in West Virginia, The Information reported Thursday .
Anthropic has signed a $44.6 billion contract for the project’s first building alone, according to Nscale’s IPO filing .

In essence, the chipmaker would be co-signing a customer’s loans, a sign of how hard the AI industry is working to keep its buildout plans afloat as investors grow jittery about the amounts of money involved.
Anthropic’s contract with Nscale covers the first 460-megawatt building at Nscale’s West Virginia campus, which is expected to use Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips.
The companies are also discussing a second deal worth roughly $45 billion for another building.

Under what’s known as a residual value guarantee, Nvidia would step in if Nscale defaulted on construction payments, temporarily take over the facility, and help find a buyer and new tenant, according to The Information .
Nscale has struggled to get its projects off the ground.
The company had about 25,000 advanced AI chips running in August , a fraction of the nearly 500,000 it plans to deploy.
Runoff from the construction site has flooded nearby homes more than once .
In September, after months of negotiations , the project won state certification.
The stakes are high for Nscale, which is seeking to go public at a valuation of up to $35 billion despite growing concerns about its ability to deliver on ambitious data center projects.
That includes $1 billion in convertible financing committed to Nscale in September.
Anthropic, one of the largest buyers of AI computing power, has spread its infrastructure spending across multiple chipmakers.
Nvidia’s earlier support for cloud providers has mostly covered leases and chip purchases, not construction.
This month, Microsoft pulled out of a planned Nscale site in England after grid power for it was pushed into the 2030s.

extraction.body: Nvidia is weighing an unprecedented move to cosign financing for Nscale's AI data center project in West Virginia, marking a dramatic shift in how chipmakers are supporting infrastructure buildout. The potential arrangement comes as investors grow increasingly nervous about the sustainability of AI spending, threatening to choke off capital for the very data centers that house Nvidia's chips. It's a striking reversal - the company that sparked the AI gold rush now finds itself potentially backstopping the picks-and-shovels builders. Nvidia is exploring a financing arrangement that would have been unthinkable just months ago - acting as a cosigner on loans for AI data center construction. The chipmaker is in discussions to back financing for Nscale's planned facility in West Virginia, effectively putting its balance sheet behind the infrastructure buildout that's critical to its own chip sales. The timing reveals just how quickly the AI infrastructure market has shifted. After Elon Musk warned of 'guppy-level death' for smaller GPU providers, capital markets have turned skittish on AI infrastructure plays. What was once easy money for data center projects has dried up, leaving companies like Nscale scrambling for creative financing solutions. Nvidia's potential involvement goes far beyond typical vendor financing. By cosigning the loan, the company would be taking on direct credit risk for a project that exists primarily to buy and deploy its chips. It's a circular arrangement that underscores both the strategic importance of AI infrastructure and the precarious state of its financing. States across the country have been competing aggressively for AI data center projects, offering tax breaks and infrastructure support. West Virginia has positioned itself as a low-cost alternative to traditional tech hubs, with abundant land and power capacity. But even with state incentives, securing financing has become increasingly difficult as lenders question the long-term profitability of AI infrastructure. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been vocal about capital constraints throttling what he calls "neocloud" growth - the wave of specialized AI infrastructure providers that have emerged to serve enterprise customers. The company's willingness to potentially cosign loans suggests it views the capital crunch as a genuine threat to its growth trajectory. If data centers can't get built, chips don't get sold. Companies like Nvidia have long offered technical support, early access to hardware, and even equity investments in promising startups. The company recently backed Indian AI startup Simplismart as it posted explosive revenue growth. But directly cosigning debt takes that support to an entirely different level of financial commitment and risk. Industry observers see the potential Nscale deal as a canary in the coal mine for AI infrastructure financing. If Nvidia feels compelled to backstop loans, it suggests traditional lenders have serious doubts about the sector's fundamentals. The AI data center market has been built on assumptions of endless demand growth and improving economics. But with concerns mounting about AI spending sustainability and environmental impact, those assumptions are facing fresh scrutiny. The move also highlights the growing concentration of power in AI infrastructure. Nvidia already controls the vast majority of AI chip sales. By effectively financing the data centers that house those chips, the company would gain even more leverage over the entire stack. That could raise antitrust concerns, though regulators have so far taken a hands-off approach to AI infrastructure consolidation. For Nscale, landing Nvidia as a cosigner would be transformative. But it would also tie the company's fate even more closely to Nvidia's ecosystem, potentially limiting flexibility in chip selection and strategic direction. The discussions come as massive infrastructure investments continue elsewhere, with SpaceX recently closing a $40 billion debt deal for AI chip infrastructure. Smaller, specialized players like Nscale face a much tougher financing environment, even with strong growth prospects. Nvidia's consideration of cosigning Nscale's data center loan represents more than just a creative financing arrangement. It's a signal that the AI infrastructure boom has entered a new, more precarious phase where even the industry's biggest winners feel compelled to prop up the ecosystem. Whether this becomes a one-off deal or a new template for infrastructure financing will depend on how capital markets evolve in the coming months.

extraction.body: AI infrastructure company Runware is making news again, just months after unveiling the Sonic Inference Pod, a modular data center built in a factory and shipped to customers ready to install. Now the company has bigger plans. It told TechCrunch it wants to build a factory that assembles these pods on a production line, as if they were cars. The idea isn’t entirely new. Companies like Crusoe and Schneider Electric also sell prefabricated pods, but Runware says it can ship its pods faster. Flaviu Radulescu, co-founder and CEO of Runware, told TechCrunch that the company plans to scale production at its Romania-based factory to 30 megawatts of data center capacity per day by 2028, or nearly 1 gigawatt per month. That’s a whole lot of capacity: At that pace, Runware would produce roughly as much in a year as the entire U.S. was expected to add in data center power this year, about 10 gigawatts . But it also reflects an industrywide push to deploy data centers faster and more efficiently. Nvidia announced, for example, the Vera Rubin AI factories and the DSX POD earlier this year. Both are also meant to make it faster and easier for companies to build their own AI data centers. The difference with Runware, though, is that it says it has actually built a factory rather than just designed the infrastructure that would let others build one. Radulescu said Runware will gradually increase production starting next year and that it already has two factories — one it has used for a few years to build the pods, and a second it started building earlier this year. The second is expected to be finished within months and go online early next year. Runware will manufacture the modular data centers on an assembly line. Customers can provide their own site to assemble them, or Runware can find one for them. Radulescu said Runware aims to bring the pods online within 48 hours. That time covers installation and set-up time, not build time. A pod once took three weeks to build but it will soon take one day as it ramps up production, says the company. Runware will provide spare parts if components fail. Customers can also rent compute from Runware or supply their own GPUs and pay a monthly fee for the pods and operations. Power and internet are charged separately, he said. The pods can also be customized to customer preferences, he said. The pods have a standard design, but can be configured to meet customer requirements and the latest GPU chips. Chips can take a long time to arrive after they’re ordered, which works in Runware’s favor. “Our pod delivery times are also shorter than current GPU lead times, giving us time to adapt the infrastructure to the hardware being ordered,” he said. “For new GPU generations, our in-house hardware team can design, build, and test components itself, allowing us to adapt quickly.” Right now, these are all plans — execution is the test. The factory will need a lot of people, inventory, supply-chain logistics, and money. There are cautionary tales about reinventing manufacturing, notably the electric vehicle startup Arrival, once valued at over $13 billion , which struggled to mass-produce electric vehicles cost-effectively compared with traditional plants. Runware, which has raised more than $60 million to date, said it plans to raise a Series B, but for now it is finishing and launching the factory with the $50 million Series A it raised last December. “Our cost structure is very different,” Radulescu said, explaining how Runware seeks to avoid Arrival’s fate. “We do have headcount and materials cost,” he continued. “But our factory staff is cost-effective relative to the value of deploying compute for AI.” He also said that designing its own systems and buying widely available, affordable parts helps keep costs low. “We’ve brought in a highly experienced plant manager from the automotive industry to work alongside our chief of hardware and help us get that execution right.” Sourcing components could also be a challenge. Though Runware says it designs and builds its own cooling and other pod systems with standard components, some parts, such as pumps and fans, come from Germany, and it still depends on Nvidia for networking. Still, Runware claims it has received $1 billion in committed interest for its Sonic pods since it began offering them to outside customers a month ago, “representing over 20 megawatts, which we’re now working to deliver,” Radulescu said. Data centers in the U.S. and abroad have come under fire for how much energy they consume and how that affects the grid and other resources. When pressed, Radulescu said his company’s pods only need power and an internet connection. They’ll use a closed-loop liquid cooling system with air-cooled radiators to release heat, so they don’t really need a water connection. “We’re working with power providers on a site pipeline covering 397 megawatts, with potential to expand to 1.2 gigawatts,” he said, referring to its list of planned sites and adding that the company is deploying its modular data centers on sites that are much smaller than those used by hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google. The sites, he continued, typically already have power, so they shouldn’t further strain the grid or disrupt the community. The pods also run “completely silent up to temperatures of 86 degrees Fahrenheit. We use energy from renewable sources whenever possible,” he continued. “We are actively working on expanding our network of energy providers and sites. We’re aiming to have renewables as our main energy source.” Runware will bring its new factory online early next year, then expand to the U.S. and other regions worldwide. Modular systems are the future and will soon become “the standard for large AI deployment,” Radulescu said. “Customers should be able to plan a hyperscale data center around factory-built pods from the beginning and have it working in months instead of years,” he added. A pod once took three weeks to build but it will soon take one day as it ramps up production, says the company. Runware will provide spare parts if components fail. Customers can also rent compute from Runware or supply their own GPUs and pay a monthly fee for the pods and operations. Power and internet are charged separately, he said.

The pods can also be customized to customer preferences, he said. The pods have a standard design, but can be configured to meet customer requirements and the latest GPU chips. Chips can take a long time to arrive after they're ordered, which works in Runware's favor. "Our pod delivery times are also shorter than current GPU lead times, giving us time to adapt the infrastructure to the hardware being ordered," he said. "For new GPU generations, our in-house hardware team can design, build, and test components itself, allowing us to adapt quickly."

Right now, these are all plans — execution is the test. The factory will need a lot of people, inventory, supply-chain logistics, and money. There are cautionary tales about reinventing manufacturing, notably the electric vehicle startup Arrival, once valued at over $13 billion , which struggled to mass-produce electric vehicles cost-effectively compared with traditional plants. Runware, which has raised more than $60 million to date, said it plans to raise a Series B, but for now it is finishing and launching the factory with the $50 million Series A it raised last December.

"Our cost structure is very different," Radulescu said, explaining how Runware seeks to avoid Arrival's fate. "We do have headcount and materials cost," he continued. "But our factory staff is cost-effective relative to the value of deploying compute for AI." He also said that designing its own systems and buying widely available, affordable parts helps keep costs low. "We've brought in a highly experienced plant manager from the automotive industry to work alongside our chief of hardware and help us get that execution right."

Sourcing components could also be a challenge. Though Runware says it designs and builds its own cooling and other pod systems with standard components, some parts, such as pumps and fans, come from Germany, and it still depends on Nvidia for networking. Still, Runware claims it has received $1 billion in committed interest for its Sonic pods since it began offering them to outside customers a month ago, "representing over 20 megawatts, which we're now working to deliver," Radulescu said.

Data centers in the U.S. and abroad have come under fire for how much energy they consume and how that affects the grid and other resources. When pressed, Radulescu said his company's pods only need power and an internet connection. They'll use a closed-loop liquid cooling system with air-cooled radiators to release heat, so they don't really need a water connection. "We're working with power providers on a site pipeline covering 397 megawatts, with potential to expand to 1.2 gigawatts," he said, referring to its list of planned sites and adding that the company is deploying its modular data centers on sites that are much smaller than those used by hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google.

The sites, he continued, typically already have power, so they shouldn't further strain the grid or disrupt the community. The pods also run "completely silent up to temperatures of 86 degrees Fahrenheit. We use energy from renewable sources whenever possible," he continued. "We are actively working on expanding our network of energy providers and sites. We're aiming to have renewables as our main energy source."

Runware will bring its new factory online early next year, then expand to the U.S. and other regions worldwide. Modular systems are the future and will soon become "the standard for large AI deployment," Radulescu said.
"Customers should be able to plan a hyperscale data center around factory-built pods from the beginning and have it working in months instead of years," he added.

That's a whole lot of capacity: At that pace, Runware would produce roughly as much in a year as the entire U.S. was expected to add in data center power this year, about 10 gigawatts . But it also reflects an industrywide push to deploy data centers faster and more efficiently.

Nvidia announced, for example, the Vera Rubin AI factories and the DSX POD earlier this year. Both are also meant to make it faster and easier for companies to build their own AI data centers. The difference with Runware, though, is that it says it has actually built a factory rather than just designed the infrastructure that would let others build one.

Radulescu said Runware will gradually increase production starting next year and that it already has two factories — one it has used for a few years to build the pods, and a second it started building earlier this year. The second is expected to be finished within months and go online early next year.

Runware will manufacture the modular data centers on an assembly line. Customers can provide their own site to assemble them, or Runware can find one for them. Radulescu said Runware aims to bring the pods online within 48 hours. That time covers installation and set-up time, not build time. A pod once took three weeks to build but it will soon take one day as it ramps up production, says the company. Runware will provide spare parts if components fail. Customers can also rent compute from Runware or supply their own GPUs and pay a monthly fee for the pods and operations. Power and internet are charged separately, he said.

The pods can also be customized to customer preferences, he said. The pods have a standard design, but can be configured to meet customer requirements and the latest GPU chips. Chips can take a long time to arrive after they're ordered, which works in Runware's favor. "Our pod delivery times are also shorter than current GPU lead times, giving us time to adapt the infrastructure to the hardware being ordered," he said. "For new GPU generations, our in-house hardware team can design, build, and test components itself, allowing us to adapt quickly."

Right now, these are all plans — execution is the test. The factory will need a lot of people, inventory, supply-chain logistics, and money. There are cautionary tales about reinventing manufacturing, notably the electric vehicle startup Arrival, once valued at over $13 billion , which struggled to mass-produce electric vehicles cost-effectively compared with traditional plants. Runware, which has raised more than $60 million to date, said it plans to raise a Series B, but for now it is finishing and launching the factory with the $50 million Series A it raised last December.

"Our cost structure is very different," Radulescu said, explaining how Runware seeks to avoid Arrival's fate. "We do have headcount and materials cost," he continued. "But our factory staff is cost-effective relative to the value of deploying compute for AI." He also said that designing its own systems and buying widely available, affordable parts helps keep costs low. "We've brought in a highly experienced plant manager from the automotive industry to work alongside our chief of hardware and help us get that execution right."

Sourcing components could also be a challenge. Though Runware says it designs and builds its own cooling and other pod systems with standard components, some parts, such as pumps and fans, come from Germany, and it still depends on Nvidia for networking. Still, Runware claims it has received $1 billion in committed interest for its Sonic pods since it began offering them to outside customers a month ago, "representing over 20 megawatts, which we're now working to deliver," Radulescu said.

Data centers in the U.S. and abroad have come under fire for how much energy they consume and how that affects the grid and other resources. When pressed, Radulescu said his company's pods only need power and an internet connection. They'll use a closed-loop liquid cooling system with air-cooled radiators to release heat, so they don't really need a water connection. "We're working with power providers on a site pipeline covering 397 megawatts, with potential to expand to 1.2 gigawatts," he said, referring to its list of planned sites and adding that the company is deploying its modular data centers on sites that are much smaller than those used by hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google.

The sites, he continued, typically already have power, so they shouldn't further strain the grid or disrupt the community. The pods also run "completely silent up to temperatures of 86 degrees Fahrenheit. We use energy from renewable sources whenever possible," he continued. "We are actively working on expanding our network of energy providers and sites. We're aiming to have renewables as our main energy source."

Runware will bring its new factory online early next year, then expand to the U.S. and other regions worldwide. Modular systems are the future and will soon become "the standard for large AI deployment," Radulescu said.
"Customers should be able to plan a hyperscale data center around factory-built pods from the beginning and have it working in months instead of years," he added.

extraction.body: Nat Curi was 20 when she first joined BFF, a version of Bumble’s dating site tailored to making friends. Pandemic-era restrictions had been lifted in Curi’s college town, but her friends were still scattered at their homes across the country. Curi, who grew up in Connecticut and attended Southern Connecticut State University, was looking for friends nearby. Curi attached a photo of herself dancing at a party. If she could have dinner with any celebrity, she wrote, it’d be Jesus. “Not in a religious way, in a nosy as f—- way,” she added in parentheses. Swiping through profiles was awkward. Some users had a different definition of friendship than Curi; she rejected those “looking for a third,” for instance. But she soon came across a profile brimming with photos of fashionable outfits, pets and travel. Curi matched with the platonic prospect, who had another match in common with her. The three formed an Instagram group chat, eventually adding a couple more women from BFF. When it came to meeting the women in person, Curi donned a pink tube top, gold jewelry, light-wash jeans and platform heels. She wondered about her hair. The women all seemed pretty girly in their profiles. Would her pink hair come across as too edgy? Curi arrived at a dive bar in Fairfield, Connecticut, jittery with nerves. “It was like your first day of college,” Curi recalls. “You’re just asking each other about your interests, why you joined BFF.” All five had the same answer - they joined because they wanted to make friends. Friend-making apps are increasingly popular. The number of people who use BFF at least once a week has grown by 80 percent year over year, according to a Bumble spokesperson. Advertisements for the app are plastered over subway stations and posted on social media feeds. BFF, which launched in 2016, is now one of many apps promising platonic matches: Timeleft, 222 and Sonder all launched in the past three years. That growth coincides with the so-called “loneliness epidemic”: The number of Americans with no close friends quadrupled from 1990 to 2021. Men have been hit hardest; 1 in 5 single men report having no close friends at all. Danny Metz, a 28-year-old who works in insurance, tried BFF out. He swiped right on guys who seemed cool and better-looking than him. But the idea of meeting up with a match felt weird. Metz deleted the app. “I’m too used to this behavior for dating girls,” he says. “I’ve only ever organically made a friend.” But that’s not so easy. As far back as 2000, Robert Putnam argued that technological isolation, urban sprawl and the disintegration of civic organizations had eroded social capital in his book, “Bowling Alone.” The settings for making friends have only grown fewer in the years since. Even in the settings that do remain, casual conversation has disappeared, says historian Sarah Gold McBride. Gold McBride, who teaches a class on friendship at the University of California at Berkeley, noticed her students would look at their phones before lectures began. “It created a bubble with themselves and their technology. They’re not having those spontaneous ‘I like your jacket’ or ‘What book are you reading?’ conversations that can spark friendship in real life,” she explains. Students told her they worried about surveillance. “Students felt nervous interacting with a stranger. If they were filmed, they could be made viral against their will, memed or put on TikTok,” Gold McBride says. “Low-stakes interactions with people can be the beginnings of new friendships. But students are fearful of it, worried they might be put on the internet.” Sara Rollens, 32, had tried to make friends in real life. On the way to a book signing, she recalled thinking, “I’m gonna go. I’m gonna meet friends.” But when she arrived, she found the other attendees to be shy. “You’ll walk up to people to say hi, and they get really freaked out,” Rollens says. “People have a hard time conversing in real life.” She turned to a friendship app but discovered they had many of the same pitfalls associated with online dating: She has deleted and redownloaded BFF over the course of four years. She’s rejected men who hoped the friend dates would turn romantic and women who hoped Rollens would join their multilevel marketing ventures. She’s been platonically love-bombed by matches. She was even ghosted by one person after three dates. Rollens has made a few acquaintances but no deep friendships. She stays on the app, she says, “just in case” it can work. Eric Balki, who researches dating app algorithms at the Faculty of Health and Medicine at Lancaster University in England, says that much like dating apps, friendship apps “are designed to keep you on there. The business model is misaligned to the demand.” If matches were optimal, he notes, users would leave the app. “It ends up making you more lonely and defeated,” he says. He compared algorithmic matching to slot machines. Every once in a while, there is a random small reward, which maintains a user’s expectation for a larger reward to come. And some users do achieve that larger reward. They find a best friend forever. The news spreads - the bell ringing is loud. Slot machines can pay out, so users return. “That one I was really nervous for,” she says. The group didn’t have one another’s names, much less contact information, and couldn’t communicate ahead of time. Curi’s hair was back to its natural brunette. She wore a pencil skirt as a tube top and paired it with baggy jeans and sandals. She didn’t click with the women at her table. “I didn’t feel like anyone was a great match or a good friendship,” Curi says. “They had a lot of questions about [my] queerness and coming out, and then they asked me about my tattoos. Nobody had tattoos. Nobody had talked to a gay person.” She overheard the table beside her, a group also formed by Timeleft. That table’s guests were closer to her own age. They talked about shows and bars Curi liked. “They were having so much fun, and I was like, ‘Damn, I wish I could meet them,’” she says. Then serendipity struck for Curi. The app sent an address of a karaoke bar for an optional, after-dinner cocktail hour. All the Timeleft tables were invited. Once she arrived at the bar, Curi jumped ship and made friends with the users she’d been eyeing at dinner. A year and a half later, they play trivia, celebrate birthdays, try new restaurants and watch “Love Island” together. She’s still friends with all of them, and they hang out at least once a week. BFF, which launched in 2016, is now one of many apps promising platonic matches: Timeleft, 222 and Sonder all launched in the past three years. That growth coincides with the so-called “loneliness epidemic”: The number of Americans with no close friends quadrupled from 1990 to 2021. Men have been hit hardest; 1 in 5 single men report having no close friends at all. Danny Metz, a 28-year-old who works in insurance, tried BFF out. He swiped right on guys who seemed cool and better-looking than him. But the idea of meeting up with a match felt weird. Metz deleted the app. “I’m too used to this behavior for dating girls,” he says. “I’ve only ever organically made a friend.” But that’s not so easy. As far back as 2000, Robert Putnam argued that technological isolation, urban sprawl and the disintegration of civic organizations had eroded social capital in his book, “Bowling Alone.” The settings for making friends have only grown fewer in the years since. Even in the settings that do remain, casual conversation has disappeared, says historian Sarah Gold McBride. Gold McBride, who teaches a class on friendship at the University of California at Berkeley, noticed her students would look at their phones before lectures began. “It created a bubble with themselves and their technology. They’re not having those spontaneous ‘I like your jacket’ or ‘What book are you reading?’ conversations that can spark friendship in real life,” she explains. Students told her they worried about surveillance. “Students felt nervous interacting with a stranger. If they were filmed, they could be made viral against their will, memed or put on TikTok,” Gold McBride says. “Low-stakes interactions with people can be the beginnings of new friendships. But students are fearful of it, worried they might be put on the internet.” Sara Rollens, 32, had tried to make friends in real life. On the way to a book signing, she recalled thinking, “I’m gonna go. I’m gonna meet friends.” But when she arrived, she found the other attendees to be shy. “You’ll walk up to people to say hi, and they get really freaked out,” Rollens says. “People have a hard time conversing in real life.” She turned to a friendship app but discovered they had many of the same pitfalls associated with online dating: She has deleted and redownloaded BFF over the course of four years. She’s rejected men who hoped the friend dates would turn romantic and women who hoped Rollens would join their multilevel marketing ventures. She’s been platonically love-bombed by matches. She was even ghosted by one person after three dates. Rollens has made a few acquaintances but no deep friendships. She stays on the app, she says, “just in case” it can work. The business model is misaligned to the demand.” If matches were optimal, he notes, users would leave the app. “It ends up making you more lonely and defeated,” he says. He compared algorithmic matching to slot machines. Every once in a while, there is a random small reward, which maintains a user’s expectation for a larger reward to come. And some users do achieve that larger reward. They find a best friend forever. The news spreads - the bell ringing is loud. Slot machines can pay out, so users return. “That one I was really nervous for,” she says. The group didn’t have one another’s names, much less contact information, and couldn’t communicate ahead of time. Curi’s hair was back to its natural brunette. She wore a pencil skirt as a tube top and paired it with baggy jeans and sandals. She didn’t click with the women at her table. “I didn’t feel like anyone was a great match or a good friendship,” Curi says. “They had a lot of questions about [my] queerness and coming out, and then they asked me about my tattoos. Nobody had tattoos. Nobody had talked to a gay person.” She overheard the table beside her, a group also formed by Timeleft. That table’s guests were closer to her own age. They talked about shows and bars Curi liked. “They were having so much fun, and I was like, ‘Damn, I wish I could meet them,’” she says. Then serendipity struck for Curi. The app sent an address of a karaoke bar for an optional, after-dinner cocktail hour. All the Timeleft tables were invited. Once she arrived at the bar, Curi jumped ship and made friends with the users she’d been eyeing at dinner. A year and a half later, they play trivia, celebrate birthdays, try new restaurants and watch “Love Island” together. She’s still friends with all of them, and they hang out at least once a week. passages: Quanda Grant, of West Philadelphia, was outside City Hall on her way to drop off her mail-in ballot.
She said she has concerns about Election Day but believes voter apathy poses a threat as well.
"Our main role on Election Day is to make sure everyone gets a chance to vote.
We are not looking to do anything other than make things run smooth," Assistant District Attorney Brian Collins said.
The Department of Justice also plans to send federal election monitors to Philadelphia.
The Philadelphia District Attorney's Office announced that its Election Task Force will be mobilized Tuesday, an effort officials have been planning since the summer.

She said she has concerns about Election Day but believes voter apathy poses a threat as well. "I do think we are going to see problems," Grant said. "We can't just keep on saying my votes not going to county, we gotta say we gotta do it and see what the outcome is," she added. City officials are taking steps to protect the voting process and its outcome. The Philadelphia District Attorney's Office announced that its Election Task Force will be mobilized Tuesday, an effort officials have been planning since the summer. Fifty assistant district attorneys will be deployed to respond to issues, and a hotline will be available for anyone who witnesses problems. "Our main role on Election Day is to make sure everyone gets a chance to vote. We are not looking to do anything other than make things run smooth," Assistant District Attorney Brian Collins said. The Department of Justice also plans to send federal election monitors to Philadelphia. Officials said they are not concerned about the move because it has been done in the past. Some voters said they welcome the increased security. "I just think that with all the hype and everything that's happened. I think whoever the poll watchers are they are more aware of that," said Tyrone Wrice of West Philadelphia. Others said they wanted to make sure they voted early. "I did have a slight concern. Thats why i came to city hall and hand out my ballot to make sure it got in there," said Colleen Chambers of Northern Liberties. Wrice emphasized the importance of casting a ballot. "The power of the vote, even though it's one, is probably the most powerful thing we have," he said. The Election Task Force will remain activated until every vote is counted. Voters in Pennsylvania who are in line by 8 p.m. cannot be turned away.

The November 2026 midterm elections are just four days away.
By Kanishka Singh WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - A US judge ordered the Justice Department on Friday to stop threatening to prosecute state and local election officials who do not comply with the

President Donald Trump on Friday insisted Republicans "have a shot" at success in the US midterms despite a feverish end to the campaign for elections that will decide control of Congress.Earlier in the day, Trump acknowledged to reporters that sitting presidents' parties often suffer in midterm elections.
A federal judge imposed a sweeping emergency order halting various aggressive tactics employed by the Trump administration in recent days to pressure election officials across the country.
Quanda Grant, of West Philadelphia, was outside City Hall on her way to drop off her mail-in ballot.
She said she has concerns about Election Day but believes voter apathy poses a threat as well.
"Our main role on Election Day is to make sure everyone gets a chance to vote.
We are not looking to do anything other than make things run smooth," Assistant District Attorney Brian Collins said.
The Department of Justice also plans to send federal election monitors to Philadelphia.
The Philadelphia District Attorney's Office announced that its Election Task Force will be mobilized Tuesday, an effort officials have been planning since the summer.

extraction.body: Quanda Grant, of West Philadelphia, was outside City Hall on her way to drop off her mail-in ballot. She said she has concerns about Election Day but believes voter apathy poses a threat as well. "I do think we are going to see problems," Grant said. "We can't just keep on saying my votes not going to county, we gotta say we gotta do it and see what the outcome is," she added. City officials are taking steps to protect the voting process and its outcome. The Philadelphia District Attorney's Office announced that its Election Task Force will be mobilized Tuesday, an effort officials have been planning since the summer. Fifty assistant district attorneys will be deployed to respond to issues, and a hotline will be available for anyone who witnesses problems. "Our main role on Election Day is to make sure everyone gets a chance to vote. We are not looking to do anything other than make things run smooth," Assistant District Attorney Brian Collins said. The Department of Justice also plans to send federal election monitors to Philadelphia. Officials said they are not concerned about the move because it has been done in the past. Some voters said they welcome the increased security. "I just think that with all the hype and everything that's happened. I think whoever the poll watchers are they are more aware of that," said Tyrone Wrice of West Philadelphia. Others said they wanted to make sure they voted early. "I did have a slight concern. Thats why i came to city hall and hand out my ballot to make sure it got in there," said Colleen Chambers of Northern Liberties. Wrice emphasized the importance of casting a ballot. "The power of the vote, even though it's one, is probably the most powerful thing we have," he said. The Election Task Force will remain activated until every vote is counted. Voters in Pennsylvania who are in line by 8 p.m. cannot be turned away.

The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.

By Lawrence Delevingne, Summer Zhen and Elizabeth Howcroft BOSTON/SINGAPORE/PARIS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, worked on Friday to shore up public confidence after a record $6.3 billion hack of its platform, promising it would cover all losses from company funds and allow clients to trade again within days. Cryptocurrency prices fell on news of the hack, which analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time. The publicly traded stocks of ‌crypto-related firms Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood slid. Binance said customer funds were safe and it is working with industry partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion, but ‌Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a post on X that $3 billion represented only about 2% of the company's total user assets and public reserves. The exchange also said on Friday afternoon US eastern time that its technical team was targeting a resumption of withdrawal services within approximately 34 hours. Binance said it is conducting a full security review and plans an ​initial proof-of-reserves snapshot in 12 hours, with the results expected to be available by Monday. Binance said it has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1 billion. Binance's other co-CEO, Richard Teng, said in a post on X that the breach was a "complex attack" that was not carried out by one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity as it went along, "making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate." The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called "hot" wallet in a way that did not ‌pass through normal approval controls, Teng said. "Rest assured that we are working nonstop to resolve this, ⁠to make the users whole, and live up to your trust," Teng wrote. Crypto prices fell broadly but losses were contained. Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368, and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178 before markets stabilized. Bitcoin last stood at $76,447 and ether at $2,226. Binance's BNB token was down about 6.4% over the past 24 hours at $696. The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth ⁠of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. "This incident is almost certainly the single-largest-known theft of any kind," British blockchain analysts Elliptic said. The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis. TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea. North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and ​South ​Korean authorities as well as cybersecurity experts. US ​President Donald Trump, asked on Friday whether North Korean hackers were behind the theft, said he did not ‌know but his administration is looking into it. "It was a hack. That's the problem. You know the old-fashioned way when you used to sign a check, take it out. These are different. People never see the money anymore. So I've always felt it was a little bit dangerous," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he thought any of the stolen funds could be retrieved. "But no, they (Binance) say they have it pretty much under control." Binance is working with the FBI and the US Secret Service, according to a person familiar with the situation. The FBI said it is "aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps." The Secret Service said that its investigators "are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle, to identify, freeze, trace and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday." Stablecoin issuer Tether said it froze nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million. Abu Dhabi's Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance's main operating license, said it is "engaging closely with Binance and ‌monitoring the incident." Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX declined to comment. It became a minority investor in Binance last year. Beyond the potential loss of assets, ​the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the crypto sector, which already was under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from ​exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said. "It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralized ​exchanges," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group. Investor Michael Saylor, among bitcoin's most prominent supporters, said in a post on X that he expects Binance to "deliver" on ensuring no customers suffered losses. "Our industry will learn from this ‌incident, strengthen security and emerge stronger and more resilient," Saylor wrote on Friday. Binance, which ​allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered ​users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report. The heist at Binance drew a relatively measured response from crypto enthusiasts online. On social media platform Reddit, discussions about the breach featured a mix of humor, confidence in the exchange's financial resources and questions about how such an enormous theft could have occurred.

Cryptocurrency prices fell on news of the hack, which analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time. The publicly traded stocks of ‌crypto-related firms Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood slid.

It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion, but ‌Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a post on X that $3 billion represented only about 2% of the company's total user assets and public reserves.

The exchange also said on Friday afternoon US eastern time that its technical team was targeting a resumption of withdrawal services within approximately 34 hours. Binance said it is conducting a full security review and plans an ​initial proof-of-reserves snapshot in 12 hours, with the results expected to be available by Monday.

Binance said it has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1 billion.

Binance's other co-CEO, Richard Teng, said in a post on X that the breach was a "complex attack" that was not carried out by one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity as it went along, "making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate."

The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called "hot" wallet in a way that did not ‌pass through normal approval controls, Teng said.
"Rest assured that we are working nonstop to resolve this, ⁠to make the users whole, and live up to your trust," Teng wrote.

BOSTON/SINGAPORE/PARIS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, worked on Friday to shore up public confidence after a record $6.3 billion hack of its platform, promising it would cover all losses from company funds and allow clients to trade again within days.

Cryptocurrency prices fell on news of the hack, which analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time. The publicly traded stocks of ‌crypto-related firms Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood slid.

Binance said customer funds were safe and it is working with industry partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion, but ‌Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a post on X that $3 billion represented only about 2% of the company's total user assets and public reserves.

The exchange also said on Friday afternoon US eastern time that its technical team was targeting a resumption of withdrawal services within approximately 34 hours. Binance said it is conducting a full security review and plans an ​initial proof-of-reserves snapshot in 12 hours, with the results expected to be available by Monday.

Binance said it has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1 billion.

Binance's other co-CEO, Richard Teng, said in a post on X that the breach was a "complex attack" that was not carried out by one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity as it went along, "making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate."

The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called "hot" wallet in a way that did not ‌pass through normal approval controls, Teng said.
"Rest assured that we are working nonstop to resolve this, ⁠to make the users whole, and live up to your trust," Teng wrote.
Crypto prices fell broadly but losses were contained.

Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368, and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178 before markets stabilized. Bitcoin last stood at $76,447 and ether at $2,226. Binance's BNB token was down about 6.4% over the past 24 hours at $696.
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth ⁠of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
"This incident is almost certainly the single-largest-known theft of any kind," British blockchain analysts Elliptic said.

The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea.
North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and ​South ​Korean authorities as well as cybersecurity experts.
US ​President Donald Trump, asked on Friday whether North Korean hackers were behind the theft, said he did not ‌know but his administration is looking into it.

"It was a hack. That's the problem. You know the old-fashioned way when you used to sign a check, take it out. These are different. People never see the money anymore. So I've always felt it was a little bit dangerous," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he thought any of the stolen funds could be retrieved. "But no, they (Binance) say they have it pretty much under control."
Binance is working with the FBI and the US Secret Service, according to a person familiar with the situation.

The FBI said it is "aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps."

The Secret Service said that its investigators "are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle, to identify, freeze, trace and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday."
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it froze nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.

Abu Dhabi's Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance's main operating license, said it is "engaging closely with Binance and ‌monitoring the incident." Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX declined to comment. It became a minority investor in Binance last year.

Beyond the potential loss of assets, ​the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the crypto sector, which already was under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from ​exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
"It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralized ​exchanges," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group.
Investor Michael Saylor, among bitcoin's most prominent supporters, said in a post on X that he expects Binance to "deliver" on ensuring no customers suffered losses.
"Our industry will learn from this ‌incident, strengthen security and emerge stronger and more resilient," Saylor wrote on Friday.
Binance, which ​allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered ​users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.
The heist at Binance drew a relatively measured response from crypto enthusiasts online.

On social media platform Reddit, discussions about the breach featured a mix of humor, confidence in the exchange's financial resources and questions about how such an enormous theft could have occurred.

The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called "hot" wallet in a ‌way that did not pass through ‌normal approval controls, Teng said.
"Rest assured that we are ⁠working nonstop to resolve this, to make the users whole, and live up to your trust," Teng wrote.

"This incident is almost certainly the single-largest-known theft of any kind," British blockchain analysts Elliptic said.

The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.

"But no, they (Binance) say they have it pretty much under control."
Binance is working with the FBI and the US Secret Service, according to a person familiar with the situation.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $US162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.

passages: Hackers working for the North Korean regime have been blamed for a record cryptocurrency heist following a cyberattack at crypto exchange Binance .

The hackers stole at least $6.3 billion in crypto from the company’s wallets, though about half of that amount was frozen as the stolen crypto traveled across various blockchains, according to security researchers.

Researchers describe the network of hackers, known in the cybersecurity industry as TraderTraitor, as a North Korean cell focused almost exclusively on stealing crypto from large companies and exchanges.
Blockchain security firm Elliptic also attributed the Binance theft to North Korean hackers.
Spokespeople for Binance did not respond to an email with questions about the breach.
Companies regularly ask third-party companies to stress-test their security to identify weaknesses that could be exploited by attackers, but it’s unclear if Binance sought such a review.
Binance said “user funds are safe,” but did not immediately provide proof of this claim.
The company said it will “publish an updated proof of reserves once the remediation is complete.”
Spokesperson Andie Cooper said in a statement shared with TechCrunch on Friday that some $3 billion has been frozen by industry partners.

The spokesperson said Binance has “begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds.”

Other times, malware bundled with regular-looking apps and games can allow hackers to steal usernames, passwords, and session tokens from infected computers, which may let them log in as if they were a legitimate employee.

The hackers stole at least $6.3 billion in crypto from the company’s wallets, though about half of that amount was frozen as the stolen crypto traveled across various blockchains, according to security researchers. The breach is by far the largest known theft of crypto in history, though the incident has not been confirmed yet to be resolved, and the amount of crypto stolen may change. In a post on X , Binance said its initial investigation showed that the hackers broke into the company’s network after targeting a “compromised” Binance engineer’s laptop, which “allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” Binance said it has seen no evidence of a leak of its private keys, which would grant the hacker near-unfettered control over the company’s stores of crypto. The crypto exchange — the world’s largest — said it has now suspended all deposits and withdrawals while its investigation into the breach continues. TechCrunch reported on Thursday that the exchange had paused withdrawals across some of its blockchains. Binance said “user funds are safe,” but did not immediately provide proof of this claim. The company said it will “publish an updated proof of reserves once the remediation is complete.” Spokesperson Andie Cooper said in a statement shared with TechCrunch on Friday that some $3 billion has been frozen by industry partners. The spokesperson said Binance has “begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds.” It’s unclear how the hack went down or under what circumstances the employee’s laptop was compromised, but it’s not uncommon for security incidents to stem from the use of compromised software on employee devices. Software is generally built from many components, including open source projects, which hackers regularly target , compromise and modify in order to steal data from devices that the affected software is installed on. Other times, malware bundled with regular-looking apps and games can allow hackers to steal usernames, passwords, and session tokens from infected computers, which may let them log in as if they were a legitimate employee. Binance will face questions about why the company’s security allowed a single employee’s laptop to access systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in funds. Spokespeople for Binance did not respond to an email with questions about the breach. TechCrunch has also asked the company who, if anyone, performed a security audit of Binance’s network and systems prior to the hack. Companies regularly ask third-party companies to stress-test their security to identify weaknesses that could be exploited by attackers, but it’s unclear if Binance sought such a review. Security researchers at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and forensic company, attributed the breach to North Korean hackers, and called it the “largest hack in history.” Researchers describe the network of hackers, known in the cybersecurity industry as TraderTraitor, as a North Korean cell focused almost exclusively on stealing crypto from large companies and exchanges. This group was also blamed for the now-second-largest heist on record, a $1.4 billion theft from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 . According to TRM, the theft of Binance’s billions in crypto took about 20 minutes. Blockchain security firm Elliptic also attributed the Binance theft to North Korean hackers. Elliptic said some of the stolen funds ended up in the same wallet that was used in a previous cyberattack on crypto exchange Bitget earlier this year, in which hackers stole $351 million . The U.S. government and its allies have long warned about the threat from North Korea, which remains cut off from the U.S. and the global financial system for its ongoing development of its nuclear weapons program. Researchers say the breakaway country’s sole motivations are to steal as much crypto as possible in order to continue developing its sanctioned weapons of mass destruction. passages: SINGAPORE/TOKYO/PARIS Oct 30 (Reuters) – Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange , in a theft that analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time.
TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea.
Both TRM and Chainalysis said they were highly confident North Korea was responsible.
North Korea has ​for years ⁠used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well ⁠as cybersecurity ​experts.
Binance logo and hacker code are seen in this illustration taken October 30, 2026.
Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
Virginia Business is the only publication dedicated to covering economic activity in every sector and every region of Virginia.
“This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it,” Binance said in a post on X.
Binance said the company had set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses, without giving details about where the funds had come from.
The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website.
Abu Dhabi’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance’s main operating licence, said it was “engaging closely with Binance and monitoring the incident”.

BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down 5.3% over the past 24 hours at $699.54, according to CoinGecko, while shaky confidence hit listed crypto exchange shares.
The company later added it had uncovered additional points of breach.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.

World Liberty Financial said it worked with custodian BitGo to freeze funds, and Binance co-founder Yi He said $27 million in stablecoins and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.
Crypto firm Ripple also froze roughly $200 million in funds, Yi said.
Binance is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the United States Secret Service (USSS), a person familiar with the situation told Reuters.

Binance is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the United States Secret Service (USSS), a person familiar with the situation told Reuters.
“This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it,” Binance said in a post on X.

The exchange said customer funds were safe and it was working with partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It said earlier on Friday it expected to resume withdrawal services in the next 48 hours. It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion.

Binance said the company had set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses, without giving details about where the funds had come from. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1 billion.

The bulk of the heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea.

“TRM attributes the attack to … North Korea’s elite hacking unit,” the firm said in an analysis posted on its website. Both TRM and Chainalysis said they were highly confident North Korea was responsible.
British blockchain analysts Elliptic also said they believed North Korea was behind the theft.
“This incident is almost certainly the single largest known theft of any kind,” Elliptic said.
North Korea has ​for years ⁠used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well ⁠as cybersecurity ​experts.
North Korea routinely denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
The US embassy in London said it had no comment on a possible investigation. The USSS did not respond to a request for comment sent via email outside of US hours.
Abu Dhabi’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance’s main operating licence, said it was “engaging closely with Binance and monitoring the incident”.
“Your money is safe and we’re covering every loss,” Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on X. “Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual.”
“It’s the biggest hack in history,” Aravind Srinivasan at market maker GSR said, as crypto prices fell broadly.
Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178 before markets stabilised.

“Our security team is tracing the full attack path through the compromised computer which may be the entry point of the incident,” Binance said. The company later added it had uncovered additional points of breach.

Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the crypto sector, which had already been under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
“It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges,” said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.

coreStoryFacts.text: TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor , describing it as an elite North Korean hacking unit.

No public criminal indictment has been filed in connection with this specific incident, and North Korean responsibility should be read as a converging set of private-sector assessments rather than a settled legal finding.

The alleged financial motive is consistent with longstanding assessments by U.S. government and international bodies that North Korean cyber operations generate hard currency for a heavily sanctioned state, including programs tied to weapons development.
Binance's preliminary investigation identified a potentially compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, though the company later noted additional points of breach.
Hackers working for the North Korean regime have been blamed for a record cryptocurrency heist following a cyberattack at crypto exchange Binance .

The hackers stole at least $6.3 billion in crypto from the company’s wallets, though about half of that amount was frozen as the stolen crypto traveled across various blockchains, according to security researchers.

Researchers describe the network of hackers, known in the cybersecurity industry as TraderTraitor, as a North Korean cell focused almost exclusively on stealing crypto from large companies and exchanges.
Blockchain security firm Elliptic also attributed the Binance theft to North Korean hackers.
Spokespeople for Binance did not respond to an email with questions about the breach.
Companies regularly ask third-party companies to stress-test their security to identify weaknesses that could be exploited by attackers, but it’s unclear if Binance sought such a review.
Binance said “user funds are safe,” but did not immediately provide proof of this claim.
The company said it will “publish an updated proof of reserves once the remediation is complete.”
Spokesperson Andie Cooper said in a statement shared with TechCrunch on Friday that some $3 billion has been frozen by industry partners.

The spokesperson said Binance has “begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds.”

Software is generally built from many components, including open source projects, which hackers regularly target , compromise and modify in order to steal data from devices that the affected software is installed on.

Other times, malware bundled with regular-looking apps and games can allow hackers to steal usernames, passwords, and session tokens from infected computers, which may let them log in as if they were a legitimate employee.

SINGAPORE/TOKYO/PARIS Oct 30 (Reuters) – Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange , in a theft that analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time.
TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea.
Both TRM and Chainalysis said they were highly confident North Korea was responsible.
North Korea has ​for years ⁠used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well ⁠as cybersecurity ​experts.
Binance logo and hacker code are seen in this illustration taken October 30, 2026.
Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.

“This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it,” Binance said in a post on X.
Binance said the company had set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses, without giving details about where the funds had come from.
The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website.
Abu Dhabi’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance’s main operating licence, said it was “engaging closely with Binance and monitoring the incident”.

BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down 5.3% over the past 24 hours at $699.54, according to CoinGecko, while shaky confidence hit listed crypto exchange shares.
The company later added it had uncovered additional points of breach.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.

World Liberty Financial said it worked with custodian BitGo to freeze funds, and Binance co-founder Yi He said $27 million in stablecoins and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.
Crypto firm Ripple also froze roughly $200 million in funds, Yi said.
Binance is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the United States Secret Service (USSS), a person familiar with the situation told Reuters.
