extraction.body: $6.36 billion moved out of Binance wallets across 10 blockchains in roughly 20 minutes, according to blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs, as reported by Reuters. That figure surpasses the 2025 Bybit theft, previously regarded as the largest known cryptocurrency heist on record. Binance estimated its own impact at approximately $6.3 billion and temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while conducting security checks, according to the company's official statement on X. Binance's preliminary investigation identified a potentially compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, though the company later noted additional points of breach. Binance's preliminary investigation pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop as a likely entry point. Attackers may have used that access to reach a service container, then submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions from there. Binance said it found no evidence that private keys were leaked. Private keys are the cryptographic credentials that directly authorize control over cryptocurrency holdings, so their absence suggests attackers exploited an operational pathway rather than the most direct form of account control. The alleged method raises questions about whether privileged employee devices and associated environments had excessive access to systems capable of authorizing withdrawals at this scale. TRM Labs, Elliptic, and Chainalysis each attributed the attack to North Korea, though those assessments rest on blockchain tracing and pattern analysis rather than a completed criminal indictment. TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor , describing it as an elite North Korean hacking unit. The firm said it reached that assessment with high confidence, according to Reuters. Elliptic cited similarities between this fund movement and patterns seen in earlier attacks linked to the same network, according to the Wall Street Journal. Chainalysis also assessed the breach as likely conducted by TraderTraitor, according to CBS News. Those assessments rest on blockchain tracing, infrastructure analysis, and attack-pattern comparison. No public criminal indictment has been filed in connection with this specific incident, and North Korean responsibility should be read as a converging set of private-sector assessments rather than a settled legal finding. The alleged financial motive is consistent with longstanding assessments by U.S. government and international bodies that North Korean cyber operations generate hard currency for a heavily sanctioned state, including programs tied to weapons development. Roughly $3 billion of the affected assets have been frozen on-chain, while the remainder is still being traced across multiple blockchains. Roughly $3 billion of the affected assets have been frozen on-chain through cooperation with blockchain partners, according to Binance's statement. The remaining funds are still being traced, which complicates recovery efforts. Binance said it revoked the affected address authorization and engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners. An updated proof of reserves is planned following remediation. User funds are safe, Binance asserted, though that claim remains unverified pending a full technical post-mortem and updated proof of reserves. User funds are safe, the company stated, and any losses will be covered through its Secure Asset Fund for Users and company reserves. That claim is a company assertion, not an independently verified finding. A completed technical post-mortem and updated proof of reserves have not yet been published. Independent verification of customer-fund status remains pending. The reported entry point raises broader questions about whether large exchanges adequately separate deployment access from financial authorization. The alleged breach path points to a structural question about privilege management at large exchanges. Deployment access and financial authorization are different functions, and the incident raises questions about whether controls separating those functions were sufficient. Binance has not yet published a full technical post-mortem. Until it does, the complete picture of how this happened remains incomplete.

The hackers stole at least $6.3 billion in crypto from the company’s wallets, though about half of that amount was frozen as the stolen crypto traveled across various blockchains, according to security researchers. The breach is by far the largest known theft of crypto in history, though the incident has not been confirmed yet to be resolved, and the amount of crypto stolen may change. In a post on X , Binance said its initial investigation showed that the hackers broke into the company’s network after targeting a “compromised” Binance engineer’s laptop, which “allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” Binance said it has seen no evidence of a leak of its private keys, which would grant the hacker near-unfettered control over the company’s stores of crypto. The crypto exchange — the world’s largest — said it has now suspended all deposits and withdrawals while its investigation into the breach continues. TechCrunch reported on Thursday that the exchange had paused withdrawals across some of its blockchains. Binance said “user funds are safe,” but did not immediately provide proof of this claim. The company said it will “publish an updated proof of reserves once the remediation is complete.” Spokesperson Andie Cooper said in a statement shared with TechCrunch on Friday that some $3 billion has been frozen by industry partners. The spokesperson said Binance has “begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds.” It’s unclear how the hack went down or under what circumstances the employee’s laptop was compromised, but it’s not uncommon for security incidents to stem from the use of compromised software on employee devices. Software is generally built from many components, including open source projects, which hackers regularly target , compromise and modify in order to steal data from devices that the affected software is installed on. Other times, malware bundled with regular-looking apps and games can allow hackers to steal usernames, passwords, and session tokens from infected computers, which may let them log in as if they were a legitimate employee. Binance will face questions about why the company’s security allowed a single employee’s laptop to access systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in funds. Spokespeople for Binance did not respond to an email with questions about the breach. TechCrunch has also asked the company who, if anyone, performed a security audit of Binance’s network and systems prior to the hack. Companies regularly ask third-party companies to stress-test their security to identify weaknesses that could be exploited by attackers, but it’s unclear if Binance sought such a review. Security researchers at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and forensic company, attributed the breach to North Korean hackers, and called it the “largest hack in history.” Researchers describe the network of hackers, known in the cybersecurity industry as TraderTraitor, as a North Korean cell focused almost exclusively on stealing crypto from large companies and exchanges. This group was also blamed for the now-second-largest heist on record, a $1.4 billion theft from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 . According to TRM, the theft of Binance’s billions in crypto took about 20 minutes. Blockchain security firm Elliptic also attributed the Binance theft to North Korean hackers. Elliptic said some of the stolen funds ended up in the same wallet that was used in a previous cyberattack on crypto exchange Bitget earlier this year, in which hackers stole $351 million . The U.S. government and its allies have long warned about the threat from North Korea, which remains cut off from the U.S. and the global financial system for its ongoing development of its nuclear weapons program. Researchers say the breakaway country’s sole motivations are to steal as much crypto as possible in order to continue developing its sanctioned weapons of mass destruction. story.title: North Korean hackers blamed for stealing record $6.3B in Binance breach

facts.text: TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor , describing it as an elite North Korean hacking unit.

No public criminal indictment has been filed in connection with this specific incident, and North Korean responsibility should be read as a converging set of private-sector assessments rather than a settled legal finding.

The alleged financial motive is consistent with longstanding assessments by U.S. government and international bodies that North Korean cyber operations generate hard currency for a heavily sanctioned state, including programs tied to weapons development.
Binance's preliminary investigation identified a potentially compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, though the company later noted additional points of breach.
Hackers working for the North Korean regime have been blamed for a record cryptocurrency heist following a cyberattack at crypto exchange Binance .

The hackers stole at least $6.3 billion in crypto from the company’s wallets, though about half of that amount was frozen as the stolen crypto traveled across various blockchains, according to security researchers.

Researchers describe the network of hackers, known in the cybersecurity industry as TraderTraitor, as a North Korean cell focused almost exclusively on stealing crypto from large companies and exchanges.
Blockchain security firm Elliptic also attributed the Binance theft to North Korean hackers.
Spokespeople for Binance did not respond to an email with questions about the breach.
Companies regularly ask third-party companies to stress-test their security to identify weaknesses that could be exploited by attackers, but it’s unclear if Binance sought such a review.
Binance said “user funds are safe,” but did not immediately provide proof of this claim.
The company said it will “publish an updated proof of reserves once the remediation is complete.”
Spokesperson Andie Cooper said in a statement shared with TechCrunch on Friday that some $3 billion has been frozen by industry partners.

The spokesperson said Binance has “begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds.”

Software is generally built from many components, including open source projects, which hackers regularly target , compromise and modify in order to steal data from devices that the affected software is installed on.

Other times, malware bundled with regular-looking apps and games can allow hackers to steal usernames, passwords, and session tokens from infected computers, which may let them log in as if they were a legitimate employee.

passages: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has data centers full of memory, but seemingly it's the 32GB of RAM in your desktop that's the problem.
In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible."

OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home.

Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud.
Some of what Altman is saying is based on an idea that data center buildouts won't slow down.
It also assumes that RAM being used in AI data centers 24/7 is more worthwhile than RAM that is used for spreadsheets, web browsing, gaming, and maybe even local AI occasionally.
The rest of the wide-ranging interview includes talk of this week's PHP vulnerabilities, sandboxing models in training, and OpenAI's research in mathematics.
Freedman is a senior editor at Tom's Hardware focusing on laptops, desktops and gaming.
A lover of all things gaming and tech, his previous work has shown up in Tom's Guide, Laptop Mag, Kotaku, PCMag and Complex, among others.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has data centers full of memory, but seemingly it's the 32GB of RAM in your desktop that's the problem. In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible." When discussing local inference on home computers with open-source models, Altman discussed the assumption that people will be able to run local AI on their own computers, the ones they may already own or want to build. Then he explained why that's a bad idea (at the 29-minute mark): "From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time," Altman said. "You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that." While OpenAI does have some open-source models, its primary business is in closed-source models that run in data centers, so he's really defending the company's business model. OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home. Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud. Some of what Altman is saying is based on an idea that data center buildouts won't slow down. It also assumes that RAM being used in AI data centers 24/7 is more worthwhile than RAM that is used for spreadsheets, web browsing, gaming, and maybe even local AI occasionally. The rest of the wide-ranging interview includes talk of this week's PHP vulnerabilities, sandboxing models in training, and OpenAI's research in mathematics. "You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that."
While OpenAI does have some open-source models, its primary business is in closed-source models that run in data centers, so he's really defending the company's business model.

OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home. Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud. Some of what Altman is saying is based on an idea that data center buildouts won't slow down. It also assumes that RAM being used in AI data centers 24/7 is more worthwhile than RAM that is used for spreadsheets, web browsing, gaming, and maybe even local AI occasionally. The rest of the wide-ranging interview includes talk of this week's PHP vulnerabilities, sandboxing models in training, and OpenAI's research in mathematics.

extraction.body: If you've been RAM shopping any time in the last year or so, you've probably noticed that memory costs quite a bit more than it used to. Part of the reason is due to the increase in RAM usage for AI, as companies purchase large batches of sticks to cover their needs. Now, Sam Altman has gone on record saying that it's "quite terrible" that some of the limited amount of RAM in the world are in people's PCs. Over in an interview on the Cheeky Pint (via IGN ), Sam Altman discussed the current state of RAM. In the interview, he brings up that people want to run open-source AI on their own hardware. However, according to Altman, that's not a great thing: From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer, and being used maybe 5% of the time. Like, you want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that. It seems his point was that, in a shortage, he would prefer RAM in data centers where it'll be put to task for hours in a day, rather than someone's computer where it'll only be used a fraction of the time. And from a "global allocation perspective," I can see what he means. But overall, I feel his statement has partially shown his hand and disposition toward consumers, particularly the last sentence: "And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that." I got the feeling that he thinks RAM sticks in his data centers are worth more than the RAM in people's PCs, whether they run AI off them or not. As if people should allow OpenAI to have the lion's share of RAM so that it can run more powerful AI models in the cloud. And that really comes off poorly in my eyes. Regardless, this is just inference and speculation from a single interview, and it's not indicative of OpenAI's entire stance around the RAM shortage. However, I'd be lying if I said it didn't worry me at least a little bit. 32GB has become the new minimum and my testing proved it for me. We want to hear from you. Remarks come as AI infrastructure providers compete for increasingly limited memory supplies.
Memory manufacturers are prioritizing demand from data centers, putting additional pressure on the consumer market and contributing to higher prices for PCs and other hardware.
In other words, Altman believes memory would be put to better use in centralized data centers, where it could continuously serve multiple users and workloads.

Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it’s “terrible” to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers.

Right now, memory companies Samsung and SK Hynix have long term deals with cloud service operators and projects like OpenAI’s Stargate that have reserved much of the world’s RAM output over the next few years.
If you've been RAM shopping any time in the last year or so, you've probably noticed that memory costs quite a bit more than it used to.
Part of the reason is due to the increase in RAM usage for AI, as companies purchase large batches of sticks to cover their needs.
Now, Sam Altman has gone on record saying that it's "quite terrible" that some of the limited amount of RAM in the world are in people's PCs.
In the interview, he brings up that people want to run open-source AI on their own hardware.
However, according to Altman, that's not a great thing:
And from a "global allocation perspective," I can see what he means.
Regardless, this is just inference and speculation from a single interview, and it's not indicative of OpenAI's entire stance around the RAM shortage.
However, I'd be lying if I said it didn't worry me at least a little bit.
From a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time.
You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment, - Sam Altman .

supportedClaims.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has data centers full of memory, but seemingly it's the 32GB of RAM in your desktop that's the problem.
In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible."

OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home.

Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud.
Some of what Altman is saying is based on an idea that data center buildouts won't slow down.
It also assumes that RAM being used in AI data centers 24/7 is more worthwhile than RAM that is used for spreadsheets, web browsing, gaming, and maybe even local AI occasionally.
The rest of the wide-ranging interview includes talk of this week's PHP vulnerabilities, sandboxing models in training, and OpenAI's research in mathematics.

Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it’s “terrible” to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers.

Right now, memory companies Samsung and SK Hynix have long term deals with cloud service operators and projects like OpenAI’s Stargate that have reserved much of the world’s RAM output over the next few years.
If you've been RAM shopping any time in the last year or so, you've probably noticed that memory costs quite a bit more than it used to.
Part of the reason is due to the increase in RAM usage for AI, as companies purchase large batches of sticks to cover their needs.
Now, Sam Altman has gone on record saying that it's "quite terrible" that some of the limited amount of RAM in the world are in people's PCs.
In the interview, he brings up that people want to run open-source AI on their own hardware.
However, according to Altman, that's not a great thing:
And from a "global allocation perspective," I can see what he means.
Regardless, this is just inference and speculation from a single interview, and it's not indicative of OpenAI's entire stance around the RAM shortage.
However, I'd be lying if I said it didn't worry me at least a little bit.
From a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time.
You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment, - Sam Altman .
Remarks come as AI infrastructure providers compete for increasingly limited memory supplies.
Memory manufacturers are prioritizing demand from data centers, putting additional pressure on the consumer market and contributing to higher prices for PCs and other hardware.
In other words, Altman believes memory would be put to better use in centralized data centers, where it could continuously serve multiple users and workloads.
However, his argument focuses on local AI inference and does not account for the many other reasons people need RAM in their PCs, including gaming, everyday applications and multitasking.

coreFacts.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has data centers full of memory, but seemingly it's the 32GB of RAM in your desktop that's the problem.
In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible."

OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home.

Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud.
Some of what Altman is saying is based on an idea that data center buildouts won't slow down.
It also assumes that RAM being used in AI data centers 24/7 is more worthwhile than RAM that is used for spreadsheets, web browsing, gaming, and maybe even local AI occasionally.
The rest of the wide-ranging interview includes talk of this week's PHP vulnerabilities, sandboxing models in training, and OpenAI's research in mathematics.
Freedman is a senior editor at Tom's Hardware focusing on laptops, desktops and gaming.
A lover of all things gaming and tech, his previous work has shown up in Tom's Guide, Laptop Mag, Kotaku, PCMag and Complex, among others.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has data centers full of memory, but seemingly it's the 32GB of RAM in your desktop that's the problem. In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible." When discussing local inference on home computers with open-source models, Altman discussed the assumption that people will be able to run local AI on their own computers, the ones they may already own or want to build. Then he explained why that's a bad idea (at the 29-minute mark): "From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time," Altman said. "You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that." While OpenAI does have some open-source models, its primary business is in closed-source models that run in data centers, so he's really defending the company's business model. OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home. Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud. Some of what Altman is saying is based on an idea that data center buildouts won't slow down. It also assumes that RAM being used in AI data centers 24/7 is more worthwhile than RAM that is used for spreadsheets, web browsing, gaming, and maybe even local AI occasionally. The rest of the wide-ranging interview includes talk of this week's PHP vulnerabilities, sandboxing models in training, and OpenAI's research in mathematics. sources.title: Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk
passages: Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it’s “terrible” to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers.

Right now, memory companies Samsung and SK Hynix have long term deals with cloud service operators and projects like OpenAI’s Stargate that have reserved much of the world’s RAM output over the next few years.

extraction.body: If you've been RAM shopping any time in the last year or so, you've probably noticed that memory costs quite a bit more than it used to. Part of the reason is due to the increase in RAM usage for AI, as companies purchase large batches of sticks to cover their needs. Now, Sam Altman has gone on record saying that it's "quite terrible" that some of the limited amount of RAM in the world are in people's PCs. Over in an interview on the Cheeky Pint (via IGN ), Sam Altman discussed the current state of RAM. In the interview, he brings up that people want to run open-source AI on their own hardware. However, according to Altman, that's not a great thing: From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer, and being used maybe 5% of the time. Like, you want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that. It seems his point was that, in a shortage, he would prefer RAM in data centers where it'll be put to task for hours in a day, rather than someone's computer where it'll only be used a fraction of the time. And from a "global allocation perspective," I can see what he means. But overall, I feel his statement has partially shown his hand and disposition toward consumers, particularly the last sentence: "And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that." I got the feeling that he thinks RAM sticks in his data centers are worth more than the RAM in people's PCs, whether they run AI off them or not. As if people should allow OpenAI to have the lion's share of RAM so that it can run more powerful AI models in the cloud. And that really comes off poorly in my eyes. Regardless, this is just inference and speculation from a single interview, and it's not indicative of OpenAI's entire stance around the RAM shortage. However, I'd be lying if I said it didn't worry me at least a little bit. 32GB has become the new minimum and my testing proved it for me. We want to hear from you. Remarks come as AI infrastructure providers compete for increasingly limited memory supplies.

extraction.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has argued that keeping large amounts of RAM in personal computers is an inefficient use of limited memory supplies, saying data centers can put the same resources to better use. He said local AI inference, which is becoming an increasingly popular alternative to cloud-based AI services, leaves memory unused most of the time, making it a poor allocation of scarce DRAM. From a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time. You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment, - Sam Altman . In other words, Altman believes memory would be put to better use in centralized data centers, where it could continuously serve multiple users and workloads. However, his argument focuses on local AI inference and does not account for the many other reasons people need RAM in their PCs, including gaming, everyday applications and multitasking. Altman's position also aligns with OpenAI's business model. Although the company offers some open-weight models, its main products are closed-source models that run in data centers and are accessed through subscriptions and cloud services. Wider adoption of local AI models could reduce users’ dependence on cloud platforms and subscriptions, although data centers would remain essential for training large models. Remarks come as AI infrastructure providers compete for increasingly limited memory supplies. Memory manufacturers are prioritizing demand from data centers, putting additional pressure on the consumer market and contributing to higher prices for PCs and other hardware. His comments add to the debate over whether the world’s limited DRAM supply should be concentrated in large AI data centers or remain available to individual users.

story.title: Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk

facts.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has data centers full of memory, but seemingly it's the 32GB of RAM in your desktop that's the problem.
In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible."

OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home.

Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud.
Some of what Altman is saying is based on an idea that data center buildouts won't slow down.
It also assumes that RAM being used in AI data centers 24/7 is more worthwhile than RAM that is used for spreadsheets, web browsing, gaming, and maybe even local AI occasionally.
The rest of the wide-ranging interview includes talk of this week's PHP vulnerabilities, sandboxing models in training, and OpenAI's research in mathematics.
Freedman is a senior editor at Tom's Hardware focusing on laptops, desktops and gaming.
A lover of all things gaming and tech, his previous work has shown up in Tom's Guide, Laptop Mag, Kotaku, PCMag and Complex, among others.
Follow him on Threads @FreedmanAE and BlueSky @andrewfreedman.net .
You can send him tips on Signal: andrewfreedman.01

Right now, memory companies Samsung and SK Hynix have long term deals with cloud service operators and projects like OpenAI’s Stargate that have reserved much of the world’s RAM output over the next few years.
If you've been RAM shopping any time in the last year or so, you've probably noticed that memory costs quite a bit more than it used to.
Part of the reason is due to the increase in RAM usage for AI, as companies purchase large batches of sticks to cover their needs.
Now, Sam Altman has gone on record saying that it's "quite terrible" that some of the limited amount of RAM in the world are in people's PCs.
In the interview, he brings up that people want to run open-source AI on their own hardware.
However, according to Altman, that's not a great thing:
And from a "global allocation perspective," I can see what he means.
Regardless, this is just inference and speculation from a single interview, and it's not indicative of OpenAI's entire stance around the RAM shortage.
However, I'd be lying if I said it didn't worry me at least a little bit.
From a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time.
You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment, - Sam Altman .
Remarks come as AI infrastructure providers compete for increasingly limited memory supplies.
Memory manufacturers are prioritizing demand from data centers, putting additional pressure on the consumer market and contributing to higher prices for PCs and other hardware.
In other words, Altman believes memory would be put to better use in centralized data centers, where it could continuously serve multiple users and workloads.
However, his argument focuses on local AI inference and does not account for the many other reasons people need RAM in their PCs, including gaming, everyday applications and multitasking.

coreFacts.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has data centers full of memory, but seemingly it's the 32GB of RAM in your desktop that's the problem.
In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible."

OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home.

Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud.
Some of what Altman is saying is based on an idea that data center buildouts won't slow down.
It also assumes that RAM being used in AI data centers 24/7 is more worthwhile than RAM that is used for spreadsheets, web browsing, gaming, and maybe even local AI occasionally.
The rest of the wide-ranging interview includes talk of this week's PHP vulnerabilities, sandboxing models in training, and OpenAI's research in mathematics.

extraction.body: Binance halted trading Thursday after hackers allegedly linked to North Korea stole more than $6 billion, the largest crypto hack in history. Why it matters : The attack comes after a wave of high-profile cyber intrusions and data breaches during "Black October," when a series of security incidents and AI -discovered bugs triggered fears of a global crisis. Driving the news: Binance co-founder Yi He said on X that the crypto exchange had suspended deposits and withdrawals. "User funds are safe," she wrote. "Binance will cover all hacking losses." An estimated $6.3 billion were drained from wallets in the incident, Binance said , although the exchange and partners managed to freeze about $3 billion that can potentially be recovered. "This is unprecedented," said Kevin March, a co-founder of JPEG Trading, a cryptocurrency trading firm that closely tracked the hack to monitor market conditions. An initial investigation linked the hack to a compromised laptop from one Binance engineer. That access allowed an attacker to gain access to Binance's systems to make withdrawals, the exchange said. Zoom in: Researchers from TRM Labs and Pangolin Intelligence found that the attack appeared to be the work of a North Korean hacking collective. "This was absolutely North Korea," Nick Carlsen, a senior TRM investigator, told the Wall Street Journal . Representatives of North Korea have previously denied allegations of hacking crypto exchanges. The country has turned hacking and scams into an industrial-scale scourge, focusing on crypto heists and a widespread practice of tricking Western companies into hiring North Korean workers . A Binance spokesperson said the exchange's security teams are "reviewing all relevant information with urgency." The big picture: If estimates hold up, the Binance hack would be the biggest crypto attack in history. In 2025, North Korea-linked hackers stole about $1.5 billion worth of crypto from the Bybit exchange. Between the lines: Crypto is a relatively common hacking target, but massive attacks can leave smaller exchanges vulnerable to collapse due to the potential for panicked withdrawals. Binance's size makes it more insulated, March said. "If this happened to any other business in crypto other than Binance, it would've been catastrophic." The exchange is capable of covering potential losses through its insurance and balance sheet, he said, although broad reverberations in crypto markets and prices remain possible. The intrigue: Reports of a breach came just hours after Polymarket confirmed it was facing a cyberattack, prompting the decentralized prediction market operator to pause trading for an hour after an attacker made off with at least $2.7 million in user funds. Researchers at Hudson Rock tied the Polymarket incident to a breach involving third-party website monitoring tool DebugBear , which said earlier Thursday it was responding to its own security incident. What to watch: Binance has yet to confirm who may be behind the attack and the total value of the currencies suspected hackers made off with. Analysts suspect North Korea could be behind it - one analysis firm says it has observed funds from this hack "commingling" with funds from another that has widely been attributed to North Korean actors The regime has repeatedly been accused of using cryptocurrency theft to generate revenue to help fund its weapons programmes, our Japan correspondent writes Edited by Craig Hoyle, with cyber correspondent Joe Tidy and technology reporters Liv McMahon and Laura Cress The US Secret Service says its investigators are working "around the clock" to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds stolen in what is thought to be the largest hack in history - worth up to $6.3bn (£4.7bn). The affected firm Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange, which earlier said it had "begun recovering" some funds after yesterday's attack. Binance co-CEO Richard Tend said the hack attacked the firm's own hot wallet by abusing something called "multi-signature protocol EIP-7702". This meant the thieves were able to bypass the usual methods of verification used by the platform - most of the money left Binance wallets in about 20 minutes , one expert told the BBC. Chainalysis, another crypto analytics firm, also says it has a "high degree of confidence" that North Korea was behind the hack. It says it observed funds stolen from Binance "commingling" with funds stolen from another hack of a different crypto exchange last month which was also widely attributed to North Korean actors. North Korea has always denied it is behind such hacking, but Tidy says "the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling". After we heard from the FBI earlier, another US government agency has commented on the hack. The US Secret Service, which is the lead federal agency for financial crimes and protecting the US financial system, says it's "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance. The agency goes on to say that it's "coordinating closely with the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia and law enforcement partners to identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice". Bitcoin's value (BTC) fell after the news of the Binance hack, with its price dropping by about four percentage points. But we should note that in the early days of crypto, BTC could lose 20% or 30% of its value in a single day after a cryptocurrency theft. So that's likely a sign that the crypto market has since matured. Binance earlier said its initial investigation suggests the security incident may have involved a "compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" which allowed the hackers to gain access and submit unauthorised transactions. Most of the $6.36bn left Binance wallets in about 20 minutes, Redbord says, starting at 20:05 GMT on Thursday. "That speed is the product of long preparation," he says. He says the delegation did not pass through the firm's normal approval controls, adding that this is why the withdrawal service needs to be paused so that investigations can be carried out. Binance is rebuilding the withdrawal service and not switching it back until it "passes rigorous testing", Teng says, adding that Binance is "on track" to resume services within 40 hours. The company is also conducting a full security review across the whole company, and completing the purchase of the remaining assets. The FBI has said in a statement it is "aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps". Richard Teng, Binance's co-CEO, has posted an update on X, explaining that what was affected in this hack was Binance's own hot wallet. He says many people are asking how Binance can prove individual's assets are not impacted. Cryptocurrency fans say the fact it's not controlled by any centralised financial institution brings with it privacy and financial freedom. With the race now on to trace crypto funds stolen from Binance, investigators will be monitoring any instances where it's converted into conventional money, because that greater visibility as it enters the real-world financial system makes it a key opportunity to intervene . Converting crypto into normal money is called off-ramping . The opposite process is called on-ramping . The world's biggest crypto exchange Binance says it has "begun recovering affected assets for users" , after it was hit by what is thought to be the biggest hack in history. Cryptocurrency worth $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was stolen in the mega-hack, and trading on platform Binance Alpha was temporarily suspended last night - read a timeline of Binance's response here . In its latest update, the firm reiterated that it has committed to cover losses through company funds , and says it has reserved over $6.3bn (£4.7bn) to cover the incident. It said frozen or protected assets remain subject to ongoing recovery and verification. Earlier, it said $3bn (£2.24bn) had already been frozen.

passages: Binance was hacked with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets.
Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far, according to a Binance security update .

Assuming frozen stablecoins are eventually returned, Binance's SAFU emergency fund, worth approximately $1.2 billion, could cover roughly a third of the remaining losses, with the balance coming from the exchange's own funds.

Chainalysis also pointed to North Korea , with co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin saying the firm assessed that the $6.4 billion Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, citing links to previous attacks.
The firm estimated that approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, with most transferred within about 20 minutes.
The FBI previously identified the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, according to the company's insights.
"The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance," Farrell said.

Speaking to CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ," Perkins said the industry must address cybersecurity challenges to reach its full potential, calling for stronger defenses and policies to hold cybercriminals accountable.
"A freeze stops the money from moving, and recovery follows through legal process," Redbord told CNBC.
A technical freeze may happen quickly, while returning funds can take months or years," Jardine told CNBC.
TRM Labs said the Binance attack shared characteristics with previous North Korea-linked incidents, including preparations made well before the theft and transaction signatures obtained in advance.
Farrell said the key indicators to watch were how quickly Binance resumes withdrawals and whether outflows remain orderly.
He added that a shortfall in customer assets could force the exchange to sell reserves, potentially triggering broader selling across crypto markets.
The Binance hack underscores the need for stronger cybersecurity standards and greater coordination among governments, according to Chris Perkins, head of Franklin Crypto at Franklin Templeton.

extraction.body: Binance was hacked with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets. Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far, according to a Binance security update . The exchange pledged to cover all losses, while blockchain investigators linked the attack to North Korea and analysts assessed the potential financial risks. Bitcoin was under pressure on Friday and was trading below $78,000. Freezing cryptocurrency prevents it from being transferred, but recovering the funds requires a separate legal process, according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs and a former U.S. federal prosecutor and Treasury official. "A freeze stops the money from moving, and recovery follows through legal process," Redbord told CNBC. Redbord said law enforcement typically obtains a court order or seizure warrant before working with stablecoin issuers to release or reissue assets and return them to their rightful owners. "Stablecoins are the most recoverable asset class in crypto because the issuer controls the token contract," he said. "Tether and Circle can freeze, burn and reissue, which allows frozen USDT and USDC to be returned to a victim." But recovering bitcoin and ether is more challenging because they have no issuer that can directly freeze the assets. Instead, investigators must trace funds through exchanges and other crypto services where they can potentially be intercepted, added Redbord. Eric Jardine, head of research at blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, said returning frozen assets requires coordination among law enforcement, exchanges and token issuers. "There is no standard recovery timeline. A technical freeze may happen quickly, while returning funds can take months or years," Jardine told CNBC. Jardine added that while bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen by an issuer, they can still be traced and potentially recovered. Investigators can trace the funds on public blockchains and intervene when they reach a cooperating exchange or another centralized platform, he said. TRM Labs attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit, based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence. The FBI previously identified the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, according to the company's insights. TRM Labs said the Binance attack shared characteristics with previous North Korea-linked incidents, including preparations made well before the theft and transaction signatures obtained in advance. The firm estimated that approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, with most transferred within about 20 minutes. TRM Labs said preparations for the attack began at least 36 hours before the theft, with the attackers using Tornado Cash, a cryptocurrency mixing service, to fund their wallets ahead of the breach. Chainalysis also pointed to North Korea , with co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin saying the firm assessed that the $6.4 billion Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, citing links to previous attacks. The attack does not currently appear to pose a significant solvency risk for Binance, according to Sean Farrell, head of digital asset strategy at Fundstrat Global Advisors. "The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance," Farrell said. Farrell estimated that around $3.3 billion in assets remained unfrozen. Assuming frozen stablecoins are eventually returned, Binance's SAFU emergency fund, worth approximately $1.2 billion, could cover roughly a third of the remaining losses, with the balance coming from the exchange's own funds. Farrell said the key indicators to watch were how quickly Binance resumes withdrawals and whether outflows remain orderly. He added that a shortfall in customer assets could force the exchange to sell reserves, potentially triggering broader selling across crypto markets. The exchange pledged to cover all losses, while blockchain investigators linked the attack to North Korea and analysts assessed the potential financial risks.
Bitcoin was under pressure on Friday and was trading below $78,000.

Freezing cryptocurrency prevents it from being transferred, but recovering the funds requires a separate legal process, according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs and a former U.S. federal prosecutor and Treasury official.
"A freeze stops the money from moving, and recovery follows through legal process," Redbord told CNBC.
Redbord said law enforcement typically obtains a court order or seizure warrant before working with stablecoin issuers to release or reissue assets and return them to their rightful owners.

"Stablecoins are the most recoverable asset class in crypto because the issuer controls the token contract," he said. "Tether and Circle can freeze, burn and reissue, which allows frozen USDT and USDC to be returned to a victim."

But recovering bitcoin and ether is more challenging because they have no issuer that can directly freeze the assets. Instead, investigators must trace funds through exchanges and other crypto services where they can potentially be intercepted, added Redbord.
Eric Jardine, head of research at blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, said returning frozen assets requires coordination among law enforcement, exchanges and token issuers.
"There is no standard recovery timeline. A technical freeze may happen quickly, while returning funds can take months or years," Jardine told CNBC.

Jardine added that while bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen by an issuer, they can still be traced and potentially recovered. Investigators can trace the funds on public blockchains and intervene when they reach a cooperating exchange or another centralized platform, he said.
TRM Labs attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit, based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence.
The FBI previously identified the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, according to the company's insights.
TRM Labs said the Binance attack shared characteristics with previous North Korea-linked incidents, including preparations made well before the theft and transaction signatures obtained in advance.
The firm estimated that approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, with most transferred within about 20 minutes.
TRM Labs said preparations for the attack began at least 36 hours before the theft, with the attackers using Tornado Cash, a cryptocurrency mixing service, to fund their wallets ahead of the breach.

Chainalysis also pointed to North Korea , with co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin saying the firm assessed that the $6.4 billion Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, citing links to previous attacks.
The attack does not currently appear to pose a significant solvency risk for Binance, according to Sean Farrell, head of digital asset strategy at Fundstrat Global Advisors.
"The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance," Farrell said.

Farrell estimated that around $3.3 billion in assets remained unfrozen. Assuming frozen stablecoins are eventually returned, Binance's SAFU emergency fund, worth approximately $1.2 billion, could cover roughly a third of the remaining losses, with the balance coming from the exchange's own funds.

"I do not think that is the setup we are dealing with, but the key tell will be how quickly withdrawals resume and whether outflows stay orderly," Farrell said.
The Binance hack underscores the need for stronger cybersecurity standards and greater coordination among governments, according to Chris Perkins, head of Franklin Crypto at Franklin Templeton.

Speaking to CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ," Perkins said the industry must address cybersecurity challenges to reach its full potential, calling for stronger defenses and policies to hold cybercriminals accountable.
"We need to make sure standards are incredibly high, but we have to really focus on the criminals," Perkins said.

Perkins called for greater international cooperation to address cybersecurity threats, pointing to regulatory coordination among G20 countries following the global financial crisis as a potential model.

passages: Binance was hacked with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets.
Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far, according to a Binance security update .

Assuming frozen stablecoins are eventually returned, Binance's SAFU emergency fund, worth approximately $1.2 billion, could cover roughly a third of the remaining losses, with the balance coming from the exchange's own funds.

Chainalysis also pointed to North Korea , with co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin saying the firm assessed that the $6.4 billion Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, citing links to previous attacks.
The firm estimated that approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, with most transferred within about 20 minutes.
The FBI previously identified the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, according to the company's insights.
"The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance," Farrell said.

Speaking to CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ," Perkins said the industry must address cybersecurity challenges to reach its full potential, calling for stronger defenses and policies to hold cybercriminals accountable.
"A freeze stops the money from moving, and recovery follows through legal process," Redbord told CNBC.
A technical freeze may happen quickly, while returning funds can take months or years," Jardine told CNBC.
TRM Labs said the Binance attack shared characteristics with previous North Korea-linked incidents, including preparations made well before the theft and transaction signatures obtained in advance.
Farrell said the key indicators to watch were how quickly Binance resumes withdrawals and whether outflows remain orderly.
He added that a shortfall in customer assets could force the exchange to sell reserves, potentially triggering broader selling across crypto markets.
The Binance hack underscores the need for stronger cybersecurity standards and greater coordination among governments, according to Chris Perkins, head of Franklin Crypto at Franklin Templeton.

extraction.body: Binance was hacked with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets. Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far, according to a Binance security update . The exchange pledged to cover all losses, while blockchain investigators linked the attack to North Korea and analysts assessed the potential financial risks. Bitcoin was under pressure on Friday and was trading below $78,000. Freezing cryptocurrency prevents it from being transferred, but recovering the funds requires a separate legal process, according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs and a former U.S. federal prosecutor and Treasury official. "A freeze stops the money from moving, and recovery follows through legal process," Redbord told CNBC. Redbord said law enforcement typically obtains a court order or seizure warrant before working with stablecoin issuers to release or reissue assets and return them to their rightful owners. "Stablecoins are the most recoverable asset class in crypto because the issuer controls the token contract," he said. "Tether and Circle can freeze, burn and reissue, which allows frozen USDT and USDC to be returned to a victim." But recovering bitcoin and ether is more challenging because they have no issuer that can directly freeze the assets. Instead, investigators must trace funds through exchanges and other crypto services where they can potentially be intercepted, added Redbord. Eric Jardine, head of research at blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, said returning frozen assets requires coordination among law enforcement, exchanges and token issuers. "There is no standard recovery timeline. A technical freeze may happen quickly, while returning funds can take months or years," Jardine told CNBC. Jardine added that while bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen by an issuer, they can still be traced and potentially recovered. Investigators can trace the funds on public blockchains and intervene when they reach a cooperating exchange or another centralized platform, he said. TRM Labs attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit, based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence. The FBI previously identified the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, according to the company's insights. TRM Labs said the Binance attack shared characteristics with previous North Korea-linked incidents, including preparations made well before the theft and transaction signatures obtained in advance. The firm estimated that approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, with most transferred within about 20 minutes. TRM Labs said preparations for the attack began at least 36 hours before the theft, with the attackers using Tornado Cash, a cryptocurrency mixing service, to fund their wallets ahead of the breach. Chainalysis also pointed to North Korea , with co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin saying the firm assessed that the $6.4 billion Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, citing links to previous attacks. The attack does not currently appear to pose a significant solvency risk for Binance, according to Sean Farrell, head of digital asset strategy at Fundstrat Global Advisors. "The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance," Farrell said. Farrell estimated that around $3.3 billion in assets remained unfrozen. Assuming frozen stablecoins are eventually returned, Binance's SAFU emergency fund, worth approximately $1.2 billion, could cover roughly a third of the remaining losses, with the balance coming from the exchange's own funds. Farrell said the key indicators to watch were how quickly Binance resumes withdrawals and whether outflows remain orderly. He added that a shortfall in customer assets could force the exchange to sell reserves, potentially triggering broader selling across crypto markets. "I do not think that is the setup we are dealing with, but the key tell will be how quickly withdrawals resume and whether outflows stay orderly," Farrell said. The Binance hack underscores the need for stronger cybersecurity standards and greater coordination among governments, according to Chris Perkins, head of Franklin Crypto at Franklin Templeton. Speaking to CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ," Perkins said the industry must address cybersecurity challenges to reach its full potential, calling for stronger defenses and policies to hold cybercriminals accountable. "We need to make sure standards are incredibly high, but we have to really focus on the criminals," Perkins said. Perkins called for greater international cooperation to address cybersecurity threats, pointing to regulatory coordination among G20 countries following the global financial crisis as a potential model. He also said AI could help improve cybersecurity by identifying and addressing vulnerabilities, even as the technology is used by both attackers and defenders. Got a confidential news tip? The share price of Intel dropped almost 30% on Friday , shaving over $11 billion from the US government's stake in the company, though the transaction remains profitable overall. Last August, the Trump administration took a 9.9% equity stake in the chipmaker at a price of $20.47 per share, according to a company press release at the time. That initial stake of 433.3 million primary shares was worth about $8.9 billion. The value shot up dramatically earlier this year, with Intel ( INTC ) closing on Thursday at $92.07 per share, implying a value to the US government of $39.9 billion. But the stock took a beating on Friday after the company reported earnings on Thursday night . The stock closed Friday down about 29% at $65.76 per share, suggesting a new paper value for the government's stake of $28.5 billion. The rapid price change underscores how government investments can take investors on a wild ride and presents a new challenge to a centerpiece of Trump's government portfolio, which now spans 40 companies, according to a CATO Institute tracker. Investors punished Intel after its Q4 revenue outlook fell short of Wall Street expectations and the company reported a worse-than-anticipated drop in PC revenue. Intel is projecting fourth quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, well below the $17 billion analysts expected. It's a major setback for CEO Lip-Bu Tan, who was hired in March 2025, and has since been on a campaign to revive the company after it missed out on the early years of the artificial intelligence boom. Intel's plunge is also a big hit to the Trump administration, which led the U.S. government into taking a 10% stake in the company over a year ago. While it's still a profitable investment, the value of those holdings dropped by about $12 billion on Friday. Nvidia also took a big stake in Intel, and its stock dropped by about $6 billion in value. Heading into Thursday's earnings report, Intel shares were up about 150% this year, buoyed by demand for central processors, which are becoming critical to agentic AI workloads. Analysts at D.A. Davidson downgraded the stock to neutral from buy on Friday in a report titled, "Not fixed yet." "We understand the PC market is being impacted at the industry level," the analysts wrote. "However it is hard to justify the current multiple when weakness is so significant." Amazon shares also sold off on Friday, slipping 1.4%, after the company reported a third-quarter miss on the top and bottom line while maintaining its capital expenditure forecast for 2026 of $220 billion. Amazon also reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, and a big increase from the previous period. The Nasdaq Composite slid 2.9%, capping off a week of rough tech earnings. Alphabet on Thursday suffered its worst day on record, plunging more than 12%. The stock fell again on Friday. Other semiconductor names also notched declines. Chip giant Nvidia fell 4%, while Broadcom dropped more than 5% and mobile chipmaker Qualcomm tumbled 11%. Investors are growing nervous about the massive AI spending from the tech giants and whether their investments will pay off. "I don't think this is a moment of reckoning but I think it's a moment where investors should take a long thought about how positioning across the space still remains crowded even though the fundamentals are strong," Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday. For Intel, the disappointing forecast reflects a PC market that's getting hammered due to soaring costs for memory and other components. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier, according to Counterpoint Research . Intel said it expects adjusted earnings per share of 25 cents this quarter on revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion. Analysts were expecting revenue of $17.1 billion and EPS of 43 cents, according to LSEG. "We see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," Intel finance chief David Zinsner, said in the release. "We will continue making disciplined investments in capacity and working capital to increase supply and support future growth." The guidance also accounts for the effects of an explosion at a fab in Israel that killed two workers and seriously injured a third earlier this month. The incident will cost the company about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters, Zinsner said. Tan said the explosion, which he called an "unfortunate and tragic accident," caused an "extended shutdown" at the plant, impacting shipments of 10-nanometer chips. Key to Tan's turnaround effort is Intel's foundry business, which has struggled to find its footing. Intel is the only U.S.-based manufacturer of advanced logic chips, and is now in high-volume production of its most advanced 18A chip out of its new fab in Arizona, providing an alternative to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co . Its next Arizona fab is expected to begin operations by the end of 2028. Intel still has no external customers for its new chips. "We're going to have a couple of customers ready to announce the next two quarters," Tan said on the call, adding that Intel is making "tremendous progress" on its coming 14A chips. This rout reduced the value of Intel’s holdings by the government by $12 billion, CNBC reports . The Trump administration had the government buy 10% stake over a year ago. extraction.body: Apple today took the unusual step of confirming when its next iOS developer beta is expected to arrive, as part of an announcement detailing the upcoming launch of Apple Intelligence in China. Here are the details. In mid-July, Reuters reported that, following a lengthy back-and-forth with Chinese regulators and multiple delays, Apple Intelligence had finally cleared a major regulatory hurdle ahead of its long-awaited launch in the country. Then, a couple of weeks ago, Bloomberg reported that Apple was planning to launch Apple Intelligence in China in December as part of iOS 27.3, although without Siri AI and other newer features. The following day, China’s state-backed media outlet The Paper reported that Tim Cook had confirmed regulatory approval for the platform, with a test version expected before the end of October. Then, just last Monday, Apple released iOS 27.2 and its counterparts, expanding Siri AI support to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. On the same day, the company announced that four more languages, including Traditional Chinese, would be supported by the end of the year. However, while that announcement confirmed additional language support for Siri AI, it offered no updates on the rollout of Apple Intelligence in China, where Siri AI itself will remain unavailable for the time being. While Apple typically releases the first beta of its next software update shortly after the previous version becomes available, iOS 27.3 has yet to materialize. Now, as spotted by MacRumors , a press release published on Apple’s Chinese Newsroom website confirms that testing of Apple Intelligence in China will begin on November 4, as part of the next iOS developer beta. Importantly, Apple has only confirmed November 4 as the start of Apple Intelligence testing in China, not necessarily the release date of iOS 27.3 beta 1 itself. In the press release , Apple confirms that users in China will get an improved Siri experience, including Type to Siri and the ability to access Alibaba’s Qwen for certain requests, but not Siri AI itself. The Qwen integration will also extend to Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence. According to Apple, users will be able to ask questions about photos and documents, including PDFs and presentations, as well as generate original content from scratch through Writing Tools. Users will be able to access Qwen by signing into their accounts or using Sign in with Apple. Other features included in the initial rollout are Live Translation in Messages, FaceTime, and Phone, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Clean Up in Photos, natural-language photo searches, priority notifications, notification summaries, and Smart Reply, among others. Apple also noted that the initial rollout will be exclusive to the iPhone, with support for other platforms coming only after the necessary regulatory approvals have been obtained. The features will be available on the iPhone 15 Pro and Pro Max, iPhone 16 and later, iPhone Air, and iPhone Duo, with both Siri and the device language required to be set to either English or Simplified Chinese. The company also confirmed that the features will become publicly available in December, with the official release of iOS 27.3. To check out Apple’s press release, follow this link . extraction.body: Apple is preparing to bring Apple Intelligence to mainland China in December, potentially ending a delay that has kept the company’s AI features out of one of its most important markets for more than two years. According to Bloomberg , Apple is planning to launch its first Apple Intelligence features in the country as part of iOS 27.3. The rollout would mark a major step for Apple in China, where regulatory requirements have prevented the company from offering the same AI experience already available across many other markets. The initial launch is expected to be deliberately limited. Apple reportedly plans to bring over several of the original Apple Intelligence capabilities first introduced in 2024, including Writing Tools, notification summaries, Genmoji and the Clean Up feature in Photos. However, the newer Siri AI experience introduced with iOS 27 is not expected to be included. Apple’s own image-generation tools are also expected to remain unavailable, while some text-generation capabilities could be restricted in certain apps. That means customers in China may receive a noticeably different version of Apple Intelligence from the experience available elsewhere. The rollout has required Apple to take a different technical approach to comply with Chinese regulations. Bloomberg reports that Apple has worked with Alibaba on safeguards for its AI system, including a filtering mechanism designed around local requirements, while Baidu is involved in areas including search and Siri. A separate South China Morning Post report says updated network access permits from China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology now list Apple Intelligence alongside Alibaba’s Qwen and Tongyi Wanxiang models for devices including the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro and several earlier iPhones. Apple has been trying to bring Apple Intelligence to China since the platform was first introduced in 2024. Earlier launch targets reportedly slipped repeatedly as the company worked through regulatory approval, local model requirements and the restrictions placed on foreign-developed generative AI services. The absence of Apple Intelligence has become increasingly important for Apple as Chinese smartphone makers continue to push AI deeper into their devices. Rivals including Huawei, Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo already offer extensive generative AI features, leaving Apple without one of the headline capabilities it promotes elsewhere around the world. Bringing Writing Tools, notification summaries and other everyday Apple Intelligence features to Chinese iPhone users would close part of the gap, while giving Apple a foundation it could expand if further approvals are secured. coreStoryFacts.text: Importantly, Apple has only confirmed November 4 as the start of Apple Intelligence testing in China, not necessarily the release date of iOS 27.3 beta 1 itself.

In the press release , Apple confirms that users in China will get an improved Siri experience, including Type to Siri and the ability to access Alibaba’s Qwen for certain requests, but not Siri AI itself.
Then, just last Monday, Apple released iOS 27.2 and its counterparts, expanding Siri AI support to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.
On the same day, the company announced that four more languages, including Traditional Chinese, would be supported by the end of the year.

In mid-July, Reuters reported that, following a lengthy back-and-forth with Chinese regulators and multiple delays, Apple Intelligence had finally cleared a major regulatory hurdle ahead of its long-awaited launch in the country.
The Qwen integration will also extend to Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence.
According to Apple, users will be able to ask questions about photos and documents, including PDFs and presentations, as well as generate original content from scratch through Writing Tools.
Apple also noted that the initial rollout will be exclusive to the iPhone, with support for other platforms coming only after the necessary regulatory approvals have been obtained.

To check out Apple’s press release, follow this link .

Apple trained its own LLM specifically for China, Reuters reported in August.

Instead, Apple is launching several of its earlier Apple Intelligence features like notification summaries, real-time translation, rewriting and proofreading tools, visual intelligence, and removing objects from photos.

extraction.body: Apple today took the unusual step of confirming when its next iOS developer beta is expected to arrive, as part of an announcement detailing the upcoming launch of Apple Intelligence in China. Here are the details. In mid-July, Reuters reported that, following a lengthy back-and-forth with Chinese regulators and multiple delays, Apple Intelligence had finally cleared a major regulatory hurdle ahead of its long-awaited launch in the country. Then, a couple of weeks ago, Bloomberg reported that Apple was planning to launch Apple Intelligence in China in December as part of iOS 27.3, although without Siri AI and other newer features. The following day, China’s state-backed media outlet The Paper reported that Tim Cook had confirmed regulatory approval for the platform, with a test version expected before the end of October. Then, just last Monday, Apple released iOS 27.2 and its counterparts, expanding Siri AI support to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. On the same day, the company announced that four more languages, including Traditional Chinese, would be supported by the end of the year. However, while that announcement confirmed additional language support for Siri AI, it offered no updates on the rollout of Apple Intelligence in China, where Siri AI itself will remain unavailable for the time being. While Apple typically releases the first beta of its next software update shortly after the previous version becomes available, iOS 27.3 has yet to materialize. Now, as spotted by MacRumors , a press release published on Apple’s Chinese Newsroom website confirms that testing of Apple Intelligence in China will begin on November 4, as part of the next iOS developer beta. Importantly, Apple has only confirmed November 4 as the start of Apple Intelligence testing in China, not necessarily the release date of iOS 27.3 beta 1 itself. In the press release , Apple confirms that users in China will get an improved Siri experience, including Type to Siri and the ability to access Alibaba’s Qwen for certain requests, but not Siri AI itself. The Qwen integration will also extend to Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence. According to Apple, users will be able to ask questions about photos and documents, including PDFs and presentations, as well as generate original content from scratch through Writing Tools. Users will be able to access Qwen by signing into their accounts or using Sign in with Apple. Other features included in the initial rollout are Live Translation in Messages, FaceTime, and Phone, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Clean Up in Photos, natural-language photo searches, priority notifications, notification summaries, and Smart Reply, among others. Apple also noted that the initial rollout will be exclusive to the iPhone, with support for other platforms coming only after the necessary regulatory approvals have been obtained. The features will be available on the iPhone 15 Pro and Pro Max, iPhone 16 and later, iPhone Air, and iPhone Duo, with both Siri and the device language required to be set to either English or Simplified Chinese.
