story.title: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom

facts.text: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft have outlined more than $740 billion in capital spending this year, exposing cracks emerging spending boom as investors question the cost of AI infrastructure.
The spending boom is also being financed through borrowing and securities sales, not only through profits.
The English-language global edition of JournalArta.
The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out.
Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s.
Not every data centre developer worries bond investors equally.
The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals.
The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked.
It now costs more than US$40,000 to insure against US$1 million of SoftBank debt.
At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000.
Those questions burst into the forefront this past week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data centre company, CoreWeave.

Prices of its bonds – the company has accrued US$72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centres – crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 per cent likelihood that CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations.
Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects.
SoftBank has borrowed heavily to make one of the biggest bets – by dollar value – on OpenAI.
The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first US$500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested US$30 billion more.
That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due.
Some of the debt has traded around US$0.90 on the US dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan.
CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description.
Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts with those of the troubled office-space provider WeWork.
Oracle planned to pay back the borrowed money on the Texas facility helped by profits from the latter complex, called Project Lighthouse, which it expected to be operational by 2028.
In response to questions about SoftBank’s increasing debt, Alex Clavel, CEO of the SoftBank Vision Funds, said the amount of debt as a percentage of SoftBank Group’s assets had not changed.
TRILLIONS of dollars in borrowed money have powered the artificial intelligence boom.
First, CoreWeave buys Nvidia and other AI chips.
Then, as with WeWork, which leases space inside office buildings owned by others, CoreWeave contracts with data centre owners to use the structures for AI computing for 15 years or more.
CoreWeave then sub-leases the space to customers, including Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI, for a shorter time frame.
Several investors said they worried about whether hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future.
Alternately, they are wary of whether the data centres could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire.
Oracle faces similar permitting issues at a data centre project in New Mexico.
The project’s developer, investment firm Blue Owl, has started construction on the facility, but Oracle is struggling to get state permits to provide enough power.

The rub is that CoreWeave is on the hook for costs on both ends: It must pay to assemble and operate the facilities before any tenant is in place, and it is committed to the space for longer than its customers may stick around.
Anand Shah, CIO of PMS & AIF at ICICI Prudential AMC, sees cracks emerging in the artificial intelligence investment boom as revenue generation fails to keep pace with spending on infrastructure.
He believes the sustainability of the massive investment cycle will depend on how effectively AI companies convert spending into revenue.“Today, the boom is in AI investment.

We are not seeing a big boom in terms of revenue,” Shah told CNBC-TV18 in an interview.He pointed to pressure on companies supplying AI infrastructure, including chip manufacturers and businesses benefiting from electrification, alongside revenue concerns among AI companies.

He argued that the country would continue to need foreign direct investment and foreign institutional investor flows unless exports increased significantly relative to imports.Shah also noted that the securities transaction tax had become a source of revenue for the government, while saying the future direction of equity taxation remained uncertain.“We need to be mindful that, unlike many other economies that run surpluses, exporting more than they consume or producing more than they consume, India is much more dependent on foreign flows,” he said.He added that attracting foreign investment would remain important until India built sufficient manufacturing strength to export substantially more than it does today.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

Previously, the FT notes, Blackstone had said the opposite: that the Claude maker would receive an investment-grade rating (indicating low risk for lenders) before 2027 rolls around.

The lab has been on a spending spree, racking up large compute power deals throughout the past 12 months, which has worried investors .

passages: Blackstone has told investors in Anthropic's latest $63 billion chip financing deal that the AI company is likely to receive a high-yield, or junk, credit rating following its IPO, said a Financial Times report citing people familiar with the matter.
The news says Blackstone expects a junk (double-B) rating post-IPO, which means higher borrowing costs and a smaller institutional buyer pool for its debt—bad for a company planning massive capex.
Even with big cash, the market will price in a higher cost of capital right when it needs funding flexibility.
The assessment marks a shift from Blackstone's earlier guidance that Anthropic could secure an investment-grade rating before the end of the year.
As Anthropic gets closer to its public market debut, investors need to watch out for the credit ratings the company receives, as they will determine its debt load in funding its AI buildout.
Broadcom's high A-tier credit rating was an important factor in helping Anthropic secure the financing.
Blackstone's funds invested $9 billion in the junior debt at a yield of more than 10%, according to the Financial Times.
However, Fitch, Moody's and S&P, the three major credit rating agencies with significant influence over corporate borrowing costs, have not officially issued credit ratings for Anthropic.

Junk-rated junior paper is where the yield is highest; if the financing structure holds and Broadcom-backed senior debt stays safe, the junior tranche can re-rate upward as rating agencies finalize reviews and investors gain clarity post-IPO.
Key Risk: Credit agencies upgrade Anthropic to investment-grade quickly, shrinking the funding-cost penalty and unlocking institutional demand.
Blackstone is an anchor investor in the financing arrangement, known as Project North Star, and is working with banks involved in distributing the debt to other investors.
Bankers representing Anthropic and rival OpenAI have reportedly lobbied major rating agencies to award the AI companies investment-grade ratings following their respective IPOs.
The uncertainty surrounding Anthropic's credit outlook also coincided with broader weakness in technology stocks.

Anthropic may struggle to secure an investment-grade credit rating immediately after its planned initial public offering, potentially increasing borrowing costs as the artificial intelligence company prepares for massive infrastructure spending. Blackstone has told investors in Anthropic's latest $63 billion chip financing deal that the AI company is likely to receive a high-yield, or junk, credit rating following its IPO, said a Financial Times report citing people familiar with the matter. The assessment marks a shift from Blackstone's earlier guidance that Anthropic could secure an investment-grade rating before the end of the year. Blackstone is an anchor investor in the financing arrangement, known as Project North Star, and is working with banks involved in distributing the debt to other investors. Anthropic filed to go public on Monday , potentially setting up one of the largest stock market listings next month. Blackstone has recently indicated that Anthropic is more likely to receive a rating in the double-B range or above, based on guidance from major credit rating agencies, the people cited in the report said. A double-B rating falls below investment grade and could restrict the company's access to institutional capital. Many insurance companies and pension funds face restrictions on taking large positions in borrowers with junk-rated debt. This could reduce the pool of investors available to finance Anthropic's infrastructure expansion. Consequently, the company may need to continue relying on suppliers with stronger credit ratings to support its borrowing arrangements. An investment-grade rating is important to Anthropic's long-term financing strategy because it would allow the company to access debt at relatively lower interest rates. Anthropic currently has more than $112 billion in cash and equivalents. Investors also anticipate that the company could raise approximately $100 billion through its IPO. A US technology-focused portfolio manager told the Financial Times that credit access was central to the company's financing ambitions. The financing concerns come as banks have completed the $63 billion Project North Star deal, which provides funding for Anthropic to lease 1.5 gigawatts of Google's semiconductors. More than $42 billion of the senior loans is guaranteed by Broadcom, which co-develops the chips and holds an investment-grade credit rating. The remaining $18 billion in junior debt is backed by Anthropic's lease payments. Senior debt generally takes priority over junior loans in the event of a default, making it more attractive to institutional investors. Broadcom's high A-tier credit rating was an important factor in helping Anthropic secure the financing. Blackstone's funds invested $9 billion in the junior debt at a yield of more than 10%, according to the Financial Times. Project North Star's $18 billion junior debt has received a double-B-plus rating with a positive outlook from Kroll Bond Rating Agency (KBRA). This represents a modest improvement from the stable outlook assigned to a similar financing arrangement, Project Big Sky, four months earlier. Morningstar DBRS also assigned the junior debt a double-B rating, according to people familiar with the matter. However, Fitch, Moody's and S&P, the three major credit rating agencies with significant influence over corporate borrowing costs, have not officially issued credit ratings for Anthropic. Bankers representing Anthropic and rival OpenAI have reportedly lobbied major rating agencies to award the AI companies investment-grade ratings following their respective IPOs. The uncertainty surrounding Anthropic's credit outlook also coincided with broader weakness in technology stocks. The Nasdaq 100 fell 3.84% in afternoon trading on Friday following an earlier sell-off triggered by concerns about the sustainability of AI spending. As Anthropic gets closer to its public market debut, investors need to watch out for the credit ratings the company receives, as they will determine its debt load in funding its AI buildout. Anthropic may struggle to secure an investment-grade credit rating immediately after its planned initial public offering, potentially increasing borrowing costs as the artificial intelligence company prepares for massive infrastructure spending.

Blackstone has told investors in Anthropic's latest $63 billion chip financing deal that the AI company is likely to receive a high-yield, or junk, credit rating following its IPO, said a Financial Times report citing people familiar with the matter.
The assessment marks a shift from Blackstone's earlier guidance that Anthropic could secure an investment-grade rating before the end of the year.
Blackstone is an anchor investor in the financing arrangement, known as Project North Star, and is working with banks involved in distributing the debt to other investors.
Anthropic filed to go public on Monday , potentially setting up one of the largest stock market listings next month.

Blackstone has recently indicated that Anthropic is more likely to receive a rating in the double-B range or above, based on guidance from major credit rating agencies, the people cited in the report said.
A double-B rating falls below investment grade and could restrict the company's access to institutional capital.
Many insurance companies and pension funds face restrictions on taking large positions in borrowers with junk-rated debt.
This could reduce the pool of investors available to finance Anthropic's infrastructure expansion.
Consequently, the company may need to continue relying on suppliers with stronger credit ratings to support its borrowing arrangements.
An investment-grade rating is important to Anthropic's long-term financing strategy because it would allow the company to access debt at relatively lower interest rates.
Anthropic currently has more than $112 billion in cash and equivalents.
Investors also anticipate that the company could raise approximately $100 billion through its IPO.
A US technology-focused portfolio manager told the Financial Times that credit access was central to the company's financing ambitions.
The financing concerns come as banks have completed the $63 billion Project North Star deal, which provides funding for Anthropic to lease 1.5 gigawatts of Google's semiconductors.
More than $42 billion of the senior loans is guaranteed by Broadcom, which co-develops the chips and holds an investment-grade credit rating.
The remaining $18 billion in junior debt is backed by Anthropic's lease payments.
Senior debt generally takes priority over junior loans in the event of a default, making it more attractive to institutional investors.
Broadcom's high A-tier credit rating was an important factor in helping Anthropic secure the financing.
Blackstone's funds invested $9 billion in the junior debt at a yield of more than 10%, according to the Financial Times.
Project North Star's $18 billion junior debt has received a double-B-plus rating with a positive outlook from Kroll Bond Rating Agency (KBRA).
This represents a modest improvement from the stable outlook assigned to a similar financing arrangement, Project Big Sky, four months earlier.
Morningstar DBRS also assigned the junior debt a double-B rating, according to people familiar with the matter.
However, Fitch, Moody's and S&P, the three major credit rating agencies with significant influence over corporate borrowing costs, have not officially issued credit ratings for Anthropic.
Bankers representing Anthropic and rival OpenAI have reportedly lobbied major rating agencies to award the AI companies investment-grade ratings following their respective IPOs.
The uncertainty surrounding Anthropic's credit outlook also coincided with broader weakness in technology stocks.

extraction.body: A record-breaking hack at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, is a reminder of the risks investors take when trusting a company to hold their digital tokens. Binance said Friday that the security breach affected about $6.3 billion in client assets , making it the largest crypto hack on record. Around $3 billion of the affected assets has been frozen on blockchain networks, and the exchange says it has begun recovering some of them. Binance's initial investigation suggests hackers gained access to the firm's withdrawal systems and were able to make unauthorized transfers from the exchange's crypto wallets, according to the company . The company says it has found no evidence that the private keys controlling those wallets were leaked and is still investigating the full scope of the breach. The company says it will cover customers' losses . Binance maintains a roughly $1 billion emergency fund known as SAFU, which was created to protect customers in the event of a security breach. The company initially said SAFU and company funds would cover the losses, and has since said it has set aside more than $6.3 billion of its own funds. For crypto investors, the Binance breach highlights one of the risks of keeping assets on an exchange. While exchanges make it easier to buy, sell and store crypto, what happens after a hack can vary widely, including whether customers get their money back. Crypto exchange hacks aren't uncommon. Hackers stole roughly $1.5 billion from Dubai-based exchange Bybit in 2025, while Seychelles-registered Bitget lost more than $387 million in a hack in September 2026. But a hack doesn't necessarily mean customers will lose their money permanently. Stolen assets can sometimes be recovered or frozen — preventing the hackers from moving or cashing them out — and exchanges may also have insurance, dedicated emergency funds or other company resources available to cover losses. In Binance's case, roughly half of the affected assets have already been frozen, preventing some of the stolen crypto from being moved. Its roughly $1 billion SAFU emergency reserve provides another backstop, if needed. Customers don't always recover stolen digital assets quickly. New Zealand exchange Cryptopia was forced into liquidation months after a 2019 hack in which about NZ$30 million in crypto was stolen. The liquidation process stretched on for years, with the first distributions finally beginning in 2024 . "When you leave crypto on an exchange, you are relying on that company's controls and its balance sheet," says Martin Mulyadi, YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting and professor of accounting at Shenandoah University. "A pledge to make customers whole is only as strong as the resources behind it." When considering where to transact in and hold crypto, start by researching the exchange itself. The Securities and Exchange Commission recommends searching for customer complaints and checking how the exchange is regulated. U.S. customers can also check whether an exchange is registered with the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, using its online database . Registration can help confirm that you're dealing with an identifiable business operating within the U.S. regulatory system, though FinCEN cautions that registration isn't an endorsement of the company. Look for language explaining who owns your crypto and what the exchange can do with it. Phrases such as "you retain title" or assets being "held for your benefit" are good signs, Mulyadi says. Check whether customer assets are kept separate from the exchange's own, which can offer extra protection if the company fails. And find out whether the exchange can lend or otherwise use your crypto, which can expose your assets to additional risk. In the user agreement, check the exchange's limitation-of-liability section, Mulyadi says, and look at what insurance coverage the exchange offers and what it actually covers. "If a refund after a hack is at the exchange's discretion, it's a goodwill gesture, not a promise," Mulyadi says. Even strong language in the terms isn't a guarantee that your assets will be safe. FTX, the popular crypto exchange that collapsed in 2022, misappropriated billions of dollars in customer funds even though its terms said those assets belonged to customers, Mulyadi says. If you don't want to hold your crypto through an exchange, there's another option known as "self-custody." With self-custody, you use your own crypto wallet and control the private keys used to authorize transactions on the blockchain. Wallets typically come with a recovery phrase — essentially a master password that can be used to restore access to the wallet if you lose it. That gives you control of your crypto without relying on an exchange, but it also makes you responsible for keeping that information safe. And for anyone who's ever lost or forgotten a password, the risks of self-custody are real. With self-custody, there is "no help desk if you lose your recovery phrase," Mulyadi says. For many investors, Mulyadi says a middle ground is keeping only what they actively trade on an exchange and holding longer-term assets themselves, as long as they understand how to safely store and recover them. "Coins on an exchange are a promise from a company; coins in your own wallet are a responsibility you can't hand off," Mulyadi says. Now, however, Tang shared some additional details about the incident. While reiterating that customer funds are "safe," he said that the hack was a bit more involved than what the statement above implies. "Our initial investigation suggests this security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions," wrote Tang."To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual. So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak," he wrote, adding that the company will share a "detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and every fact is verified - and publish an updated Proof of Reserves once remediation is complete."Furthermore, according to the BBC, Binance has uncovered "additional points of breach," so it may not be just the one laptop that was compromised. Fortunately for Binance and its users, a substantial portion of the stolen funds has been frozen by the issuers. In response to Elon Musk's snarky comments about the incident, CZ said that roughly $3 billion in funds has been frozen. The company also has a SAFU fund worth more than $1 billion, and CZ pointed out that the company holds more than $1 billion in SpaceX shares, in an obvious jab at Musk.

sources.title: What to know about the $6.3B hack on Binance, likely the biggest-ever crypto theft - News4JAX
passages: Here's what we know about the hack, possible North Korean involvement and Binance's investigation.
Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record.
Blockchain firms have pointed to the attack coming from a North Korean hacking unit.
Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X.
Many are calling this the biggest crypto theft on record
Gox have had a more substantial impact in terms of the bitcoin amount affected, he said.
Asked whether North Korea was involved, Trump said: “We’re looking at that.”
“An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes,” TRM said.
“Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists."

Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is “working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice.”
In February of last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked.
The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack.
Binance worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets.
“Cyber threats are becoming more sophisticated and widespread as ever, and it is likely only a matter of time before an even larger hack, with even greater financial fallout, makes headlines.”
“We are working nonstop to resolve this,” Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said Friday in a video posted to X.
Binance said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional “points of breach.”

“This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet,” he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' “private keys,” or unique authorizations, digitally and that are connected to the internet.
“User assets are held under Binance's established security architecture," he said.
"The vast majority sits in cold wallets” — which are offline and used for secure storage — “and are only moved into a hot wallet when a user makes withdrawal.”
Binance has said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two.

Experts have said that North Korea turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities in recent years as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.
Where experts — and Binance — say things went wrong

extraction.body: Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. Blockchain firms have pointed to the attack coming from a North Korean hacking unit. The company said it has reserved more than $6.34 billion of company funds to cover the stolen assets and was beginning to recover assets for users. Binance worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets. The cryptocurrency exchange has promised to cover all losses, and it has been sharing regular updates on its social media channels as it uncovers more information about the hack. “We are working nonstop to resolve this,” Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said Friday in a video posted to X. In an exchange Friday with reporters at the White House, President Donald Trump said U.S. officials were investigating the Binance hack. Asked whether North Korea was involved, Trump said: “We’re looking at that.” Here's what we know about the hack, possible North Korean involvement and Binance's investigation. North Korean hackers are suspected in the attack Binance said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional “points of breach.” U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm TRM, in a post on its website late Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea’s elite hacking unit. “We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said. “An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes,” TRM said. “Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists." Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X. Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is “working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice.” Experts have said that North Korea turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities in recent years as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties. In December 2022, South Korea’s spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets over the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea’s capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the world's best . Many are calling this the biggest crypto theft on record While about half of the stolen assets were frozen, there is evidence that the hackers already are transferring and converting some of what wasn’t recovered, said Garrick Hileman, an independent cryptocurrency analyst. “Like in money laundering, you bring in the stolen goods and launder those through a mixer or tumbler,” he said. “You mix it in with other cryptos, and it’s harder to track.” How long it will take the hackers to turn that into something usable isn’t clear, he said. “The bottom line is there are places in the world where you can take your bitcoin and get that converted,” Hileman said. TRM and several other crypto firms and experts have said the hack represents the largest cryptocurrency theft on record. In February of last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack. TRM listed the Bybit hack when it referenced similarities between the Binance hack and previous attacks linked to TraderTraitor. Binance's founder, Changpeng Zhao , wrote on X that while Binance's hack might be the largest in terms of its dollar value, previous attacks on other companies like the crypto exchange Mt. Gox have had a more substantial impact in terms of the bitcoin amount affected, he said. Experts warn this scale of hacking could become more commonplace. “A cyber attack of this level is a matter of when, not if, particularly alongside the rise of AI,” said Andy Ward, a senior vice president at Absolute Security. “Cyber threats are becoming more sophisticated and widespread as ever, and it is likely only a matter of time before an even larger hack, with even greater financial fallout, makes headlines.” Where experts — and Binance — say things went wrong The hack has raised questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, co-founder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab. “This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet,” he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' “private keys,” or unique authorizations, digitally and that are connected to the internet. Teng, Binance’s co-CEO, confirmed in a nearly five-minute video posted on X Friday that Binance's own hot wallet was affected. “User assets are held under Binance's established security architecture," he said. "The vast majority sits in cold wallets” — which are offline and used for secure storage — “and are only moved into a hot wallet when a user makes withdrawal.” Teng said Binance's tech and security teams are “still deep” in investigating the hack. He said it was not carried out by one person and that the attackers used complex tactics, including a "self-destruct mechanism" that is making the incident more difficult to investigate. “We are working with law enforcement, blockchain intelligence firms, token issuers and other exchanges to trace and recover stolen funds," Teng said. "We will do everything within our power to make sure that these bad actors will be held accountable.” Binance has said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. coreStoryFacts.text: Binance said Friday that the security breach affected about $6.3 billion in client assets , making it the largest crypto hack on record.
Around $3 billion of the affected assets has been frozen on blockchain networks, and the exchange says it has begun recovering some of them.

But a hack doesn't necessarily mean customers will lose their money permanently. Stolen assets can sometimes be recovered or frozen — preventing the hackers from moving or cashing them out — and exchanges may also have insurance, dedicated emergency funds or other company resources available to cover losses. In Binance's case, roughly half of the affected assets have already been frozen, preventing some of the stolen crypto from being moved. Its roughly $1 billion SAFU emergency reserve provides another backstop, if needed. Customers don't always recover stolen digital assets quickly. New Zealand exchange Cryptopia was forced into liquidation months after a 2019 hack in which about NZ$30 million in crypto was stolen. The liquidation process stretched on for years, with the first distributions finally beginning in 2024 . "When you leave crypto on an exchange, you are relying on that company's controls and its balance sheet," says Martin Mulyadi, YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting and professor of accounting at Shenandoah University. "A pledge to make customers whole is only as strong as the resources behind it." When considering where to transact in and hold crypto, start by researching the exchange itself. The Securities and Exchange Commission recommends searching for customer complaints and checking how the exchange is regulated. U.S. customers can also check whether an exchange is registered with the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, using its online database . Registration can help confirm that you're dealing with an identifiable business operating within the U.S. regulatory system, though FinCEN cautions that registration isn't an endorsement of the company. Look for language explaining who owns your crypto and what the exchange can do with it. Phrases such as "you retain title" or assets being "held for your benefit" are good signs, Mulyadi says. Check whether customer assets are kept separate from the exchange's own, which can offer extra protection if the company fails. And find out whether the exchange can lend or otherwise use your crypto, which can expose your assets to additional risk. In the user agreement, check the exchange's limitation-of-liability section, Mulyadi says, and look at what insurance coverage the exchange offers and what it actually covers. "If a refund after a hack is at the exchange's discretion, it's a goodwill gesture, not a promise," Mulyadi says. Even strong language in the terms isn't a guarantee that your assets will be safe. FTX, the popular crypto exchange that collapsed in 2022, misappropriated billions of dollars in customer funds even though its terms said those assets belonged to customers, Mulyadi says. If you don't want to hold your crypto through an exchange, there's another option known as "self-custody." With self-custody, you use your own crypto wallet and control the private keys used to authorize transactions on the blockchain. Wallets typically come with a recovery phrase — essentially a master password that can be used to restore access to the wallet if you lose it. That gives you control of your crypto without relying on an exchange, but it also makes you responsible for keeping that information safe. And for anyone who's ever lost or forgotten a password, the risks of self-custody are real. With self-custody, there is "no help desk if you lose your recovery phrase," Mulyadi says. For many investors, Mulyadi says a middle ground is keeping only what they actively trade on an exchange and holding longer-term assets themselves, as long as they understand how to safely store and recover them. "Coins on an exchange are a promise from a company; coins in your own wallet are a responsibility you can't hand off," Mulyadi says. passages: The first question that comes to mind after hearing that Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, was hacked to the tune of $6.2 billion is: How the heck can this even happen?The hack, which lasted several hours, saw the attacker drain Binance's wallets, with hundreds of millions of dollars in BTC, ETH, USDC, USDT, and other cryptocurrencies.
The total tally, according to Binance co-CEO Richard Tang, was $6.3 billion.
Crypto sleuth Wazz put it at $6.17 billion by following crypto wallets, and Binance founder Changpeng 'CZ' Zhao didn't share the actual number, but he did confirm the ballpark.
If a single compromised laptop can result in billions being stolen, Binance had better rethink its security practices.
The same group was named responsible by the FBI for the $1.5 billion attack on crypto exchange Bybit back in 2025.

So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak," he wrote, adding that the company will share a "detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and every fact is verified - and publish an updated Proof of Reserves once remediation is complete."Furthermore, according to the BBC, Binance has uncovered "additional points of breach," so it may not be just the one laptop that was compromised.
CET Crypto analysis firm TRM claims with "high confidence" that the hack has been done by North Korea's "elite hacking unit" called TraderTraitor.
Fortunately for Binance and its users, a substantial portion of the stolen funds has been frozen by the issuers.

sources.title: What to know about the $6.3B hack on Binance, likely the biggest-ever crypto theft - News4JAX
passages: Here's what we know about the hack, possible North Korean involvement and Binance's investigation.
Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record.
Blockchain firms have pointed to the attack coming from a North Korean hacking unit.
Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X.
Many are calling this the biggest crypto theft on record
Gox have had a more substantial impact in terms of the bitcoin amount affected, he said.
Asked whether North Korea was involved, Trump said: “We’re looking at that.”
“An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes,” TRM said.
“Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists."

Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is “working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice.”
In February of last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked.
The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack.
Binance worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets.
“Cyber threats are becoming more sophisticated and widespread as ever, and it is likely only a matter of time before an even larger hack, with even greater financial fallout, makes headlines.”
“We are working nonstop to resolve this,” Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said Friday in a video posted to X.
Binance said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional “points of breach.”

“This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet,” he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' “private keys,” or unique authorizations, digitally and that are connected to the internet.
“User assets are held under Binance's established security architecture," he said.
"The vast majority sits in cold wallets” — which are offline and used for secure storage — “and are only moved into a hot wallet when a user makes withdrawal.”
Binance has said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two.

Experts have said that North Korea turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities in recent years as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.
Where experts — and Binance — say things went wrong

extraction.body: Binance has suffered the biggest hack in crypto history , but that's done little to shake confidence in bitcoin , according to market analysts and researchers. On Thursday, the world's largest exchange by daily trading volume said that roughly $6.3 billion were affected in an exploit. Security firm TRM Labs linked the security incident to North Korea. The hack sparked a slight sell-off in bitcoin . On Friday, the cryptocurrency traded at $77,065 around 1:34 p.m. ET, down about 4% on the day. By comparison, the token has fallen 8.3% on average in the first 24 hours following past crypto exchange exploits, according to data from institutional crypto platform Anchorage Digital. The digital asset has remained relatively resilient because the hack on Binance had nothing to do with the security of the bitcoin network itself, according to Sam Callahan, director of bitcoin strategy and research at crypto treasury firm OranjeBTC. "Investors recognize an important distinction: Bitcoin itself was not hacked," Callahan told CNBC. "This was a security breach at a centralized exchange, not a failure of the Bitcoin network." Although Binance has suffered the largest hack in crypto history, it's far from the only digital asset exchange to fall victim to bad actors and lead bitcoin to tumble. In the early 2010s, bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox was hacked a handful of times, wreaking havoc on the price of bitcoin. The token fell as much as 23.7% in the first 24 hours after an attack on Mt. passages: Binance was hacked with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets.
Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far.

Assuming frozen stablecoins are eventually returned, Binance’s SAFU emergency fund, worth approximately $1.2 billion, could cover roughly a third of the remaining losses, with the balance coming from the exchange’s own funds.

Chainalysis also pointed to North Korea, with co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin saying the firm assessed that the $6.4 billion Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, citing links to previous attacks.
The firm estimated that approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, with most transferred within about 20 minutes.
The FBI previously identified the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, according to the company’s insights.
“The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance,” Farrell said.
TRM Labs said the Binance attack shared characteristics with previous North Korea-linked incidents, including preparations made well before the theft and transaction signatures obtained in advance.
Farrell said the key indicators to watch were how quickly Binance resumes withdrawals and whether outflows remain orderly.
He added that a shortfall in customer assets could force the exchange to sell reserves, potentially triggering broader selling across crypto markets.
The Binance hack underscores the need for stronger cybersecurity standards and greater coordination among governments, according to Chris Perkins, head of Franklin Crypto at Franklin Templeton.

extraction.body: Reach Africa's business leaders, investors and decision-makers. Binance was hacked with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets. Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far. The exchange pledged to cover all losses, while blockchain investigators linked the attack to North Korea and analysts assessed the potential financial risks. Bitcoin was under pressure on Friday and was trading below $78,000. Freezing cryptocurrency prevents it from being transferred, but recovering the funds requires a separate legal process, according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs and a former U.S. federal prosecutor and Treasury official. “A freeze stops the money from moving, and recovery follows through legal process,” Redbord told CNBC. Redbord said law enforcement typically obtains a court order or seizure warrant before working with stablecoin issuers to release or reissue assets and return them to their rightful owners. “Stablecoins are the most recoverable asset class in crypto because the issuer controls the token contract,” he said. “Tether and Circle can freeze, burn and reissue, which allows frozen USDT and USDC to be returned to a victim.” But recovering bitcoin and ether is more challenging because they have no issuer that can directly freeze the assets. Instead, investigators must trace funds through exchanges and other crypto services where they can potentially be intercepted, added Redbord. Eric Jardine, head of research at blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, said returning frozen assets requires coordination among law enforcement, exchanges and token issuers. “There is no standard recovery timeline. A technical freeze may happen quickly, while returning funds can take months or years,” Jardine told CNBC. Jardine added that while bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen by an issuer, they can still be traced and potentially recovered. Investigators can trace the funds on public blockchains and intervene when they reach a cooperating exchange or another centralized platform, he said. TRM Labs attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit, based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence. The FBI previously identified the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, according to the company’s insights. TRM Labs said the Binance attack shared characteristics with previous North Korea-linked incidents, including preparations made well before the theft and transaction signatures obtained in advance. The firm estimated that approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, with most transferred within about 20 minutes. TRM Labs said preparations for the attack began at least 36 hours before the theft, with the attackers using Tornado Cash, a cryptocurrency mixing service, to fund their wallets ahead of the breach. Chainalysis also pointed to North Korea, with co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin saying the firm assessed that the $6.4 billion Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, citing links to previous attacks. The attack does not currently appear to pose a significant solvency risk for Binance, according to Sean Farrell, head of digital asset strategy at Fundstrat Global Advisors. “The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance,” Farrell said. Farrell estimated that around $3.3 billion in assets remained unfrozen. Assuming frozen stablecoins are eventually returned, Binance’s SAFU emergency fund, worth approximately $1.2 billion, could cover roughly a third of the remaining losses, with the balance coming from the exchange’s own funds. Farrell said the key indicators to watch were how quickly Binance resumes withdrawals and whether outflows remain orderly. He added that a shortfall in customer assets could force the exchange to sell reserves, potentially triggering broader selling across crypto markets. “I do not think that is the setup we are dealing with, but the key tell will be how quickly withdrawals resume and whether outflows stay orderly,” Farrell said. The Binance hack underscores the need for stronger cybersecurity standards and greater coordination among governments, according to Chris Perkins, head of Franklin Crypto at Franklin Templeton. Speaking to CNBC’s “Squawk Box Asia,” Perkins said the industry must address cybersecurity challenges to reach its full potential, calling for stronger defenses and policies to hold cybercriminals accountable. “We need to make sure standards are incredibly high, but we have to really focus on the criminals,” Perkins said. Perkins called for greater international cooperation to address cybersecurity threats, pointing to regulatory coordination among G20 countries following the global financial crisis as a potential model. He also said AI could help improve cybersecurity by identifying and addressing vulnerabilities, even as the technology is used by both attackers and defenders.

On-chain data shows the first large outflow from a Binance hot wallet at 8.24pm GMT on Thursday. Binance paused withdrawals shortly after 10pm. Soon afterwards, co-founder Changpeng Zhao posted on X: “It does look like a hack on Binance.”

According to Binance’s preliminary investigation, the attacker got in through a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer, then used it to reach an internal service and submit unauthorised withdrawals. Binance says it has found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked. At least one blockchain security firm has disputed that account. Binance has promised to cover all losses from its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and from company funds.

The breach has a direct UK connection. In 2021 the FCA barred Binance’s UK arm from carrying on regulated activity. Binance then stopped taking new UK customers in October 2023, although existing accounts continued to trade. In August, Binance was reported to be preparing an application under the FCA’s new crypto regime. Binance has not said how many UK customers are affected by the freeze.
Read next: WTW just made a big move on crypto insurance - shrewd, or big risk?

Binance is covering the loss itself. It set up SAFU in 2018 and still owns and manages it. The fund is held entirely in bitcoin and is worth roughly US$1bn to US$1.2bn, depending on the price of bitcoin. That covers less than a fifth of the estimated loss, so most of the money will come from Binance’s balance sheet.

Much of the specialist capacity for crypto theft sits in London. Evertas writes its cover with backing from a Lloyd’s syndicate member. In June, WTW bought Redefind, an MGA that writes crypto theft insurance on Lloyd’s paper. Capacity has grown this year, but publicly reported limits are a small fraction of a US$6.3bn loss.
Recovering the frozen funds will take time. Redbord told CNBC that returning frozen stablecoins to their owners usually requires legal proceedings, and there is no standard timeline.

The North Korean link will send claims teams straight to their wordings. Under Lloyd’s Market Bulletin Y5381 , standalone cyber policies written at Lloyd’s since 31 March 2023 must exclude two things. The first is war. The second is any state-backed attack that significantly impairs a state’s ability to function or its security capabilities. The bulletin also requires each policy to set out a robust basis for attributing an attack to a state.

That test is aimed at attacks with national-scale consequences. Whether a theft from a private exchange meets it is open to argument, and wordings vary between policies. Brokers have warned of grey areas since the mandate was announced. Clear Group’s George Grimshaw has told Insurance Business that cyber cover is “not going to cover anything when it comes to war or state-backed attacks”. Under war exclusions, the insurer generally carries the burden of proving the exclusion applies.

Formal attribution will matter. After the Bybit theft, the FBI named TraderTraitor within a week. A similar statement this time would strengthen the hand of any insurer arguing that the loss was state-backed.
Read next: War exclusions protect insurers as cyber spillover risk emerges

The FCA published its final cryptoasset rules on 30 June. Its authorisation gateway opened on 30 September and closes on 28 February 2027, and the regime comes into force on 25 October 2027. PwC’s summary says that firms involved in trading, custody, intermediation and staking will all need authorisation.

The senior managers and certification regime is part of the new framework. Directors of newly authorised crypto firms will therefore carry personal accountability, which is likely to make them look harder at D&O cover. All this is happening while the market absorbs the largest crypto loss on record. Lloyd’s had already warned that rapid cyber growth may be outstripping the market’s capacity to absorb risk .
Read next: Lloyd’s new cyber mandate spurs “grey area” fears
The Binance breach follows Bitget’s loss of roughly US$350m in September. TRM Labs says North Korea-linked groups took about 76% of all crypto hack value in the first four months of 2026.

Prices fell overnight. Bitcoin dropped more than 3% to a six-week low, and BNB, Binance’s own token, fell between 5% and 8%. Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group, told Reuters the breach could prompt investors to reassess counterparty, solvency and liquidity risk at centralised exchanges.

Kevin March, co-founder of JPEG Trading, told The Wall Street Journal he expected Binance to manage the loss. Its rivals are watching. Few exchanges hold reserves that could absorb a single loss on this scale.
This story is developing and will be updated.
Read next: Markel introduces cyber war cover for indirect losses from state-linked attacks

extraction.body: The $6.3 billion security breach at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has renewed concerns about the safety of digital assets and the risks of keeping investments on centralised trading platforms. While the exchange has pledged to cover all losses and around $3 billion worth of assets have reportedly been frozen, the incident raises a larger question: how can crypto platforms prevent such attacks rather than simply compensate investors after a breach?Binance's preliminary investigation has pointed to a possible compromise of a developer engineer's laptop, which may have allowed an attacker to access an internal service and initiate unauthorised withdrawals. The incident highlights the risks associated with internal access to systems handling large amounts of digital assets.Vineet Budki, Partner and CEO of Sigma Capital, believes the solution lies in stronger security measures, better industry cooperation and greater investor awareness.In an interview with CNBC-TV18, Budki said cyberattacks were not new to the digital world, but the growing use of online platforms for financial transactions had increased the potential consequences of a security breach. He also emphasised that investors and exchanges need to rethink how crypto assets are stored and protected.Here is what the Binance hack tells us about the vulnerabilities of crypto platforms and the measures needed to address them.Why are crypto exchanges vulnerable to hacks?Budki believes crypto hacks are part of a wider cybersecurity problem that has affected internet platforms and financial institutions for years. Web 3 has taken this further by allowing people to transact through digital platforms.This has increased the financial stakes involved in cyberattacks."Anything that involves a transaction carries the risk of being hacked," Budki said.He pointed to incidents such as the theft of $80 million from the Bank of Bangladesh in 2016 and the Mt. Gox and WazirX hacks to underline that security breaches are not unique to any one segment of the digital economy.The Binance incident also raises questions about the security of internal systems. If an employee's compromised device can provide access to services that authorise transactions, exchanges need to ensure that such access cannot be exploited to move large amounts of assets.According to Budki, technology will continue to improve, but attackers will also find new ways to exploit vulnerabilities. This makes security an ongoing challenge for platforms handling digital transactions.What should crypto investors do to protect their assets?The Binance breach also highlights why investors should not concentrate their cryptocurrency holdings on a single exchange.Budki said risk diversification should extend beyond the choice of asset classes to include how digital assets are held. Investors should consider their overall exposure to crypto alongside investments in real estate, gold and other assets.He also advised against keeping all cryptocurrency holdings on one trading platform. Instead, investors should consider splitting their holdings between exchanges and private wallets.This brings self-custody into focus. Unlike assets held on an exchange, cryptocurrency stored in a private wallet gives investors greater control over how their holdings are accessed and transferred."Not your wallet, not your money," Budki said.His point is that investors who leave their assets on an exchange depend on the platform's security systems and controls. Even established exchanges with substantial security resources can face breaches, making it important for investors to avoid relying entirely on a single custodian.Why refunding investors is not enoughBinance has pledged to cover the losses arising from the breach. While Budki believes such a commitment can restore confidence in the founder, he does not see compensation as a long-term answer to the industry's security challenges.A founder's ability to reimburse investors can provide reassurance, particularly when the exchange has sufficient financial resources. However, returning money after a hack does not address the weaknesses that allowed the breach to happen.Budki compared this with the banking system, where the focus should be on strengthening institutions and scrutinising their processes rather than relying on refunds after a collapse.He believes the cryptocurrency industry needs similar safeguards. This could include a dedicated body to develop solutions against hacking groups such as the Lazarus Group, which has been linked to attacks on several exchanges.The objective should be to establish stronger preventive mechanisms so that exchanges are better equipped to identify threats and stop attacks before they result in substantial losses.What security measures should crypto exchanges strengthen?Budki believes exchanges need multiple layers of security, backed by independent oversight and continuous monitoring.He identified third-party security audits as an important measure and suggested that exchanges could also explore using banks as custodians to strengthen the protection of digital assets.Another critical area is the management of hot and cold wallets.Cold wallets are not connected to the internet and are therefore less exposed to online attacks. Hot wallets, by contrast, are accessible through the internet and are needed to facilitate transactions.Since exchanges need to maintain some assets in hot wallets to process withdrawals and other transactions, securing these systems is particularly important.Budki said exchanges should deploy multiple security solutions and have independent teams monitoring their systems around the clock. The speed at which funds can be moved during an attack makes the ability to detect suspicious activity and respond quickly crucial.Referring to the Binance breach, in which most of the funds were reportedly moved within about 20 minutes, he questioned whether better monitoring could have stopped the attack much earlier."Could it have been stopped in five minutes? Could it have been stopped in under one minute?" he asked.Can the crypto industry prevent stolen funds from moving?Security measures within individual exchanges are only part of the solution. Budki believes companies across the cryptocurrency ecosystem also need to work together to restrict the movement of stolen assets after a breach.He pointed to the response by Tether and Circle, which froze cryptocurrency worth hundreds of millions of dollars following the incident, as an example of what industry cooperation can achieve.Such coordination could help limit the movement of stolen funds, although the same approach is not possible with every cryptocurrency. Budki noted that freezing assets such as Bitcoin and Ethereum is not possible in the same way.He believes exchanges, stablecoin issuers and other industry participants need to work towards more effective ways of responding to attacks.Budki also suggested exploring insurance products for cryptocurrency deposits, with large providers potentially offering protection against losses arising from security breaches.For the industry, the challenge is to move beyond relying on individual exchanges to deal with attacks after they happen. Stronger internal security, faster responses and cooperation between market participants will be essential to reducing the risks faced by investors.The Binance breach may be followed by compensation for affected users, but Budki's argument is that lasting confidence in crypto platforms will depend on their ability to prevent such incidents in the first place.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

coreStoryFacts.text: "Investors recognize an important distinction: Bitcoin itself was not hacked," Callahan told CNBC.
"This was a security breach at a centralized exchange, not a failure of the Bitcoin network."

"The speed of Binance's response, its deep financial resources, and its assurances that no user funds would be lost have helped restore market confidence and prevent potential panic," Hallarn told CNBC.
Binance has suffered the biggest hack in crypto history , but that's done little to shake confidence in bitcoin , according to market analysts and researchers.

"We believe Binance has more than enough liquidity to cover the hole and we expect the exchange to remain solvent while reimbursing user funds," Compass Point analyst Ed Engel said Friday in a note to clients.
The hack sparked a slight sell-off in bitcoin .
Gox was hacked a handful of times, wreaking havoc on the price of bitcoin.
Binance also has a $1.2 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users to offset losses from security breaches and other events.
The firm could also be eligible for loans that would minimize its solvency risks, if history is any indication, according to investment bank Compass Point.
Binance said it has started recovering affected assets, which has likely assuaged some of investors' concerns, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR.
Just 6% of bitcoin is held in exchange-traded funds, according to data from bitcoin analytics platform Bitbo.
That suggests many bitcoins are still being held by long-term believers in the asset and its cypherpunk origins, Lawant said.
Binance was hacked with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets.
Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far.

Assuming frozen stablecoins are eventually returned, Binance’s SAFU emergency fund, worth approximately $1.2 billion, could cover roughly a third of the remaining losses, with the balance coming from the exchange’s own funds.

Chainalysis also pointed to North Korea, with co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin saying the firm assessed that the $6.4 billion Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, citing links to previous attacks.
The firm estimated that approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, with most transferred within about 20 minutes.
The FBI previously identified the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, according to the company’s insights.
“The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance,” Farrell said.
TRM Labs said the Binance attack shared characteristics with previous North Korea-linked incidents, including preparations made well before the theft and transaction signatures obtained in advance.
Farrell said the key indicators to watch were how quickly Binance resumes withdrawals and whether outflows remain orderly.
He added that a shortfall in customer assets could force the exchange to sell reserves, potentially triggering broader selling across crypto markets.
The Binance hack underscores the need for stronger cybersecurity standards and greater coordination among governments, according to Chris Perkins, head of Franklin Crypto at Franklin Templeton.

extraction.body: Binance has suffered the biggest hack in crypto history , but that's done little to shake confidence in bitcoin , according to market analysts and researchers. On Thursday, the world's largest exchange by daily trading volume said that roughly $6.3 billion were affected in an exploit. Security firm TRM Labs linked the security incident to North Korea. The hack sparked a slight sell-off in bitcoin . On Friday, the cryptocurrency traded at $77,065 around 1:34 p.m. ET, down about 4% on the day. By comparison, the token has fallen 8.3% on average in the first 24 hours following past crypto exchange exploits, according to data from institutional crypto platform Anchorage Digital. The digital asset has remained relatively resilient because the hack on Binance had nothing to do with the security of the bitcoin network itself, according to Sam Callahan, director of bitcoin strategy and research at crypto treasury firm OranjeBTC. "Investors recognize an important distinction: Bitcoin itself was not hacked," Callahan told CNBC. "This was a security breach at a centralized exchange, not a failure of the Bitcoin network." Although Binance has suffered the largest hack in crypto history, it's far from the only digital asset exchange to fall victim to bad actors and lead bitcoin to tumble. In the early 2010s, bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox was hacked a handful of times, wreaking havoc on the price of bitcoin. The token fell as much as 23.7% in the first 24 hours after an attack on Mt. Gox in February 2014, per Anchorage Digital data. More recently, crypto exchange Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to an exploit targeting its trading platform. Last month, crypto platform Bitget was drained of more than $350 million in digital assets. What's different about the Binance hack is that it hasn't sparked the same loss in confidence in crypto markets that occurred after other major crypto security incidents, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR. Binance said it has started recovering affected assets, which has likely assuaged some of investors' concerns, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR. "The speed of Binance's response, its deep financial resources, and its assurances that no user funds would be lost have helped restore market confidence and prevent potential panic," Hallarn told CNBC. Tether, Circle and several other crypto firms said they had frozen roughly $3 billion in funds stolen in the heist. That should help mitigate losses tied to the attack, the executive noted. Binance also has a $1.2 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users to offset losses from security breaches and other events. The firm could also be eligible for loans that would minimize its solvency risks, if history is any indication, according to investment bank Compass Point. "We believe Binance has more than enough liquidity to cover the hole and we expect the exchange to remain solvent while reimbursing user funds," Compass Point analyst Ed Engel said Friday in a note to clients. "ByBit also received a bridge loan after its $1.5bn hack last year; therefore, we believe Binance has financing options." GSR's Hallarn noted that this latest rotation out of technology stocks may also be to blame for some of the pressure on bitcoin. "Since the exploit, bitcoin has largely traded in lockstep with other risk assets, including equities, which sold off overnight amid concerns over AI-related earnings," Hallarn told CNBC. The iShares A.I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) was down more than 8% on the day. Still, Anchorage Digital head of research David Lawant noted that current holders of bitcoin are more likely to hold their tokens through short-term headwinds than holders of other risk-on assets at the moment. Just 6% of bitcoin is held in exchange-traded funds, according to data from bitcoin analytics platform Bitbo. That suggests many bitcoins are still being held by long-term believers in the asset and its cypherpunk origins, Lawant said. "Bitcoin and crypto are not these hot-topic [assets like tech stocks] that investors are fleeing in and out," Lawant said. "The current holder base is a pretty strong one that is able to look at these things with a slightly longer-term view. That's playing a big role in how bitcoin is behaving well in this negative market environment." extraction.body: Reach Africa's business leaders, investors and decision-makers. Binance was hacked with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets. Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far. The exchange pledged to cover all losses, while blockchain investigators linked the attack to North Korea and analysts assessed the potential financial risks. Bitcoin was under pressure on Friday and was trading below $78,000. Freezing cryptocurrency prevents it from being transferred, but recovering the funds requires a separate legal process, according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs and a former U.S. federal prosecutor and Treasury official. “A freeze stops the money from moving, and recovery follows through legal process,” Redbord told CNBC. Redbord said law enforcement typically obtains a court order or seizure warrant before working with stablecoin issuers to release or reissue assets and return them to their rightful owners. “Stablecoins are the most recoverable asset class in crypto because the issuer controls the token contract,” he said. “Tether and Circle can freeze, burn and reissue, which allows frozen USDT and USDC to be returned to a victim.” But recovering bitcoin and ether is more challenging because they have no issuer that can directly freeze the assets. Instead, investigators must trace funds through exchanges and other crypto services where they can potentially be intercepted, added Redbord. Eric Jardine, head of research at blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, said returning frozen assets requires coordination among law enforcement, exchanges and token issuers. “There is no standard recovery timeline. A technical freeze may happen quickly, while returning funds can take months or years,” Jardine told CNBC. Jardine added that while bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen by an issuer, they can still be traced and potentially recovered. Investigators can trace the funds on public blockchains and intervene when they reach a cooperating exchange or another centralized platform, he said. TRM Labs attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit, based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence. The FBI previously identified the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, according to the company’s insights. TRM Labs said the Binance attack shared characteristics with previous North Korea-linked incidents, including preparations made well before the theft and transaction signatures obtained in advance. The firm estimated that approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, with most transferred within about 20 minutes. TRM Labs said preparations for the attack began at least 36 hours before the theft, with the attackers using Tornado Cash, a cryptocurrency mixing service, to fund their wallets ahead of the breach. Chainalysis also pointed to North Korea, with co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin saying the firm assessed that the $6.4 billion Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, citing links to previous attacks. The attack does not currently appear to pose a significant solvency risk for Binance, according to Sean Farrell, head of digital asset strategy at Fundstrat Global Advisors. “The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance,” Farrell said. Farrell estimated that around $3.3 billion in assets remained unfrozen. Assuming frozen stablecoins are eventually returned, Binance’s SAFU emergency fund, worth approximately $1.2 billion, could cover roughly a third of the remaining losses, with the balance coming from the exchange’s own funds. Farrell said the key indicators to watch were how quickly Binance resumes withdrawals and whether outflows remain orderly. He added that a shortfall in customer assets could force the exchange to sell reserves, potentially triggering broader selling across crypto markets. “I do not think that is the setup we are dealing with, but the key tell will be how quickly withdrawals resume and whether outflows stay orderly,” Farrell said. The Binance hack underscores the need for stronger cybersecurity standards and greater coordination among governments, according to Chris Perkins, head of Franklin Crypto at Franklin Templeton. Speaking to CNBC’s “Squawk Box Asia,” Perkins said the industry must address cybersecurity challenges to reach its full potential, calling for stronger defenses and policies to hold cybercriminals accountable. “We need to make sure standards are incredibly high, but we have to really focus on the criminals,” Perkins said. Perkins called for greater international cooperation to address cybersecurity threats, pointing to regulatory coordination among G20 countries following the global financial crisis as a potential model. He also said AI could help improve cybersecurity by identifying and addressing vulnerabilities, even as the technology is used by both attackers and defenders.
