extraction.body: AI infrastructure company Runware is making news again, just months after unveiling the Sonic Inference Pod, a modular data center built in a factory and shipped to customers ready to install. Now the company has bigger plans. It told TechCrunch it wants to build a factory that assembles these pods on a production line, as if they were cars. The idea isn’t entirely new. Companies like Crusoe and Schneider Electric also sell prefabricated pods, but Runware says it can ship its pods faster. Flaviu Radulescu, co-founder and CEO of Runware, told TechCrunch that the company plans to scale production at its Romania-based factory to 30 megawatts of data center capacity per day by 2028, or nearly 1 gigawatt per month. That’s a whole lot of capacity: At that pace, Runware would produce roughly as much in a year as the entire U.S. was expected to add in data center power this year, about 10 gigawatts . But it also reflects an industrywide push to deploy data centers faster and more efficiently. Nvidia announced, for example, the Vera Rubin AI factories and the DSX POD earlier this year. Both are also meant to make it faster and easier for companies to build their own AI data centers. The difference with Runware, though, is that it says it has actually built a factory rather than just designed the infrastructure that would let others build one. Radulescu said Runware will gradually increase production starting next year and that it already has two factories — one it has used for a few years to build the pods, and a second it started building earlier this year. The second is expected to be finished within months and go online early next year. Runware will manufacture the modular data centers on an assembly line. Customers can provide their own site to assemble them, or Runware can find one for them. Radulescu said Runware aims to bring the pods online within 48 hours. That time covers installation and set-up time, not build time. A pod once took three weeks to build but it will soon take one day as it ramps up production, says the company. Runware will provide spare parts if components fail. Customers can also rent compute from Runware or supply their own GPUs and pay a monthly fee for the pods and operations. Power and internet are charged separately, he said. The pods can also be customized to customer preferences, he said. The pods have a standard design, but can be configured to meet customer requirements and the latest GPU chips. Chips can take a long time to arrive after they’re ordered, which works in Runware’s favor. “Our pod delivery times are also shorter than current GPU lead times, giving us time to adapt the infrastructure to the hardware being ordered,” he said. “For new GPU generations, our in-house hardware team can design, build, and test components itself, allowing us to adapt quickly.” Right now, these are all plans — execution is the test. The factory will need a lot of people, inventory, supply-chain logistics, and money. There are cautionary tales about reinventing manufacturing, notably the electric vehicle startup Arrival, once valued at over $13 billion , which struggled to mass-produce electric vehicles cost-effectively compared with traditional plants. Runware, which has raised more than $60 million to date, said it plans to raise a Series B, but for now it is finishing and launching the factory with the $50 million Series A it raised last December. “Our cost structure is very different,” Radulescu said, explaining how Runware seeks to avoid Arrival’s fate. “We do have headcount and materials cost,” he continued. “But our factory staff is cost-effective relative to the value of deploying compute for AI.” He also said that designing its own systems and buying widely available, affordable parts helps keep costs low. “We’ve brought in a highly experienced plant manager from the automotive industry to work alongside our chief of hardware and help us get that execution right.” Sourcing components could also be a challenge. Though Runware says it designs and builds its own cooling and other pod systems with standard components, some parts, such as pumps and fans, come from Germany, and it still depends on Nvidia for networking. Still, Runware claims it has received $1 billion in committed interest for its Sonic pods since it began offering them to outside customers a month ago, “representing over 20 megawatts, which we’re now working to deliver,” Radulescu said. Data centers in the U.S. and abroad have come under fire for how much energy they consume and how that affects the grid and other resources. When pressed, Radulescu said his company’s pods only need power and an internet connection. They’ll use a closed-loop liquid cooling system with air-cooled radiators to release heat, so they don’t really need a water connection. “We’re working with power providers on a site pipeline covering 397 megawatts, with potential to expand to 1.2 gigawatts,” he said, referring to its list of planned sites and adding that the company is deploying its modular data centers on sites that are much smaller than those used by hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google. The sites, he continued, typically already have power, so they shouldn’t further strain the grid or disrupt the community. The pods also run “completely silent up to temperatures of 86 degrees Fahrenheit. We use energy from renewable sources whenever possible,” he continued. “We are actively working on expanding our network of energy providers and sites. We’re aiming to have renewables as our main energy source.” Runware will bring its new factory online early next year, then expand to the U.S. and other regions worldwide. Modular systems are the future and will soon become “the standard for large AI deployment,” Radulescu said. “Customers should be able to plan a hyperscale data center around factory-built pods from the beginning and have it working in months instead of years,” he added. Radulescu said Runware will gradually increase production starting next year and that it already has two factories — one it has used for a few years to build the pods, and a second it started building earlier this year. The second is expected to be finished within months and go online early next year.

Runware will manufacture the modular data centers on an assembly line. Customers can provide their own site to assemble them, or Runware can find one for them. Radulescu said Runware aims to bring the pods online within 48 hours. That time covers installation and set-up time, not build time. A pod once took three weeks to build but it will soon take one day as it ramps up production, says the company. Runware will provide spare parts if components fail. Customers can also rent compute from Runware or supply their own GPUs and pay a monthly fee for the pods and operations. Power and internet are charged separately, he said.

The pods can also be customized to customer preferences, he said. The pods have a standard design, but can be configured to meet customer requirements and the latest GPU chips. Chips can take a long time to arrive after they’re ordered, which works in Runware’s favor. “Our pod delivery times are also shorter than current GPU lead times, giving us time to adapt the infrastructure to the hardware being ordered,” he said. “For new GPU generations, our in-house hardware team can design, build, and test components itself, allowing us to adapt quickly.”

Right now, these are all plans — execution is the test. The factory will need a lot of people, inventory, supply-chain logistics, and money. There are cautionary tales about reinventing manufacturing, notably the electric vehicle startup Arrival, once valued at over $13 billion , which struggled to mass-produce electric vehicles cost-effectively compared with traditional plants. Runware, which has raised more than $60 million to date, said it plans to raise a Series B, but for now it is finishing and launching the factory with the $50 million Series A it raised last December.

“Our cost structure is very different,” Radulescu said, explaining how Runware seeks to avoid Arrival’s fate. “We do have headcount and materials cost,” he continued. “But our factory staff is cost-effective relative to the value of deploying compute for AI.” He also said that designing its own systems and buying widely available, affordable parts helps keep costs low. “We’ve brought in a highly experienced plant manager from the automotive industry to work alongside our chief of hardware and help us get that execution right.”

Sourcing components could also be a challenge. Though Runware says it designs and builds its own cooling and other pod systems with standard components, some parts, such as pumps and fans, come from Germany, and it still depends on Nvidia for networking. Still, Runware claims it has received $1 billion in committed interest for its Sonic pods since it began offering them to outside customers a month ago, “representing over 20 megawatts, which we’re now working to deliver,” Radulescu said.

Data centers in the U.S. and abroad have come under fire for how much energy they consume and how that affects the grid and other resources. When pressed, Radulescu said his company’s pods only need power and an internet connection. They’ll use a closed-loop liquid cooling system with air-cooled radiators to release heat, so they don’t really need a water connection. “We’re working with power providers on a site pipeline covering 397 megawatts, with potential to expand to 1.2 gigawatts,” he said, referring to its list of planned sites and adding that the company is deploying its modular data centers on sites that are much smaller than those used by hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google.

The sites, he continued, typically already have power, so they shouldn’t further strain the grid or disrupt the community. The pods also run “completely silent up to temperatures of 86 degrees Fahrenheit. We use energy from renewable sources whenever possible,” he continued. “We are actively working on expanding our network of energy providers and sites. We’re aiming to have renewables as our main energy source.”

Runware will bring its new factory online early next year, then expand to the U.S. and other regions worldwide. Modular systems are the future and will soon become “the standard for large AI deployment,” Radulescu said.
“Customers should be able to plan a hyperscale data center around factory-built pods from the beginning and have it working in months instead of years,” he added.

extraction.body: Nat Curi was 20 when she first joined BFF, a version of Bumble’s dating site tailored to making friends. Pandemic-era restrictions had been lifted in Curi’s college town, but her friends were still scattered at their homes across the country. Curi, who grew up in Connecticut and attended Southern Connecticut State University, was looking for friends nearby. Curi attached a photo of herself dancing at a party. If she could have dinner with any celebrity, she wrote, it’d be Jesus. “Not in a religious way, in a nosy as f—- way,” she added in parentheses. Swiping through profiles was awkward. Some users had a different definition of friendship than Curi; she rejected those “looking for a third,” for instance. But she soon came across a profile brimming with photos of fashionable outfits, pets and travel. Curi matched with the platonic prospect, who had another match in common with her. The three formed an Instagram group chat, eventually adding a couple more women from BFF. When it came to meeting the women in person, Curi donned a pink tube top, gold jewelry, light-wash jeans and platform heels. She wondered about her hair. The women all seemed pretty girly in their profiles. Would her pink hair come across as too edgy? Curi arrived at a dive bar in Fairfield, Connecticut, jittery with nerves. “It was like your first day of college,” Curi recalls. “You’re just asking each other about your interests, why you joined BFF.” All five had the same answer - they joined because they wanted to make friends. Friend-making apps are increasingly popular. The number of people who use BFF at least once a week has grown by 80 percent year over year, according to a Bumble spokesperson. Advertisements for the app are plastered over subway stations and posted on social media feeds. BFF, which launched in 2016, is now one of many apps promising platonic matches: Timeleft, 222 and Sonder all launched in the past three years. That growth coincides with the so-called “loneliness epidemic”: The number of Americans with no close friends quadrupled from 1990 to 2021. Men have been hit hardest; 1 in 5 single men report having no close friends at all. Danny Metz, a 28-year-old who works in insurance, tried BFF out. He swiped right on guys who seemed cool and better-looking than him. But the idea of meeting up with a match felt weird. Metz deleted the app. “I’m too used to this behavior for dating girls,” he says. “I’ve only ever organically made a friend.” But that’s not so easy. As far back as 2000, Robert Putnam argued that technological isolation, urban sprawl and the disintegration of civic organizations had eroded social capital in his book, “Bowling Alone.” The settings for making friends have only grown fewer in the years since. Even in the settings that do remain, casual conversation has disappeared, says historian Sarah Gold McBride. Gold McBride, who teaches a class on friendship at the University of California at Berkeley, noticed her students would look at their phones before lectures began. “It created a bubble with themselves and their technology. They’re not having those spontaneous ‘I like your jacket’ or ‘What book are you reading?’ conversations that can spark friendship in real life,” she explains. Students told her they worried about surveillance. “Students felt nervous interacting with a stranger. If they were filmed, they could be made viral against their will, memed or put on TikTok,” Gold McBride says. “Low-stakes interactions with people can be the beginnings of new friendships. But students are fearful of it, worried they might be put on the internet.” Sara Rollens, 32, had tried to make friends in real life. On the way to a book signing, she recalled thinking, “I’m gonna go. I’m gonna meet friends.” But when she arrived, she found the other attendees to be shy. “You’ll walk up to people to say hi, and they get really freaked out,” Rollens says. “People have a hard time conversing in real life.” She turned to a friendship app but discovered they had many of the same pitfalls associated with online dating: She has deleted and redownloaded BFF over the course of four years. She’s rejected men who hoped the friend dates would turn romantic and women who hoped Rollens would join their multilevel marketing ventures. She’s been platonically love-bombed by matches. She was even ghosted by one person after three dates. Rollens has made a few acquaintances but no deep friendships. She stays on the app, she says, “just in case” it can work. Eric Balki, who researches dating app algorithms at the Faculty of Health and Medicine at Lancaster University in England, says that much like dating apps, friendship apps “are designed to keep you on there. The business model is misaligned to the demand.” If matches were optimal, he notes, users would leave the app. “It ends up making you more lonely and defeated,” he says. He compared algorithmic matching to slot machines. Every once in a while, there is a random small reward, which maintains a user’s expectation for a larger reward to come. And some users do achieve that larger reward. They find a best friend forever. The news spreads - the bell ringing is loud. Slot machines can pay out, so users return. “That one I was really nervous for,” she says. The group didn’t have one another’s names, much less contact information, and couldn’t communicate ahead of time. Curi’s hair was back to its natural brunette. She wore a pencil skirt as a tube top and paired it with baggy jeans and sandals. She didn’t click with the women at her table. “I didn’t feel like anyone was a great match or a good friendship,” Curi says. “They had a lot of questions about [my] queerness and coming out, and then they asked me about my tattoos. Nobody had tattoos. Nobody had talked to a gay person.” She overheard the table beside her, a group also formed by Timeleft. That table’s guests were closer to her own age. They talked about shows and bars Curi liked. “They were having so much fun, and I was like, ‘Damn, I wish I could meet them,’” she says. Then serendipity struck for Curi. The app sent an address of a karaoke bar for an optional, after-dinner cocktail hour. All the Timeleft tables were invited. Once she arrived at the bar, Curi jumped ship and made friends with the users she’d been eyeing at dinner. A year and a half later, they play trivia, celebrate birthdays, try new restaurants and watch “Love Island” together. She’s still friends with all of them, and they hang out at least once a week. As the lead writer covering the Gonzaga men’s basketball team, he tells the stories behind the game and gets fans a bit closer to their favorite players. When it came to meeting the women in person, Curi donned a pink tube top, gold jewelry, light-wash jeans and platform heels. She wondered about her hair. The women all seemed pretty girly in their profiles. Would her pink hair come across as too edgy?

Curi arrived at a dive bar in Fairfield, Connecticut, jittery with nerves. “It was like your first day of college,” Curi recalls. “You’re just asking each other about your interests, why you joined BFF.” All five had the same answer - they joined because they wanted to make friends.

Friend-making apps are increasingly popular. The number of people who use BFF at least once a week has grown by 80 percent year over year, according to a Bumble spokesperson. Advertisements for the app are plastered over subway stations and posted on social media feeds. BFF, which launched in 2016, is now one of many apps promising platonic matches: Timeleft, 222 and Sonder all launched in the past three years.

That growth coincides with the so-called “loneliness epidemic”: The number of Americans with no close friends quadrupled from 1990 to 2021. Men have been hit hardest; 1 in 5 single men report having no close friends at all.

Danny Metz, a 28-year-old who works in insurance, tried BFF out. He swiped right on guys who seemed cool and better-looking than him. But the idea of meeting up with a match felt weird. Metz deleted the app. “I’m too used to this behavior for dating girls,” he says. “I’ve only ever organically made a friend.”

But that’s not so easy. As far back as 2000, Robert Putnam argued that technological isolation, urban sprawl and the disintegration of civic organizations had eroded social capital in his book, “Bowling Alone.” The settings for making friends have only grown fewer in the years since.

Even in the settings that do remain, casual conversation has disappeared, says historian Sarah Gold McBride. Gold McBride, who teaches a class on friendship at the University of California at Berkeley, noticed her students would look at their phones before lectures began. “It created a bubble with themselves and their technology. They’re not having those spontaneous ‘I like your jacket’ or ‘What book are you reading?’ conversations that can spark friendship in real life,” she explains.

Students told her they worried about surveillance. “Students felt nervous interacting with a stranger. If they were filmed, they could be made viral against their will, memed or put on TikTok,” Gold McBride says. “Low-stakes interactions with people can be the beginnings of new friendships. But students are fearful of it, worried they might be put on the internet.”

Sara Rollens, 32, had tried to make friends in real life. On the way to a book signing, she recalled thinking, “I’m gonna go. I’m gonna meet friends.” But when she arrived, she found the other attendees to be shy. “You’ll walk up to people to say hi, and they get really freaked out,” Rollens says. “People have a hard time conversing in real life.”

She turned to a friendship app but discovered they had many of the same pitfalls associated with online dating: She has deleted and redownloaded BFF over the course of four years. She’s rejected men who hoped the friend dates would turn romantic and women who hoped Rollens would join their multilevel marketing ventures. She’s been platonically love-bombed by matches. She was even ghosted by one person after three dates.
Rollens has made a few acquaintances but no deep friendships. She stays on the app, she says, “just in case” it can work.

Eric Balki, who researches dating app algorithms at the Faculty of Health and Medicine at Lancaster University in England, says that much like dating apps, friendship apps “are designed to keep you on there. The business model is misaligned to the demand.”
If matches were optimal, he notes, users would leave the app. “It ends up making you more lonely and defeated,” he says.

He compared algorithmic matching to slot machines. Every once in a while, there is a random small reward, which maintains a user’s expectation for a larger reward to come. And some users do achieve that larger reward. They find a best friend forever. The news spreads - the bell ringing is loud. Slot machines can pay out, so users return.

“That one I was really nervous for,” she says. The group didn’t have one another’s names, much less contact information, and couldn’t communicate ahead of time. Curi’s hair was back to its natural brunette. She wore a pencil skirt as a tube top and paired it with baggy jeans and sandals.

She didn’t click with the women at her table. “I didn’t feel like anyone was a great match or a good friendship,” Curi says. “They had a lot of questions about [my] queerness and coming out, and then they asked me about my tattoos. Nobody had tattoos. Nobody had talked to a gay person.”

She overheard the table beside her, a group also formed by Timeleft. That table’s guests were closer to her own age. They talked about shows and bars Curi liked. “They were having so much fun, and I was like, ‘Damn, I wish I could meet them,’” she says.

Then serendipity struck for Curi. The app sent an address of a karaoke bar for an optional, after-dinner cocktail hour. All the Timeleft tables were invited. Once she arrived at the bar, Curi jumped ship and made friends with the users she’d been eyeing at dinner.
A year and a half later, they play trivia, celebrate birthdays, try new restaurants and watch “Love Island” together. She’s still friends with all of them, and they hang out at least once a week.

passages: Quanda Grant, of West Philadelphia, was outside City Hall on her way to drop off her mail-in ballot.
She said she has concerns about Election Day but believes voter apathy poses a threat as well.

extraction.body: Quanda Grant, of West Philadelphia, was outside City Hall on her way to drop off her mail-in ballot. She said she has concerns about Election Day but believes voter apathy poses a threat as well. "I do think we are going to see problems," Grant said. "We can't just keep on saying my votes not going to county, we gotta say we gotta do it and see what the outcome is," she added. City officials are taking steps to protect the voting process and its outcome. The Philadelphia District Attorney's Office announced that its Election Task Force will be mobilized Tuesday, an effort officials have been planning since the summer. Fifty assistant district attorneys will be deployed to respond to issues, and a hotline will be available for anyone who witnesses problems. "Our main role on Election Day is to make sure everyone gets a chance to vote. We are not looking to do anything other than make things run smooth," Assistant District Attorney Brian Collins said. The Department of Justice also plans to send federal election monitors to Philadelphia. Officials said they are not concerned about the move because it has been done in the past. Some voters said they welcome the increased security. "I just think that with all the hype and everything that's happened. I think whoever the poll watchers are they are more aware of that," said Tyrone Wrice of West Philadelphia. Others said they wanted to make sure they voted early. "I did have a slight concern. Thats why i came to city hall and hand out my ballot to make sure it got in there," said Colleen Chambers of Northern Liberties. Wrice emphasized the importance of casting a ballot. "The power of the vote, even though it's one, is probably the most powerful thing we have," he said. The Election Task Force will remain activated until every vote is counted. Voters in Pennsylvania who are in line by 8 p.m. cannot be turned away.

By Lawrence Delevingne, Summer Zhen and Elizabeth Howcroft

BOSTON/SINGAPORE/PARIS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, worked on Friday to shore up public confidence after a record $6.3 billion hack of its platform, promising it would cover all losses from company funds and allow clients to trade again within days.

Cryptocurrency prices fell on news of the hack, which analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time. The publicly traded stocks of ‌crypto-related firms Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood slid.

Binance said customer funds were safe and it is working with industry partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion, but ‌Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a post on X that $3 billion represented only about 2% of the company's total user assets and public reserves.

The exchange also said on Friday afternoon US eastern time that its technical team was targeting a resumption of withdrawal services within approximately 34 hours. Binance said it is conducting a full security review and plans an ​initial proof-of-reserves snapshot in 12 hours, with the results expected to be available by Monday.

Binance said it has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1 billion.

Binance's other co-CEO, Richard Teng, said in a post on X that the breach was a "complex attack" that was not carried out by one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity as it went along, "making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate."

The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called "hot" wallet in a way that did not ‌pass through normal approval controls, Teng said.
"Rest assured that we are working nonstop to resolve this, ⁠to make the users whole, and live up to your trust," Teng wrote.
Crypto prices fell broadly but losses were contained.

Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368, and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178 before markets stabilized. Bitcoin last stood at $76,447 and ether at $2,226. Binance's BNB token was down about 6.4% over the past 24 hours at $696.
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth ⁠of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
"This incident is almost certainly the single-largest-known theft of any kind," British blockchain analysts Elliptic said.

The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea.
North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and ​South ​Korean authorities as well as cybersecurity experts.
US ​President Donald Trump, asked on Friday whether North Korean hackers were behind the theft, said he did not ‌know but his administration is looking into it.

"It was a hack. That's the problem. You know the old-fashioned way when you used to sign a check, take it out. These are different. People never see the money anymore. So I've always felt it was a little bit dangerous," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he thought any of the stolen funds could be retrieved. "But no, they (Binance) say they have it pretty much under control."
Binance is working with the FBI and the US Secret Service, according to a person familiar with the situation.

The FBI said it is "aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps."

The Secret Service said that its investigators "are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle, to identify, freeze, trace and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday."
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it froze nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.

Abu Dhabi's Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance's main operating license, said it is "engaging closely with Binance and ‌monitoring the incident." Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX declined to comment. It became a minority investor in Binance last year.

Beyond the potential loss of assets, ​the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the crypto sector, which already was under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from ​exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
"It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralized ​exchanges," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group.
Investor Michael Saylor, among bitcoin's most prominent supporters, said in a post on X that he expects Binance to "deliver" on ensuring no customers suffered losses.
"Our industry will learn from this ‌incident, strengthen security and emerge stronger and more resilient," Saylor wrote on Friday.
Binance, which ​allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered ​users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.
The heist at Binance drew a relatively measured response from crypto enthusiasts online.

On social media platform Reddit, discussions about the breach featured a mix of humor, confidence in the exchange's financial resources and questions about how such an enormous theft could have occurred.

BOSTON/SINGAPORE/PARIS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, worked on Friday to shore up public confidence after a record $6.3 billion hack of its platform, promising it would cover all losses from company funds and allow clients to trade again within days.

Cryptocurrency prices fell on news of the hack, which analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time. The publicly traded stocks of ‌crypto-related firms Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood slid.

Binance said customer funds were safe and it is working with industry partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion, but ‌Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a post on X that $3 billion represented only about 2% of the company's total user assets and public reserves.

The exchange also said on Friday afternoon US eastern time that its technical team was targeting a resumption of withdrawal services within approximately 34 hours. Binance said it is conducting a full security review and plans an ​initial proof-of-reserves snapshot in 12 hours, with the results expected to be available by Monday.

Binance said it has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1 billion.

Binance's other co-CEO, Richard Teng, said in a post on X that the breach was a "complex attack" that was not carried out by one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity as it went along, "making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate."

The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called "hot" wallet in a way that did not ‌pass through normal approval controls, Teng said.
"Rest assured that we are working nonstop to resolve this, ⁠to make the users whole, and live up to your trust," Teng wrote.
Crypto prices fell broadly but losses were contained.

Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368, and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178 before markets stabilized. Bitcoin last stood at $76,447 and ether at $2,226. Binance's BNB token was down about 6.4% over the past 24 hours at $696.
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth ⁠of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
"This incident is almost certainly the single-largest-known theft of any kind," British blockchain analysts Elliptic said.

The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea.
North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and ​South ​Korean authorities as well as cybersecurity experts.
US ​President Donald Trump, asked on Friday whether North Korean hackers were behind the theft, said he did not ‌know but his administration is looking into it.

"It was a hack. That's the problem. You know the old-fashioned way when you used to sign a check, take it out. These are different. People never see the money anymore. So I've always felt it was a little bit dangerous," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he thought any of the stolen funds could be retrieved. "But no, they (Binance) say they have it pretty much under control."
Binance is working with the FBI and the US Secret Service, according to a person familiar with the situation.

The FBI said it is "aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps."

The Secret Service said that its investigators "are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle, to identify, freeze, trace and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday."
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it froze nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.

Abu Dhabi's Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance's main operating license, said it is "engaging closely with Binance and ‌monitoring the incident." Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX declined to comment. It became a minority investor in Binance last year.

Beyond the potential loss of assets, ​the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the crypto sector, which already was under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from ​exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
"It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralized ​exchanges," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group.
Investor Michael Saylor, among bitcoin's most prominent supporters, said in a post on X that he expects Binance to "deliver" on ensuring no customers suffered losses.
"Our industry will learn from this ‌incident, strengthen security and emerge stronger and more resilient," Saylor wrote on Friday.
Binance, which ​allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered ​users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.
The heist at Binance drew a relatively measured response from crypto enthusiasts online.

On social media platform Reddit, discussions about the breach featured a mix of humor, confidence in the exchange's financial resources and questions about how such an enormous theft could have occurred.
